lessons.title: Fundamental liberties, and how a restriction is tested
lessons.summary: The rights in Part II of the Constitution, the closed list of reasons Parliament may cut them down, and an argument the courts have not settled.

sections.keypoint: A law that punishes an ordinary complaint is where constitutional argument actually starts.

body.text: Aminah posts a photograph of a broken road and asks why nobody has fixed it. A week later she is told that the post breaks the law. Can a law really say that?

The Federal Constitution gives Aminah a right to speak, and it also lets Parliament cut that right down. Almost every real argument in this area is about the cutting down rather than about the right itself.

sections.keypoint: Part II sets out the rights; the fight is almost never about whether the right exists.

body.text: Constitutional argument in Malaysia rarely fails because nobody could find the relevant right. It fails because the restriction survives, and the restriction is where the analytical work actually sits.
Part II of the Federal Constitution sets out the basic rights of a person in Malaysia. Lawyers call them the **fundamental liberties**, and the four you will meet most often are these.

items: Article 5 — liberty of the person, meaning that your freedom may be taken away only in a way the law allows.
Article 8 — equality before the law, and the equal protection of the law for everybody.
Article 10 — freedom of speech, freedom to meet together, and freedom to form groups.
Article 11 — freedom of religion, and the right to profess and practise it.

body.text: These are not simply fine words on a page. Article 4(1) makes the Constitution the highest law in the country, which is what turns the list into something a court can enforce.
Article 4(1) makes the Constitution the supreme law of the Federation, so any law that is inconsistent with it is void to the extent of that inconsistency.
*Void* means of no legal effect at all, from the very beginning. Notice the last few words as well: the law is void only so far as it clashes, and the rest of the Act keeps working.

sections.keypoint: Article 10(1)(a) gives citizens free speech, and Article 10(2)(a) lets Parliament cut it down on listed grounds.
sections.h: A right, and the power to cut it down

body.text: Aminah is a citizen, and her post criticises the way a state agency spends public money, so start with the right she is relying on.
Article 10(1)(a): every citizen has the right to freedom of speech and expression.

Look hard at the word **citizen**, which is doing a great deal of work in that sentence. Article 10(1) belongs to citizens alone, while Article 5 is wider because it speaks of *persons* and so covers anybody in the country. If the person you are helping is not a citizen, Article 10 will not help them, and that single word ends some arguments before they begin.

body.prompt: Aminah is a citizen, and Article 10(1)(a) gives her the right to speak. Before you read on — can a law still make her post an offence?
options: No — the Constitution gives her the right, so a law against it is void
Yes, but only for the reasons the Constitution itself lists
Yes, for any reason Parliament thinks is a good one
body.reveal: The second one. If you picked the first, that is what the word *right* normally means, and it is a fair instinct to have. This Constitution does not work that way. It hands the right over in one Article and lets Parliament cut it down in the next. The third answer is the other half of the trap. Parliament's reasons are not free either. They have to come off a list, and the list is in Article 10(2).

body.text: The right is not the end of the story, because Parliament may pass a law that restricts it — though not for any reason it happens to like.

Article 10(2)(a): Parliament may by law impose on the right conferred by 10(1)(a) such restrictions as it deems necessary or expedient in the interest of the security of the Federation, friendly relations with other countries, public order or morality, and restrictions designed to protect the privileges of Parliament or to provide against contempt of court, defamation, or incitement to any offence.
Put simply: Parliament may cut the right down, but only for the reasons that Article names.

Those grounds are the security of the Federation, friendly relations with other countries, public order, and morality. Parliament may also restrict speech to protect its own privileges, and to guard against contempt of court, defamation, or encouraging somebody to commit an offence.
**Defamation** means harming a person's reputation by what you say or write. **Contempt of court** covers behaviour that obstructs a court or undermines its authority.
That list is closed, and nothing may be added to it by a court or by Parliament. If a law restricts speech for some reason outside the list, Article 10(2)(a) never permitted it in the first place.
This gives you a strong opening argument that needs no theory at all. Ask whether the restriction fits one of the named grounds, and if it does not, the law is simply not authorised.

body.title: The question to ask before any theory
body.caption: The list in Article 10(2) is closed. A restriction that fits none of the named grounds fails on that alone, and the argument never has to reach proportionality.
body.alt: A question — does the restriction fit a ground named in Article 10(2)? — branching two ways. Yes: the argument moves on to how hard a judge may look at necessity. No: the restriction fails, because nothing may be added to the list by a court or by Parliament.
body.question: Does the restriction fit a ground named in Art 10(2)?

branches.label: Move to how hard a judge may look
It fails on that alone
branches.note: the list is closed; nothing may be added

sections.keypoint: How hard a court may look behind a restriction is unsettled — Pung Chen Choon and Sivarasa both stand.
sections.h: How hard may a judge look?

body.text: Now suppose the restriction does fit one of those grounds — may a judge then go on and ask whether it was really necessary? Two lines of Malaysian authority pull in different directions, and it is worth knowing both rather than picking the one you prefer.

PP v Pung Chen Choon: the words “deems necessary or expedient” leave the necessity of a restriction largely to Parliament; the court's role is to ask whether the restriction falls within a permitted head.
body.source: PP v Pung Chen Choon [1994] 1 MLJ 566 (FC)

body.text: Sivarasa Rasiah: fundamental liberties are to be read generously, restrictions must be reasonable, and proportionality is imported through Art 8(1).
body.source: Sivarasa Rasiah v Badan Peguam Malaysia [2010] 2 MLJ 333 (FC)

body.text: Put simply: on the first view the court checks only that the restriction fits one of the listed grounds. On the second it goes further and asks whether the restriction was reasonable.
**Proportionality** is a formal name for a plain question: is the harm the law does to the right worse than the good the law achieves?

Muhammad Hilman is the case where that second approach did real work. The Court of Appeal struck down a rule limiting the political speech of students, holding the restriction unreasonable, which shows the reasonableness line is more than talk.

body.title: Two lines of authority, both still standing

items: “Deems necessary or expedient” leaves necessity largely to Parliament.
The court asks whether the restriction fits a ground that Article 10(2) names.
It does not weigh whether the restriction was really needed.
The check is real, but it is a check on fit rather than on degree.
Fundamental liberties are to be read generously.
A restriction must be reasonable, not merely listed.
Proportionality enters through Article 8(1).
Muhammad Hilman is where this approach did real work, striking down a rule limiting student political speech.

body.text: Do not write that Sivarasa overruled Pung Chen Choon, because it did not, and both decisions still stand with the tension between them unresolved. Hold both, argue that the question of *which ground* is for the court on either view, and keep reasonableness as your second argument rather than your only one.

sections.keypoint: Five steps: name the right, check the holder, find the restricting law, test the head, then test reasonableness.
sections.h: Building the argument, step by step

items: Name the right, and check that the person can actually hold it — for Article 10(1), that means being a citizen.
Name the law that restricts the right, and say exactly what it forbids.
Ask whether the restriction fits one of the grounds listed in Article 10(2), remembering that the question belongs to the court and not to Parliament.
Only then argue that the restriction is unreasonable or out of proportion.
State the result under Article 4(1): the law is void so far as it clashes, and not void entirely.

body.text: Step three carries most of the weight, and there is a reason for that. If Parliament could decide for itself that a law fitted a ground, Article 4(1) would have nothing left to bite on.

An Act punishes “any statement likely to cause public disquiet about the conduct of the police”, and its long title says that it protects public order. But public order is about disorder — riots, fights, disturbance in the street. People feeling uneasy about the police is not disorder, so the label Parliament chose does not settle the question — the court decides that for itself.

body.q: An Act restricts speech in order to protect the dignity of a government department. Where does the argument end?
options: The law was never authorised — that reason is not on the Article 10(2) list
The court weighs the harm to speech against the good the law does
Parliament decided the reason was a good one, and that settles it
body.why: The list in Article 10(2)(a) is closed. The dignity of a department is not on it, so the restriction was never permitted and there is nothing further to weigh. The trap is the second answer. Reasonableness is a real argument, but reaching for it here walks past the simpler one that wins outright.

body.text: What a law *does* matters more than how it is written. A law that never mentions speech can still restrict speech, and the court looks at the effect rather than at the drafting.

It gives you a journalist charged under an invented provision, and a prosecutor who argues that the word “deems” hands the whole question to Parliament. A good answer meets that argument head on instead of reciting the right.

quiz.q: Who holds the right in Article 10(1)(a)?
options: Every person in the Federation
Every natural person
Citizens and permanent residents
Citizens
quiz.why: Article 10(1) says citizens. Article 5 says persons, which is wider. Check who you are dealing with first.

quiz.q: What does Article 10(2)(a) allow?
options: The government of the day to impose any restriction it likes
The courts to invent new grounds for restricting speech
State legislatures to restrict speech
Parliament to restrict speech, but only on the grounds the Article names
quiz.why: The grounds are a closed list. And whether a restriction fits one of them is for the court, not for Parliament's own label.

quiz.q: How do Pung Chen Choon and Sivarasa stand together?
options: Sivarasa overruled Pung Chen Choon
Pung Chen Choon overruled Sivarasa
Both still stand, and the tension between them is unresolved
Both have been overruled
quiz.why: Writing that one killed off the other is a mistake. Hold both and argue in the alternative.
quiz.source: PP v Pung Chen Choon [1994] 1 MLJ 566 (FC); Sivarasa Rasiah v Badan Peguam Malaysia [2010] 2 MLJ 333 (FC)

quiz.q: A law never mentions freedom of speech, but in practice it restricts speech. What follows?
options: It falls outside Article 10 entirely
It is presumed valid
The court looks at what the law does, not at how it is worded
Only the drafter's stated purpose counts
quiz.why: Effect matters more than form. That is what makes the whole analysis worth doing.
quiz.source: Federal Constitution Art 10; a restriction is judged by its effect on the right, not by its wording

quiz.q: A law clashes with the Constitution. What happens to it?
options: It is void so far as it clashes
The whole Act dies
It can be set aside later if someone objects
It stays in force until Parliament repeals it
quiz.why: Article 4(1). Only the offending part falls away. Cutting out the bad part is the ordinary course.

lessons.title: Homicide: the structure of sections 299 and 300
lessons.summary: Culpable homicide is the big category, murder is a smaller category sitting inside it, and the exceptions push a case back down again.

sections.keypoint: Start from the section rather than a theory of killing; the Code defines its own offences.
sections.h: Start with the Code, not with a theory

body.text: A man dies after a fight outside a shop, and somebody is arrested that same night. What exactly should he be charged with, and who decides?
In Malaysia the answer sits in a book called the Penal Code. Every offence has its own section, and each section writes in the state of mind it needs — no more and no less.
So the first move in any criminal problem is always the same. Find the section, read it, and do not reason from a general feeling about guilt.
Unlawful killing shows this better than anything else in the Code. The structure is clean once you have seen it, and thoroughly confusing if you arrive with English categories in your head.

sections.keypoint: Three steps in order: culpable homicide under s 299, then murder under s 300, then any Exception.
sections.h: Three steps, always in this order

body.text: Section 299 says what **culpable homicide** is, which is the Code's name for unlawful killing. Section 300 then says when culpable homicide counts as **murder**, and the exceptions to section 300 say when it drops back down again.

Section 299: culpable homicide is causing death by an act done with the intention of causing death, or with the intention of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, or with the knowledge that the act is likely to cause death.

Put simply: it is culpable homicide if the person meant to kill, or meant to cause an injury that was likely to kill. It is also culpable homicide if they knew that what they were doing was likely to kill.
Culpable homicide is the big category and murder is a smaller category sitting inside it. Every murder is culpable homicide, but not every culpable homicide is murder.

So never ask “is this murder or culpable homicide?” as though the two were rivals. Ask first whether it is culpable homicide at all, and then ask whether it is the kind that section 300 turns into murder.

body.title: The route through a homicide problem
body.caption: Always in this order. Going straight to section 300 because someone died inverts the structure and usually picks the wrong limb.
body.alt: Three steps: establish culpable homicide under s 299, then ask whether a limb of s 300 elevates it to murder, then whether an Exception brings it back down.

steps.label: Murder?
steps.note: one of the four limbs of s 300

body.text: Every limb of the analysis assumes something that is easy to skip past. The prosecution must establish that the accused's own act caused the death, and where an intervening cause is genuinely arguable that question has to be answered separately.

sections.keypoint: Four limbs make it murder, and (c) — an injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature — does most of the work.
sections.h: The four ways it becomes murder

body.text: Rosli and Daud argue outside a kedai runcit late one evening. Rosli picks up a metal pipe lying by the drain and swings it once at Daud's head, and Daud dies that night. Rosli tells the police that he never meant to kill anybody.

body.prompt: Rosli swung the pipe once, and he tells the police he never meant to kill anybody. Before you read on — does that keep this out of murder?
options: No — it can be murder if he meant to cause the wound he caused
Yes — murder means meaning to kill, and he did not
It turns on whether Rosli knew that a pipe could kill a man
body.reveal: The second one. Hold on to the first answer, though. It is what the word murder means in ordinary speech, and the Code is about to take that meaning away from you. Section 300 has four routes in, and only one of them asks about an intention to kill. The third answer is the near miss. What Rosli knew matters under some limbs, and not under the limb that will catch him.

body.text: Section 300 has four limbs, lettered (a) to (d), and any one of them turns culpable homicide into murder.

items: (a) The act is done with the intention of causing death — that is, meaning to kill.
(b) The act is done meaning to cause an injury that the accused knows is likely to kill this particular person.
(c) The act is done meaning to cause the injury actually caused, and that injury is enough, in the ordinary course of nature, to cause death.
(d) The act is so obviously dangerous that it must in all probability cause death, or cause an injury likely to cause death. The accused had no excuse for running that risk.

body.text: Section 300(c) is two questions: did the accused intend to inflict the injury actually inflicted, and is that injury objectively sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
body.source: Penal Code, s 300(c); PP v Visuvanathan [1978] 1 MLJ 159, applying Virsa Singh v State of Punjab AIR 1958 SC 465 (Supreme Court of India)

body.text: Put simply: did you mean to cause the wound you caused, and would a wound like that normally kill?

The second question has nothing to do with what was in the accused's head, because it is answered by the doctor who examined the body. That is why limb (c) is the one the prosecution reaches for most often.

Go back to Rosli. He meant to strike Daud's head with the pipe, and that is the injury Daud suffered, and a pathologist will say that a blow like that normally kills. Limb (c) is made out, and the fact that Rosli did not realise it could kill is simply not the question.

It is tempting to run limb (a) because a person died. On a single blow with something picked up in the moment, (a) is hard to prove and (c) is straightforward. Choosing the wrong limb means proving a harder case than the law asks for.

sections.keypoint: Exceptions push murder back down: provocation, exceeding private defence, sudden fight.
sections.h: The exceptions: murder pushed back down

body.text: Suppose a limb of section 300 is made out on the facts. The offence is then murder, unless one of the exceptions to the section applies.

The exceptions do not set anybody free, and that is the thing to hold on to. They reduce murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder, which is a lesser offence carrying a lesser sentence. Treating provocation as a way out altogether is the commonest mistake in this area, because it is a reduction and not an escape.
Exception 1: culpable homicide is not murder if the offender, whilst deprived of the power of self-control by grave and sudden provocation, causes the death of the person who gave the provocation.
Put simply: you were pushed past self-control by something serious that had just happened, and you killed the person who did it.
Two words carry all the weight and they fail in different ways. **Grave** asks how serious the provocation was, while **sudden** asks whether there was time for temper to cool.

Halim's neighbour has insulted his late mother, on and off, for two years. One evening Halim takes a parang and kills him for it. The provocation may well be grave, but it is hard to call it sudden, because two years is a long time in which to cool down.
An Explanation to the section makes whether provocation was grave and sudden a question of fact, and that is what allows words alone to count as provocation.

Three provisos cut the exception down, and any one of them will sink it. The provocation must not have been sought out or brought on by the offender himself. It must not come from something done in obedience to the law, or by a public servant acting lawfully. Nor may it come from somebody who is lawfully defending themselves.

Exception 4 covers a sudden fight, where the killing happens in the heat of passion on a sudden quarrel. The offender must not take undue advantage or act in a cruel or unusual way, and the exception is worth checking on any facts involving a scuffle.

body.q: Grave and sudden provocation is made out on the facts. What happens to the accused?
options: He walks free — provocation is a complete defence
The offence drops to culpable homicide not amounting to murder
He is still convicted of murder, and only the sentence changes
body.why: Exception 1 reduces the offence. It does not excuse the killing, and it does not merely soften the sentence. The first answer is the commonest mistake in this area, because the word *defence* sounds like a way out. The third is the other one. The conviction itself changes, from section 302 to section 304.

sections.keypoint: Sections 302 and 304 carry the punishments, and the sentencing law changed in 2023.

body.text: Section 302 punishes murder, and section 304 punishes culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
Section 304 splits by state of mind, because the intention limb and the knowledge limb carry different maximum sentences. So the limb you settled on earlier is what decides which maximum applies.

The mandatory death penalty for murder was abolished in 2023, and sentencing is now at the court's discretion. Do not state a range from memory or from an older book — read the current provision. This is the single most likely thing on this page to have moved since it was written.

sections.keypoint: One blow, a clear post-mortem, and arguable provocation — the problem is built to test exactly this.

body.text: Work the problem question, which is built to test exactly this. It gives you a single blow, a clear pathologist's report, and provocation that is arguably grave and doubtfully sudden.
The work is in taking section 300(c) as two separate questions, and then arguing both sides of suddenness rather than asserting one of them.

quiz.q: How do sections 299 and 300 fit together?
options: They are two separate offences of equal weight
Section 300 sets the sentence for section 299
Culpable homicide is the big category; murder is a smaller one inside it
Section 299 applies only where section 300 does not
quiz.why: Every murder is culpable homicide. Not every culpable homicide is murder.

quiz.q: Section 300(c) asks two questions. What are they?
options: Did the accused intend death, and did death follow
Was the act very dangerous, and did the accused know it
Did the accused intend the injury actually caused, and is that injury enough in the ordinary course of nature to cause death
Was there provocation, and was it grave and sudden
quiz.why: The second question is answered by the pathologist, not by the accused. That is why (c) is often easier to prove than (a).

quiz.q: One blow is struck with an object picked up in the moment, and the victim dies. Which limb is the natural one to run?
quiz.why: It is tempting to run (a) because someone died. On these facts an intention to kill is hard to prove, and (c) is straightforward.

quiz.q: What does Exception 1 to section 300 require?
options: Grave and sudden provocation that destroyed self-control, and the death of the person who gave it
Any provocation at all
Provocation together with planning
Provocation given by someone else
quiz.why: And it does not set the accused free. It reduces murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

quiz.q: What should you never state from memory about the sentence for murder?
options: Which court tries it
The range — the mandatory death penalty went in 2023 and sentencing is now discretionary
How the offence is classified
The elements of the offence
quiz.why: Sentencing provisions move. Always read a current source.

lessons.title: Property offences: how possession was obtained
lessons.summary: Theft, criminal breach of trust and cheating look alike from the outside. One question separates them, and it is not what was taken.

sections.keypoint: Three incidents in one shop on one afternoon, and three different offences.
sections.h: One Saturday in a hardware shop

body.text: Siti works the till at a small hardware shop in Klang, and three things happen there in one afternoon.

items: A customer pays RM200 in cash, and Siti puts it straight into her own pocket and records no sale.
On her way out she takes a drill worth RM150 from the display shelf.
She tells the owner that a supplier needs RM300 up front, but there is no such supplier and she keeps the money.

body.prompt: Three dishonest acts, one Saturday afternoon. Before you read on — which of them is theft?
options: The drill only
All three — every time, she took something that was not hers
The drill, and the RM200 out of the till
body.reveal: Only the drill. If you said all three, that is how the afternoon looks from outside, and it is the charge a hurried officer would bring. The Code does not sort offences by what was taken. It sorts them by how the property got into her hands, and Siti got hold of those three things in three different ways.

body.text: All three are dishonest, and in all three the property belonged to somebody else. Yet these are three different offences under three different sections, and an officer who charges all of them as theft has got two of them wrong.

sections.keypoint: The question is never what was taken but how the accused came to have it.

body.text: The tempting question is “what did she take?”, and that is the wrong question. The right one is how she came to have the property in the first place.

items: Taken out of somebody else's possession, and without the consent of that person — that is theft.
Received lawfully, and then treated by her as though it were her own — that is criminal breach of trust.
Handed over willingly by its owner, but only because she lied to him — that is cheating.

body.text: Who owns the thing is not the test, because in all three of them the property belongs to somebody else. That common feature is what makes each of them an offence, and possession and consent are what tell the three apart.

body.title: One question separates the three offences
body.caption: Not what was taken, and not how much it was worth. How possession was obtained.
body.alt: A question about how possession was obtained, branching three ways. Never given: theft under section 378, moved out of possession without consent. Given lawfully: criminal breach of trust under section 405, entrusted and then misappropriated. Given but by a trick: cheating under section 415, where delivery was induced by deception.
body.question: How did the accused come to have the property?

branches.label: Theft
branches.note: s 378 — moved out of possession without consent

body.text: One further element runs through all three offences and is easy to overlook. Every one of them requires **dishonesty**, so an honest belief that you were entitled to the property is capable of answering any of the three charges.

sections.keypoint: Theft under s 378: moved out of someone's possession, without consent, dishonestly.

body.text: Section 378: whoever, intending to take dishonestly any movable property out of the possession of any person without that person's consent, moves that property in order to such taking, commits theft.
Put simply: you take a thing that is not yours out of somebody else's hands, without their agreement, and you move it.
Two elements do the work here: the property must come out of somebody else's possession, and it must be taken without the consent of the person who had it.

Two smaller points matter as well, and both of them catch people out. Only movable property can be stolen, so land cannot be, and the offence is complete the moment the property is moved with a view to taking it. Getting away with the goods afterwards is not required at all.

The drill was sitting on the shop's shelf and in the shop's possession, and nobody had handed it to Siti or put her in charge of it. Taking it off the shelf and walking out with it is therefore theft.

sections.keypoint: Criminal breach of trust under s 405: it came to them lawfully, and was then misappropriated.

body.text: Section 405: whoever, being in any manner entrusted with property, or with any dominion over property, dishonestly misappropriates or converts it to his own use, or dishonestly uses or disposes of it in violation of any direction of law or legal contract, commits criminal breach of trust.
Put simply: the property was put into your hands for a purpose, and you kept it or used it as though it were your own.
**Entrusted** means that the property was put into your hands to hold or to handle on somebody else's behalf.

Here the accused starts out with the property lawfully, so nothing comes out of anybody else's possession, because she already had it herself. The wrong lies in keeping for herself, or using as her own, the thing she was trusted with.

Siti was allowed to take payment from customers, so the RM200 reached her hands lawfully, in her job as cashier. Pocketing it is criminal breach of trust rather than theft, because nothing was taken out of anybody else's possession.
Where the accused is a clerk or a servant, a heavier form of the offence applies, and that is the form that fits most employee cases.

Whether an employee has possession of what passes through their hands, or only custody of it, is a genuine question that turns on what exactly they were entrusted with. Being a cashier does not put the whole shop in Siti's hands, so argue the point rather than simply assuming it.

sections.keypoint: Cheating under s 415: consent was given, but a deception induced it.

body.text: Section 415: whoever, by deceiving any person, fraudulently or dishonestly induces the person so deceived to deliver any property to any person, commits cheating.
Put simply: you tell somebody a lie, and because of the lie they hand something over.

Cheating is the odd one out, because here the victim agrees and the property is handed over willingly. What poisons the agreement is the lie that produced it, and the lie is the thing you have to prove.
The owner handed Siti RM300 for a supplier who did not exist. He agreed to part with the money, but he agreed to it only because of the lie he had been told, and that is cheating.

Where the lie leads to property being handed over, the punishment section is section 420 rather than the general one. Charging under the wrong punishment section is a real error and not a matter of style.

body.q: Puan Lim hands her neighbour RM500 and asks him to pay her electricity bill. He spends it on himself instead. Which offence fits?
options: Theft — he used money that was not his
Cheating — he must have lied to get hold of it
Criminal breach of trust — the money was put into his hands for a purpose
body.why: The money reached him lawfully, and for a stated purpose, so nothing came out of anybody's possession. That is section 405. Theft is the trap, because spending someone else's money feels exactly like stealing it. Cheating fails too: nothing in the facts says a lie is what made her hand the money over.

sections.keypoint: Take each incident separately and ask the one question again; a bundle of facts is not one charge.
sections.h: Facts that arrive in a bundle

body.text: Real cases come as one story with several incidents inside it, and it is tempting to label them all the same way. Take each incident on its own and ask the one question of each.
One set of facts can support more than one charge, and charging in the alternative is ordinary practice. Saying which charge is the better one, and why, is worth more than picking one and moving on.

sections.keypoint: The problem gives you an officer who wants to charge all three as theft, and he is wrong twice.

lessons.title: Formation: the moment a contract exists
lessons.summary: Section 4 of the Contracts Act fixes a different moment for each kind of message, and section 5 decides the race between an acceptance and a withdrawal.

sections.keypoint: A room, a message, and a second tenant — whether there is a contract turns on one moment.

body.text: Encik Raju advertises a room in Cheras at RM450 a month. Mei Ling messages him on Tuesday to say that she will take it. On Wednesday he tells her the room has gone to somebody else.
Whether Mei Ling has a contract depends on the exact moment one came into being, if it ever did. Malaysian law fixes that moment by statute, and the statute is precise about it.

sections.keypoint: Malaysian contract law is a statute, and it does not always match the English cases.
sections.h: A statute, not the common law

body.text: Malaysian contract law is written down in a statute. The Contracts Act 1950 sets out the rules of formation, and those rules do not always match the English ones that a common law textbook will give you.

Copying English contract law across without checking the Act is the most reliable way to get a Malaysian contract question wrong. Formation is the clearest example, because the Act writes down the posting rules in a form that produces different answers from the English cases.

sections.keypoint: Section 2(a) defines a proposal; acceptance turns it into a promise.

body.text: Section 2(a): when one person signifies to another his willingness to do or to abstain from doing anything, with a view to obtaining the assent of that other, he is said to make a proposal.
Put simply: a proposal is telling somebody that you are willing to do something, in order to get their agreement to it.

The Act says **proposal** where an English book says offer, and **promise** where it says acceptance. The ideas are the same, and the sensible course is to use the vocabulary of the statute you are working in.

A proposal has to be told apart from an **invitation to treat**, which is a signal that you are open to receiving proposals rather than a proposal itself. Goods displayed with a price, a newspaper advertisement and a notice of an auction are the standard examples. That distinction comes from the case law rather than from the Act itself.

Encik Raju's advertisement for the room is an invitation to treat, not a proposal. Mei Ling's message saying that she will take it is the proposal. Raju has to accept that proposal before either of them is bound to anything.

sections.keypoint: Section 4 fixes a different moment for each kind of message, and delivery is not knowledge.

body.text: Section 4 is the provision that decides most formation problems. The point to notice is that it fixes a different moment for each kind of message, and a different moment again depending on which side is relying on it. There is no single rule here to reach for.
Section 4(1): communication of a proposal is complete when it comes to the knowledge of the person to whom it is made.

body.prompt: Mei Ling posts her acceptance on Monday. It reaches Encik Raju on Thursday, and he reads it that evening. Before you read on — from which day is Raju bound?
options: Thursday, when he read it and knew about it
Neither — a letter binds nobody until both sides confirm
Monday, when she put the letter into the post
body.reveal: Monday. It feels wrong that a man can be bound by a letter he has not opened, and that feeling is not silly. The Act is lopsided here on purpose. Sending is enough against the proposer, and only against him. Mei Ling herself is not bound until Thursday, when Raju knows. One posting, two different moments.

body.text: Section 4(2): communication of an acceptance is complete — (a) as against the proposer, when it is put in a course of transmission to him, so as to be out of the power of the acceptor; and (b) as against the acceptor, when it comes to the knowledge of the proposer.
Put simply: sending the acceptance binds the proposer straight away, but it does not bind the acceptor until the proposer knows about it.
A **revocation** is a withdrawal — the proposer taking his offer back before it has been accepted. Section 4(3) gives a revocation the same two-sided treatment as an acceptance.

Section 4(3): communication of a revocation is complete — (a) as against the person who makes it, when it is put into a course of transmission; and (b) as against the person to whom it is made, when it comes to his knowledge.
Put simply: sending a withdrawal commits the sender straight away, but it does nothing at all to the other side until that side actually knows of it.

Read those provisions together and a pattern appears. Sending is enough to bind the person the message is aimed at in exactly one case: an acceptance, as against the proposer. Everywhere else the Act asks for knowledge, and that lopsidedness is deliberate.

body.caption: The four moments section 4 fixes

columns.label: Complete as against the other party

rows: Proposal — s 4(1)
When it comes to that person's knowledge
Acceptance — s 4(2)
When put into a course of transmission, out of the acceptor's power
When it comes to the proposer's knowledge
Revocation — s 4(3)
When put into a course of transmission
When it comes to that person's knowledge
body.note: The trap is the last cell. **Delivery is not knowledge** — an unopened letter on a desk has been delivered and not communicated, and a problem that mentions one is testing exactly that.

sections.keypoint: A proposal can be revoked until acceptance is complete against the proposer — which is why the moment matters.

body.text: Section 5(1): a proposal may be revoked at any time before the communication of its acceptance is complete as against the proposer, but not afterwards.
Put section 5(1) beside section 4(2)(a) and the deadline becomes exact. The proposer may take his offer back until the moment the acceptance is sent, and not one minute after that.
Put it beside section 4(3)(b) and the other half of the race appears. His withdrawal does not touch the acceptor until the acceptor actually knows about it.

Raju posts an offer to Mei Ling on 3 March. On 10 March he changes his mind and posts a letter withdrawing it. That letter is delivered to Mei Ling's office on the afternoon of 12 March, but she does not open it until 14 March. She had already posted her acceptance at nine in the morning on 12 March. That acceptance bound Raju the moment it went into the postbox. The withdrawal reached Mei Ling only on 14 March, when she read it, so it was too late and there is a contract.

Delivery is not the same thing as knowledge. Section 4(3)(b) asks for knowledge, and a letter lying unopened on a desk has not been communicated to anybody at all. This is the step that most answers skip over.

body.q: Raju's letter withdrawing his offer is delivered to Mei Ling's office on Monday. She opens it on Wednesday. When is the withdrawal complete against her?
options: Monday — the letter was in her hands
The day Raju posted it
Wednesday — that is when she knew of it
body.why: Section 4(3)(b) asks for knowledge, and an unopened letter on a desk is not knowledge. The first answer is the step most answers skip: delivery is not communication. The third is the right rule read off the wrong half of the subsection. Posting binds Raju, and it does nothing to Mei Ling.

body.text: Section 6 lists the ways a proposal comes to an end. They are notice of revocation, lapse of the time allowed, and failure to fulfil a condition. A proposal also ends on the death or mental disorder of the proposer, where the acceptor knows of it before accepting.

sections.keypoint: A promise to hold an offer open binds nobody without consideration.

body.text: Raju tells Mei Ling that the room is hers if she decides within fourteen days. Three days later he lets it to somebody else instead. Was he allowed to do that?

He was, unless she gave him something for the promise to wait. A promise to keep an offer open is itself a promise, and a promise that is not paid for does not bind. What each side gives in return for the other's promise is called **consideration**.
A promise to keep an offer open for a stated period is not binding unless supported by consideration; the proposer may revoke within the period.
body.source: Macon Works & Trading Sdn Bhd v Phang Hon Chin [1976] 2 MLJ 177

body.text: It is easy to over-apply this rule. All it means is that the proposer *could* have revoked in time, not that he actually did so. Check the timing under sections 4 and 5 before concluding either way.

lessons.title: Consideration under a statute, not the common law
lessons.summary: Section 2(d) differs from English law in two ways that decide cases, and section 26 rescues three promises that would otherwise fail.

sections.keypoint: A promise to give money, freely made and then withdrawn, is usually unenforceable — and that surprises people.

body.text: Puan Rohana tells her nephew that she will give him RM3,000 because she is proud of him. Two months later she changes her mind and says nothing more about it. Can he sue her for the money?

body.prompt: Puan Rohana promised her nephew RM3,000 because she was proud of him. Then she changed her mind. Can he sue her for it?
options: Yes — she said it plainly and she meant it
Only if she had put it in writing
No — he gave her nothing in return
body.reveal: The second one. If you picked the first, you are holding the ordinary moral view of a promise, and the law is about to part company with it. It asks a narrower question: what did the other side give? Writing alone will not rescue a bare promise, though writing matters later in this lesson.

body.text: Usually he cannot. A promise on its own is not a contract, and Malaysian law asks what the other side gave in return for it. What the other side gives is called **consideration**, and it is the price of a promise.

This is the topic where borrowing English law does the most damage. The English rules are famous, and the Malaysian definition is statutory and different. Two of those differences decide ordinary cases, and both of them sit in a single sentence of the Act.

sections.keypoint: Section 2(d) is wider than English law: past consideration counts, and it may move from a third party.

body.text: Section 2(d): when, at the desire of the promisor, the promisee or any other person has done or abstained from doing, or does or abstains from doing, or promises to do or to abstain from doing, something, such act or abstinence or promise is called a consideration for the promise.
Put simply: consideration is whatever the other side does, does not do, or promises, because you asked for it. It may be something already finished, and it may come from a third person.
Two phrases in that section should stand out, because each of them departs from English law.

items: “Has done or abstained from doing” — an act already finished can count. The English rule that past consideration is no consideration does not apply here.
“The promisee or any other person” — the consideration need not come from the person the promise was made to, because a stranger to the promise may supply it.

body.text: Kepong Prospecting is the case usually cited for the first point. The Privy Council there treated services rendered before the agreement as good consideration under section 2(d).
Past consideration is good consideration in Malaysia, and consideration need not move from the promisee.
body.source: Contracts Act 1950, s 2(d); Kepong Prospecting Ltd v Schmidt [1968] 1 MLJ 170 (PC)

body.text: In June Pak Samad asks Ah Meng to repair his fence, and says nothing at all about paying him. Ah Meng goes ahead and does the work. In July Pak Samad promises him RM300 for it. The work was finished before the promise, but it was done at Pak Samad's request, so under section 2(d) it can be good consideration.

This does not abolish the doctrine of privity. **Privity of contract** means that only a party to a contract can sue on it. Consideration may come from a stranger, but a stranger still cannot bring the claim. Keep the two rules apart, because Kepong Prospecting gets cited for both and they are easily run together.

The words “at the desire of the promisor” remain a real requirement. An act nobody asked for, done out of ordinary kindness, is not obviously consideration even though it is past. That is the point at which section 26 becomes the safer argument to run.

sections.keypoint: Section 26 voids a bare promise, then saves three of them — and limb (a) needs writing AND registration.

body.text: Section 26: an agreement made without consideration is void, unless — (a) it is in writing and registered, and made on account of natural love and affection between parties standing in a near relation to each other; (b) it is a promise to compensate, wholly or in part, a person who has already voluntarily done something for the promisor; or (c) it is a promise, in writing and signed by the person to be charged, to pay wholly or in part a debt of which the creditor might have enforced payment but for the law of limitation.
Put simply: no consideration, no contract — with three escapes, and each escape has a form to follow.

items: (a) It is in writing and registered, and made on account of natural love and affection between parties standing in a near relation to each other.
(b) It is a promise to compensate, wholly or in part, a person who has already voluntarily done something for the promisor.
(c) It is a promise in writing, signed by the person to be charged, to pay a debt the creditor could have enforced but for the law of limitation.

body.text: **Limitation** is the period within which an action must be brought. Once that period has run out the debt is still owed, but the courts will no longer enforce it.
Each exception carries its own formality, and it is usually the formality rather than the substance that decides the case.

items: Limb (a) needs writing *and* registration, which is a demanding pair. Writing on its own is not enough, and this is the limb most often stated only halfway.
Limb (b) needs the earlier act to have been voluntary and done for the promisor. It is the safe route for the good turn that nobody asked for.
Limb (c) needs writing signed by the person who is to pay, and a debt that is time-barred rather than merely unpaid.

body.text: Ah Meng finds Puan Rohana's cat and brings it home, without being asked to. A week later she signs a note promising him RM500 for his trouble. Section 2(d) is awkward here, because nobody had asked him to do anything at all. Section 26(b) fits squarely, since it covers a promise to compensate a person who has already voluntarily done something for the promisor. That is the limb to argue first.

A father promises his daughter RM20,000 out of natural love and affection when she finishes her degree. They are plainly in a near relation, and the love and affection is expressly the reason. But nothing was put in writing and nothing was registered, so section 26(a) is not satisfied and the promise is void.

Failing that second promise for want of an intention to create legal relations gives the right outcome for the wrong reason. The Act hands you a clear formality, so reach for the provision rather than for a general idea.

body.caption: Section 26: the three saved promises
rows: Writing **and** registration; natural love and affection; parties in a near relation
Writing alone is not enough — this is the limb most often stated incompletely
A promise to compensate a past act that was voluntary and done for the promisor
The act must have been voluntary, and done *for the promisor*
A written, signed promise to pay a debt barred by limitation
The debt must actually be time-barred, not merely unpaid

sections.keypoint: Inadequate consideration does not void an agreement, though it may bear on whether consent was free.

body.text: Puan Rohana sells her motorbike to her cousin for RM100 when the bike is plainly worth RM4,000. Is the sale void because the price is absurd?

Explanation 2 to s 26: an agreement is not void merely because the consideration is inadequate, but inadequacy may be taken into account in determining whether the promisor's consent was freely given.

So the courts do not police whether a bargain was a good one. A wildly one-sided bargain is, however, evidence that something went wrong in the making of it — pressure, perhaps, or a misunderstanding.

sections.keypoint: Three promises, and a colleague who has advised that all three fail out of an English textbook.

body.text: The problem question gives you three promises and a junior colleague who has advised that all three of them fail. His grounds are taken straight out of an English textbook.
Two of the three promises actually succeed. The exercise is noticing which of his propositions is English law that the Malaysian Act has displaced.

quiz.q: How does section 2(d) differ from English law?
options: Consideration must be adequate
Past consideration is good, and consideration need not come from the promisee
Consideration must be in writing
Consideration must come from the promisee alone
quiz.why: Both differences decide cases, and both come straight from the words of the section.

quiz.q: Does section 2(d) mean a stranger to a contract can sue on it?
options: Yes
No — a stranger to the contract still cannot sue on it
Yes, for written contracts
Only where the consideration came from the stranger
quiz.why: Consideration may come from a stranger. Who may sue is a separate question, and the answer is privity.

options: Writing and registration, natural love and affection, and parties in a near relation
Writing alone

Adequacy is entirely for the parties
quiz.why: It is the bridge between consideration and the provisions on free consent.

options: Section 26(a)
Section 26(c)
Section 26(b)
None — it fails
quiz.why: The act must have been voluntary and done for the promisor. That is the safe route where nobody asked for it.

lessons.title: From arrest to charge
lessons.summary: How the Criminal Procedure Code sorts offences into classes, and what those classes decide about arrest, remand and bail.

sections.keypoint: Arrested on a Friday night: how long can they hold him, can he see a lawyer, and can he get out?

body.text: Danial is arrested at eleven on a Friday night outside a mamak shop. His sister wants to know three things. How long can they hold him, can she get him a lawyer, and can he get out on bail?

Criminal procedure looks like a mountain of detail until you notice one thing. A small number of labels, set out in a schedule at the back of the Criminal Procedure Code, answer most of the questions people actually ask.

body.prompt: Danial's sister wants to know whether the police needed a warrant, and whether he can get bail. Before you read on — what decides those two answers?
options: How serious the offence looks, and whether he seems likely to run
Which class the offence falls into in a schedule at the back of the Code
What the magistrate thinks once Danial is brought to court
body.reveal: A schedule, in both cases. The other two answers describe something real, and neither of them is where you start. Seriousness and the risk of flight are what a court weighs once it has a discretion at all, and whether it has one is settled by the classification. So look the offence up first. Nearly every question the sister asked is answered by that single step.

sections.keypoint: Look the offence up in the First Schedule before reasoning about any of it.

body.text: Three questions come up again and again. May the police arrest without a warrant, may they investigate without an order, and is bail available? All three are settled by looking the offence up. They are not worked out by reasoning about them.
A **warrant** is a written order from a court authorising an arrest. The Code sorts every offence into classes that decide when one is needed.
The First Schedule to the CPC classifies each offence as seizable or non-seizable, and as bailable, non-bailable or unbailable. Look the offence up before reasoning about the procedure.

body.title: One lookup answers three questions
body.caption: The classification comes first and the powers follow from it. Arguing about whether an arrest was reasonable, before checking which column the offence sits in, is the common way to get this wrong.
body.alt: A question — how does the First Schedule classify this offence? — branching two ways. Seizable: the police may arrest without a warrant and investigate without an order. Non-seizable: a warrant or a magistrate's order is generally needed for both.
body.question: How does the First Schedule classify the offence?

body.text: Malaysia says *seizable* where England says *arrestable*. Borrowing the English word signals that you are working from an English book, and the two classifications are not identical. So it is more than a difference of naming.

sections.keypoint: Article 5(3) and 5(4) are the floor: grounds, a lawyer, and a magistrate within twenty-four hours.
sections.h: Arrest, and the floor beneath it

body.text: For a seizable offence a police officer may arrest without a warrant. For a non-seizable offence the general position is that a warrant or an order is required first.
But those powers sit underneath constitutional guarantees that apply whatever the classification, and that is usually where the real argument is.
Article 5(3): a person arrested shall be informed as soon as may be of the grounds of his arrest and shall be allowed to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of his choice.
Put simply: they must tell you why you are being held, and let you see a lawyer of your own choosing.

Article 5(4): a person arrested and not released shall without unreasonable delay, and in any case within twenty-four hours, be produced before a magistrate and shall not be further detained without the magistrate's authority.

The twenty-four hours does not count the time needed to travel to the magistrate. Holding somebody longer needs a **remand order**, which is a magistrate's permission to keep a person in custody while the investigation continues.
The magistrate is deciding whether continued detention is genuinely justified for that investigation. The hearing is not meant to be a formality.

body.title: The clock from arrest to a magistrate
body.caption: Twenty-four hours is a ceiling on police custody, not on detention. Past it the decision belongs to a magistrate, who is meant to ask whether the investigation genuinely needs the time.
body.alt: Four steps. Arrest. Then, as soon as may be, the grounds of arrest and access to a lawyer of your own choosing under Article 5(3). Then production before a magistrate within twenty-four hours under Article 5(4), not counting travel time. Then either a remand order extending detention, or release.

steps.label: Grounds, and a lawyer
steps.note: Art 5(3), as soon as may be

steps.label: Remand, or release
steps.note: the magistrate decides, not the police

body.text: The right to a lawyer under Article 5(3) is not always given effect at the moment of arrest. The case law on when access must be allowed is worth reading in full rather than in summary. This is a live and contested area.

body.q: Danial was arrested at eleven on Friday night. It is Sunday morning and he has not been before a magistrate. What has gone wrong?
options: Nothing — the police may hold him while they investigate
Article 5(4) required him to be produced before a magistrate within twenty-four hours
Nothing, so long as he has been allowed to see a lawyer
body.why: Twenty-four hours is the outer limit, and only the travelling time to the magistrate is left out of the count. Holding him longer needs a remand order, and only a magistrate can give one. The first answer treats an unfinished investigation as its own authority to detain, which is the thing Article 5(4) refuses. The third mixes up two separate guarantees. A lawyer under 5(3) buys the police no extra hours.

sections.keypoint: Bail is release before trial, and whether it is a right or a discretion depends on the classification.

body.text: **Bail** is release from custody before trial. The accused usually promises to come back to court, and money or a surety stands as security for that promise.

Bail in Malaysia turns mostly on the classification of the offence rather than on a general discretion in the judge. That is a real difference from the English approach a common law textbook will describe.

items: Bailable — bail is available as of right.
Non-bailable — bail is at the court's discretion.
Unbailable — bail is not available at all.

body.text: So the first question is never whether bail ought to be granted. It is which of those three boxes the offence sits in, and the Schedule answers that.

Special legislation frequently displaces the ordinary rules, and security and drugs legislation in particular carry their own bail provisions. Check whether the charge is under the Penal Code or under a particular Act before applying the general position.

sections.keypoint: A charge must give enough particulars of time, place and person to be answered.

body.text: A seizable offence may be investigated without an order, while a non-seizable one generally needs one. The investigation produces the investigation papers, which go to the Deputy Public Prosecutor, and the decision to prosecute belongs to the Public Prosecutor.
The charge must state the offence, and enough particulars of time, place, and the person or thing concerned, to give the accused notice of what he is charged with.

A defective charge is not automatically fatal, and the usual question is whether the accused was prejudiced or misled by it. But the drafting rules exist for a plain reason. Nobody can answer a case they have not been told.

sections.keypoint: At the close of the prosecution case the court tests the evidence properly, not just whether some exists.
sections.h: The halfway point of a trial

body.text: The prosecution calls its witnesses and then closes its case. The court asks at that point whether a **prima facie case** has been made out, which means whether there is a case for the accused to answer.
If there is, the accused is called on to enter his defence. If there is not, he is acquitted there and then.
A prima facie case requires the court to undertake a maximum evaluation of the prosecution evidence — to test its credibility — and to ask whether, if unrebutted, it would warrant a conviction.
Put simply: the judge must weigh how believable the prosecution's evidence really is, and ask whether it would be enough to convict if nobody answered it.

The word *maximum* is doing real work there. A minimum evaluation would ask only whether there is some evidence on each element. That would put an accused to his defence on evidence no reasonable court could convict on.

If the defence is called, the accused may give evidence on oath, make an unsworn statement from the dock, or say nothing at all. Each of those has different consequences. Conviction still requires proof beyond reasonable doubt on the whole of the evidence.

sections.keypoint: Read the First Schedule itself rather than a summary of it.

body.text: There are no flashcards or problems for this module yet. The most useful thing you can do is read the First Schedule itself, rather than a summary of it.

Follow one offence all the way through: its classification, the arrest power that follows from it, and the bail position that follows from that. The structure becomes obvious once you have done it once.

lessons.title: Negligence, in four questions
lessons.summary: Duty, breach, causation and remoteness, taken in that order — and the two places where Malaysian law has taken its own line.

sections.keypoint: A junction, a broken leg, and four questions that have to be taken in order.

body.text: Faizal is riding home on his motorbike when a car turns across the junction without looking. His leg is broken and the bike is written off. Who pays for that, and for how much of it?

A claim of this kind is called **negligence**, which is careless conduct causing foreseeable damage in breach of a duty. The person who brings the claim is the **plaintiff**, and the person sued is the **defendant**.

Almost every negligence problem is answered by four questions taken in order. Answering them out of order is the commonest way to make a mess of the whole thing, so establish each one before you move to the next.

items: Duty — did the driver owe Faizal a duty to take care?
Breach — did the driver fall below the standard the law asks for?
Causation — did that carelessness actually cause the harm, in fact and in law?
Remoteness — was that kind of harm reasonably foreseeable?

body.text: Damage is required as well. Negligence gives nobody a claim on its own, so no loss means no claim, however careless the conduct happened to be.

body.title: The four questions, in order
body.caption: The order is not stylistic. Each step assumes the one before it, and an answer that argues remoteness before establishing breach is arguing about nothing.
body.alt: Four questions, in order. Duty: was one owed to this claimant? Breach: did the defendant fall below the standard? Causation: in fact, and in law. Remoteness: was the damage of a foreseeable kind?

sections.keypoint: Duty: foreseeability, proximity, and whether it is fair, just and reasonable to impose one.

body.text: Where the situation is a familiar one, a duty already exists and a single sentence disposes of it. Two road users, a doctor and a patient, an employer and an employee are all settled cases, and Faizal's accident is one of them.
The longer test is reserved for genuinely new situations, where nobody has yet decided whether a duty is owed at all.
The three-stage test: reasonable foreseeability of harm, a relationship of proximity between the parties, and whether it is fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty.
body.source: Caparo Industries plc v Dickman [1990] 2 AC 605 (HL), adopted in Malaysia in Majlis Perbandaran Ampang Jaya v Steven Phoa Cheng Loon [2006] 2 MLJ 389 (FC)

body.text: **Proximity** here means closeness of relationship rather than closeness in metres. It asks how directly the defendant's conduct bore on this particular plaintiff, and it is the middle step of that test.
Running the three-stage test on an ordinary road accident wastes the time you needed for causation. Save it for the situation nobody has met before.

The three-stage test comes from an English case, *Caparo Industries plc v Dickman* [1990] 2 AC 605 (HL). Ampang Jaya is the Malaysian authority to cite here, and it is worth reading rather than citing at second hand. It also deals with the hard question of when a public authority is liable. Lok Kok Beng later revisited the approach and is the other case to know.

Pure economic loss and psychiatric injury have their own restrictive rules. **Pure economic loss** is money lost where nobody was injured and no property was damaged. These are separate categories rather than harder versions of an ordinary duty, so name them as such instead of running the three-stage test and hoping.

sections.keypoint: Breach is measured against the reasonable person — and on advising of risks Malaysia left Bolam behind.

body.text: The standard is objective. The question is what a reasonable person would have done in the defendant's position, and the defendant's own inexperience does not lower it. A professional is measured against the reasonably competent member of that profession.

Whether the standard was met is worked out by weighing four things against each other. How likely was the harm, how serious would it be, what would precautions have cost, and how useful is the activity to everybody else?
Those four factors are how you argue breach instead of merely asserting it.

A contractor leaves an open trench across the five-foot way outside a kedai runcit overnight, with no lamp and no barrier round it. Injury is likely, a broken hip is serious, a cone and a light would have cost almost nothing, and there was no urgency about the work. Breach is straightforward to argue on those four factors.

Doctors are the first of the two places where Malaysian law parts company with English law. The older English test said a doctor was not negligent if a responsible body of medical opinion would have done the same thing. It is called **Bolam**, after the English High Court decision in *Bolam v Friern Hospital Management Committee* [1957] 1 WLR 582.

On a doctor's duty to advise of risks, Malaysia has departed from the Bolam test and adopted the approach in Rogers v Whitaker: the question is what a reasonable patient would want to know, not what a responsible body of medical opinion would disclose.
body.source: Foo Fio Na v Dr Soo Fook Mun [2007] 1 MLJ 593 (FC), adopting Rogers v Whitaker (1992) 175 CLR 479 (High Court of Australia)

body.text: Put simply: the test is no longer what other doctors would have mentioned. It is what this patient would have wanted to be told before agreeing. The Australian case that rule takes its wording from is *Rogers v Whitaker* (1992) 175 CLR 479.

Foo Fio Na is a genuine Malaysian departure, and an English textbook will mislead you here. But it is confined to advice and the disclosure of risk. The Federal Court settled that in *Zulhasnimar bt Hasan Basri v Dr Kuppu Velumani P* [2017] 5 MLJ 438. For diagnosis and treatment the Bolam test still applies, subject to qualification.

body.q: A surgeon does not mention a small but serious risk before an operation. Most surgeons would not have mentioned it either. In Malaysia, does that answer the claim?
options: Yes — a responsible body of medical opinion would have done the same
Yes, provided the operation itself was carried out competently
No — the question is what a reasonable patient would want to know
body.why: On advice and the disclosure of risk, Malaysia follows Rogers v Whitaker rather than Bolam. The first answer *is* the Bolam test, and it is what an English textbook hands you, which is precisely what makes it the trap. The third changes the subject. Doing the operation well is a different duty from telling the patient what might go wrong.

sections.keypoint: Causation is but-for first, then whether anything later broke the chain.

body.text: Factual causation is the but-for test. Would the damage have happened anyway, but for the breach? If it would have happened regardless, the breach caused nothing at all, however negligent it looks.

A doctor negligently fails to examine a patient who is already dying of a poison for which there is no treatment. The failure is plainly a breach of duty. It caused nothing, because the patient would have died in any event, so the claim fails at causation rather than at breach.

Legal causation asks a different question: did something break the chain between the breach and the harm? Lawyers call such a thing a **novus actus interveniens**, which is a new intervening act that breaks the chain of causation.

The new act may be something the plaintiff did, something a third party did, or a natural event. The question is whether it was so unreasonable or so unforeseeable that it lifts responsibility off the defendant.

sections.keypoint: The kind of damage must be foreseeable; the extent need not, and the claimant's own fault reduces rather than defeats.

body.text: Even a breach that caused the harm does not make the defendant pay for everything that followed. The law draws a line at harm of a kind nobody could have seen coming.
Damage is too remote unless it is of a kind that was reasonably foreseeable. The precise manner of its occurrence and its extent need not be.
body.source: The Wagon Mound; standard common law

body.text: Put simply: the *kind* of harm has to be foreseeable. Exactly how it came about, and how bad it turned out to be, do not.

body.prompt: Faizal was not wearing a helmet when the car turned across the junction. Before you read on — what does that do to his claim?
options: Nothing — the driver caused the collision, not the missing helmet
It cuts his damages by a share the court thinks fair
It ends the claim, because he was breaking the law himself
body.reveal: It cuts them. The other two answers are honest instincts, and the law sits between them. The driver did cause the collision, so the claim survives. But Faizal made his own head injury worse, and the court will not ask the driver to pay for that part of it. Carelessness by the person suing reduces the award instead of defeating it.

body.text: Two doctrines then reduce or defeat what is actually recovered. The first is **contributory negligence**, which is the plaintiff's own carelessness reducing the award. It cuts the damages rather than defeating the claim, and in Malaysia it is statutory.
Contributory negligence: damages are reduced to such extent as the court thinks just and equitable having regard to the claimant's share in the responsibility.

Faizal was not wearing a helmet. The car driver still caused the collision, but the head injury was worse than it would have been. The court cuts his damages by a share it thinks just and equitable. It does not throw his claim out.

The second is **volenti non fit injuria**, meaning that no injury is done to a person who consents to run the risk. It is a complete defence and correspondingly rare, because it needs real knowledge of the risk and real agreement to accept it.

Watch the limitation period, which is the period within which an action must be brought. A tort claim is generally barred six years after the cause of action accrued. In negligence that clock starts when the damage occurs, and not when the careless act was done.

Between them they hold both of the places where Malaysian negligence has gone its own way, and both are commonly examined because an English answer gets them wrong.

lessons.title: Title by registration, and the limits of indefeasibility
lessons.summary: The Torrens system, section 340 of the National Land Code, and the case that had to be overruled before the section worked as it was meant to.

sections.keypoint: Forty years of farming, a name on a title, and a document in a drawer — what actually makes it his?

body.text: Pak Din has farmed the same two acres outside Kuala Selangor for forty years. His name is on the title at the land office, and the document itself lives in a tin under his bed.
One morning a stranger arrives with papers and says the land is his. He has a title too, in his own name, issued by the same land office. Only one of the two of them can be right.
Malaysian land law has a hard and clear rule about which. Understanding why the rule is so hard is the whole of this lesson.

body.prompt: Pak Din has farmed the land for forty years and has a title in his name. The stranger has a title in his name too, from the same land office. Before you read on — who does the law say owns it?
options: Pak Din, because forty years of working it must count for something
Whichever of them the register at the land office names now
Neither, until a court decides between the two documents
body.reveal: The register decides, and it decides on its own. Not the years. Not the tin under the bed. Not who seems more deserving. If your instinct was the first answer, hold on to that feeling. It is the instinct this system was built to overrule. The rest of the lesson is about what that costs.

sections.keypoint: Title by registration, not registration of title: the register creates the interest rather than recording it.

body.text: Malaysian land law runs on a system called **Torrens**, named after the man who designed it. One single idea organises everything else in the subject.

The register kept at the land office is not evidence of who owns the land. It *is* the ownership. A person becomes the owner by being registered, and not by holding a good bundle of old papers that registration then writes down.
Title by registration, not registration of title. The register is conclusive, and a purchaser deals with the register rather than investigating the history behind it.
body.source: National Land Code; the Torrens principle

body.text: The point of arranging things that way is to make buying land cheap and safe. A buyer checks the register and stops there, instead of paying somebody to trace deeds back through fifty years and three families.
Everything difficult in this subject comes from the cases where that promise collides with a real victim of fraud or forgery.

Section 6 of the Civil Law Act 1956 shuts English land law out, and this is the reason why. English doctrines about equitable interests and notice would cut across the conclusiveness of the register, and that conclusiveness is the whole mechanism.

sections.keypoint: Section 340 promises an indefeasible title, then lists the exceptions that qualify the promise.

body.text: The promise the Code makes is that a registered owner cannot be shifted. The technical word for that is **indefeasible**, and indefeasibility simply means a registered title that cannot be set aside.
Section 340(1): the title or interest of any person for the time being registered as proprietor, or in whose name any lease, charge or easement is registered, is indefeasible.
Put simply: whoever is on the register owns it, and that goes for a lease, a charge or an easement registered against the land as well.
Subsection (2) then sets out the exceptions, and the list is short and closed. Indefeasibility is defeated in three situations.

items: The registration was obtained by fraud or misrepresentation, and the registered owner was a party to it or knew of it.
The registration was obtained by forgery, or by an instrument that was void or insufficient.
The title was unlawfully acquired in the purported exercise of a power given by written law.

body.text: Then comes the proviso, and the whole subject turns on it. A title that could be set aside under subsection (2) is still protected once it reaches somebody who bought it in good faith and paid for it.
**In good faith** means honestly, and without knowing about the fraud. **Valuable consideration** means the buyer actually paid something, rather than being handed the land as a gift.

body.q: A forger transfers Pak Din's land into his own name. Is the forger's registered title safe?
options: Yes — once registered, a title cannot be touched
Yes, if the land office accepted the documents
No — forgery is one of the exceptions in section 340
body.why: Section 340 gives an indefeasible title, then takes it back in the listed cases, and forgery is one of them. The person registered *by* the forgery is not protected. What happens to someone who later buys from him is a different question, and it is the one the next section is about.

sections.keypoint: Deferred indefeasibility: the immediate transferee under a forgery loses; the next honest buyer does not.

body.text: Somebody forges Pak Din's signature and transfers the land to Ah Kow, who is in on the scheme. Ah Kow is registered as the owner. He then sells the land on to Salmah for RM180,000. Salmah knows nothing about the forgery and pays the full asking price.

Ah Kow's title can be undone, because he is the immediate transferee under a forged instrument. Salmah's title cannot be touched at all. Pak Din loses the land, and has to chase Ah Kow for money instead.

Deferred indefeasibility: the immediate registered proprietor whose registration was procured by fraud or forgery takes a defeasible title. A subsequent bona fide purchaser for value takes an indefeasible one.
body.source: National Land Code, s 340(2) and the proviso to s 340(3)

body.text: Put simply: the forger's buyer can be unwound, but the next innocent buyer down the line cannot. The line is drawn one transaction later than a first reading of the section suggests.
There is a reason for drawing it there. The innocent buyer is exactly the person the register exists to protect, and protecting her is what makes the register worth relying on.

This is hard on Pak Din, and it is meant to be a trade-off rather than a kindness. The system buys cheap and certain conveyancing at the price of leaving some genuine victims with a claim for money instead of their land.

sections.keypoint: Tan Ying Hong overruled Adorna Properties, and nothing in the earlier judgment says it was wrong.
sections.h: The case that had to be overruled

body.text: This is the best example in Malaysian law of the doctrine of precedent doing real work. It is worth knowing as a piece of history, quite as much as for the rule itself.

In Adorna Properties the Federal Court read section 340 as giving **immediate** indefeasibility. On that reading even Ah Kow, the first transferee under the forged instrument, ended up with a title nobody could touch.
The consequence was that a registered owner could lose their land to a forger's buyer and have no remedy at all. That turned the protective purpose of the exceptions upside down.
Tan Ying Hong overruled Adorna Properties and restored deferred indefeasibility: a registration obtained by forgery is defeasible in the hands of the immediate transferee.
body.source: Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San [2010] 2 MLJ 1 (FC)

body.text: Textbooks and judgments written before 2010 may still state the Adorna position. Check the date of anything you read on indefeasibility, because the years in between produced decisions applying a rule that is no longer good law.

body.title: Nine years of the wrong rule
body.caption: Nothing in the text of the earlier judgment tells you it was wrong. This is what a citator is for, and why free Malaysian research cannot stop at the text.
body.alt: Three points. The National Land Code 1965, section 340: registered title is indefeasible, subject to the exceptions in section 340(2). In 2001 Adorna Properties adopted immediate indefeasibility, so a forged transfer gave the transferee a good title. In 2010 Tan Ying Hong departed from Adorna and restored deferred indefeasibility.

events.note: s 340: registered title indefeasible, subject to the exceptions in s 340(2)

events.label: Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San (FC)

sections.keypoint: The Code allows a closed set of dealings — transfer, lease, charge, easement — and the vocabulary is its own.

body.text: The Code allows a closed set of registrable **dealings**, which are transfer, lease, charge and easement. The vocabulary is not the English one either.

Land here is *charged* rather than mortgaged, and a **charge** is the Code's security interest over registered land. The chargee's remedies are statutory: an order for sale, or possession, on the terms the Code lays down.

A **caveat** is an entry that freezes dealings while a claim is worked out. It creates no interest in the land at all, and what it does is stop dealings being registered while it stands. That buys the person who entered it time to prove the claim in court.
Private, registrar's, lien-holder's and trust caveats each have their own conditions attached to them.
A caveat entered without a caveatable interest exposes the person who entered it to a claim for compensation. It is not a free way to block somebody else's sale.

Then read Tan Ying Hong, to see what the Federal Court thought had gone wrong.
