lessons.title: The company as a person, and the duties that follow
lessons.summary: Separate legal personality, the narrow circumstances in which a court looks behind it, and what the Companies Act 2016 asks of directors.

sections.keypoint: Two siblings, one catering company, and the question of whose debt it is.

body.text: Kavitha and her brother run a catering business together. They register a company called Sedap Catering Sdn Bhd, and each of them takes half of the shares.
The company borrows RM60,000 for a new oven, and eighteen months later the business fails. The bank wants its money back. Who exactly owes it?

body.prompt: Sedap Catering has failed and the bank wants its RM60,000 back. Before you read on — who owes it?
options: Kavitha and her brother, half each — it is their business
Kavitha, because she signed the loan papers for the company
The company, and nobody else
body.reveal: The company. In every ordinary sense the business is the two of them, and the first answer is how anyone would describe it over the phone. The law says something else, and that one move is the foundation of the whole subject. The third answer is the near miss. Signing for a company is signing as the company, unless you also give a personal guarantee.

body.text: The answer is the company, and not Kavitha. That answer is stranger than it first looks, and everything else in company law follows from it.

sections.keypoint: A company is a person in law, and its members are not liable simply for being members.

body.text: A company registered under the Act is treated as a person in its own right, separate from the people who own it and run it. It can own property, make contracts, and sue and be sued in its own name.
It also carries on existing as members come and go, which an ordinary partnership does not.
A company is a body corporate with legal personality separate from its members. Its members are not, by reason only of membership, liable for its obligations.
body.source: Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd [1897] AC 22; Companies Act 2016

body.text: Put simply: the company owes its own debts, and being a shareholder does not by itself make you liable for them.

Salomon is the case that settled it. The House of Lords upheld the separateness even though one man owned nearly all the shares, ran the business himself, and was also its secured creditor. The company was not his agent and it was not a sham. It was simply a different person.
**Limited liability** is a consequence of that idea rather than the idea itself. Because the company owes the debt, a member risks only whatever is still unpaid on their shares.

Sedap Catering owes the bank RM60,000 and has RM4,000 left in its account. The bank can take the RM4,000. It cannot take Kavitha's car or her personal savings, unless she signed a personal guarantee for the loan.

body.title: Two persons, and only one of them owes the bank

items: Owns shares in Sedap Catering Sdn Bhd.
Does not own the ovens; the company does.
Risks only what she agreed to pay for her shares.
Her car and her savings are not available to the bank.
A person in its own right, able to own property and to be sued.
Owns the ovens and owes the RM60,000.
Its RM4,000 is what the bank can take.
Carries on existing as members come and go.

sections.keypoint: Courts look behind that personality rarely, and control alone is never a reason.

body.text: Sometimes a court will look behind the separate personality and treat the company and the person controlling it as one. Lawyers call this **lifting the veil**, the veil being the separation between a company and its members.
The circumstances in which it happens are much narrower than most people expect. Saying that the veil should be lifted because the result feels unfair is not an argument at all.

items: Statute — an Act expressly places liability on directors or members. This is by far the commonest route.
Fraud or evasion — the company form is used to escape an obligation that already existed, or to conceal wrongdoing.
Agency — the company is genuinely acting as agent for its controller on ordinary agency principles, rather than merely being controlled by them.

body.text: Control alone is never enough. A company owned entirely by another company is still a separate person from its parent, and a company with a single member is still separate from that member. That is precisely what Salomon decided, so an answer that lifts the veil because the defendant owned all the shares has not identified a ground.

body.q: A man owns every share in his company and makes every decision himself. The company cannot pay a supplier. Can the supplier come after him personally?
options: No, unless there is a ground to lift the veil, such as statute, fraud or genuine agency
Yes — he owns the whole thing, so the company is really him
Yes, because a company with a single owner is not truly separate
body.why: Control is never a ground on its own. That is the precise point Salomon decided, on facts very like these. The first and third answers are the same mistake in two costumes. A ground has to be named, and *this feels unfair* is not one of them.

sections.keypoint: The Companies Act 2016 changed the structure, so a pre-2017 textbook is describing a repealed Act.

body.text: The Companies Act 2016 replaced the 1965 Act and made structural changes that older textbooks simply do not reflect. Three of them are worth knowing before you read anything else on the subject.

items: The memorandum and articles of association were replaced by a single, optional **constitution**. A company may have none at all, and then the Act supplies its internal rules.
A private company may now be formed and run with a single member and a single director.
Authorised capital and the par value of shares were abolished, so shares are issued without a nominal value.

body.text: This is the module where an out-of-date text does the most damage. If a book refers to the memorandum and articles, or to authorised capital, as current law, it predates 2016 and should be treated as history.

sections.keypoint: Directors must act for a proper purpose and in good faith, with reasonable care, skill and diligence.

body.text: The Act sets out the core duties of a director. They sit alongside the older equitable and common law duties rather than replacing them.
A director shall at all times exercise his powers in accordance with the Act, for a proper purpose and in good faith in the best interest of the company.
Put simply: use the powers of the office for the reason they were given, honestly, and in the company's interests rather than your own.
The second duty is about competence rather than loyalty, and its shape is worth looking at closely.

A director shall exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence with the knowledge, skill and experience which may reasonably be expected of a director having the same responsibilities, and any additional knowledge, skill and experience which the director in fact has.

Put simply: there is a floor set by the job itself, and it rises for a director who happens to know more. An accountant on the board is held to more than the minimum, and a director who takes no interest in the company is not held to less.

Kavitha's brother never reads the accounts and signs whatever is put in front of him. He cannot answer a claim by saying that he did not understand any of it. The standard is what a director in his position ought reasonably to have known.
Two further points recur. The duty is owed to the company, not to individual shareholders, and not in the ordinary case to creditors either.
And a director must not use their position, or the company's property, information or opportunity, to gain a benefit for themselves or to cause harm to the company.

A director hears in a board meeting about a contract the company is chasing, and quietly takes it for himself. That the company might have failed to win it anyway is usually no answer. The objection is to using his position and the information, not to the loss.

sections.keypoint: The duty is owed to the company, which is why a single unhappy member usually cannot sue on it.

body.text: Because the duty is owed to the company, the company is the proper claimant when the duty is broken. That is where the rule comes from that a single member cannot ordinarily sue for a wrong done to the company.

Two statutory routes exist around that rule. A **derivative action** is a member suing on the company's behalf, with the court's leave. An **oppression** claim is a member's own remedy for being treated unfairly in the conduct of the company's affairs.
Keep the two apart. A derivative action vindicates the company's right, while an oppression claim vindicates the member's own. Confusing them is a standard way of answering the wrong question.

body.title: Whose right is being vindicated?
body.caption: Answer that first and the route follows. Pleading an oppression claim as though it vindicated the company's right is a standard way of losing an otherwise good case.
body.alt: A question — whose right was broken? — branching two ways. The company's: a derivative action, brought by a member on the company's behalf, with the court's leave. The member's own: an oppression claim, brought in the member's own name.
body.question: Whose right was broken?

branches.label: Derivative action
branches.note: a member sues on its behalf, with leave

branches.label: Oppression claim
branches.note: brought in the member's own name

lessons.title: Relevancy is the gate
lessons.summary: The Evidence Act is a closed list of what may be proved, which makes it a different system from the English law of admissibility.

sections.keypoint: A neighbour wants to tell the court the accused has a bad temper. Can she?
sections.h: A witness with something to say

body.text: A man is on trial for injuring his neighbour in a quarrel. A woman from three doors down wants to tell the court that the accused has always had a bad temper. Will the judge let her?

body.prompt: The neighbour wants to tell the court that the accused has always had a bad temper. Before you read on — will the judge let her?
options: Yes, if the judge thinks it helps to decide the case
Only if a section of the Evidence Act makes that fact relevant
No — what a person is generally like is never evidence
body.reveal: A section, or nothing. The first answer is how a trial looks from outside, and it is roughly where English evidence starts. Relevant material goes in unless a rule keeps it out. The Act turns that round. Nothing comes in unless a section lets it in. The third answer overshoots. Character is relevant in Malaysia, but only in narrow circumstances that a section sets out.

body.text: In Malaysia the answer does not come from a general sense of what is fair. It comes from asking which section of the Evidence Act makes that fact relevant. If no section does, it does not come in at all.

sections.keypoint: The Act is a closed list: evidence of facts in issue and facts it declares relevant, and of no others.
sections.h: Why an English textbook misleads here

body.text: The Evidence Act 1950 descends from the Indian Evidence Act of 1872, drafted by Stephen, and it is a code. That means it sets out the whole of the subject in its own terms, rather than restating what the judges had decided.
It is not organised the way English evidence is organised, and reading it as though it were will lead you astray.
The English approach asks whether a piece of evidence is admissible. It starts from a general principle that relevant evidence goes in, unless some rule of exclusion pushes it back out again.
The Act turns that whole arrangement upside down. Part I sets out the categories of fact that are relevant, and nothing outside those categories may be proved at all.
Evidence may be given of facts in issue and of such other facts as are declared relevant by the Act, and of no others.
Put simply: the Act is a closed list of what may be proved. Nothing gets in on general grounds of fairness or common sense.

body.title: Two ways of arranging the same question

items: Start from a general principle: relevant evidence is admissible.
Then apply exclusionary rules that keep particular things out.
Hearsay is a rule of exclusion with a list of exceptions hanging off it.
The question is: **is there a rule that excludes this?**
Part I declares the categories of fact that are relevant.
Nothing outside those categories may be proved at all.
There is no general hearsay rule. Statements by absent persons are simply not made relevant, except where a section makes them so.
The question is: **which section makes this fact relevant?**

body.text: So the question is never simply “is this relevant?” in the ordinary sense of the word. The question you have to answer is “which section of the Act makes this fact relevant?”. If you cannot name a section, the evidence does not come in, and an argument about relevance with no section behind it has missed the structure of the whole Act.

sections.keypoint: Know the shape of the relevancy sections rather than holding all of them at once.

body.text: Part I of the Act works through those categories one at a time. You do not need to hold them all in your head at once, but you should know the shape of the list and be able to find the right one.

items: Facts forming part of the same transaction — the res gestae provision.
Facts which are the occasion, cause or effect of facts in issue.
Motive, preparation, and the conduct of a party before or after the events in question.
Facts that are necessary in order to explain or to introduce a relevant fact.
Admissions made by a party, and confessions as a special class of admission.
Statements made by persons who cannot themselves be called as witnesses.
Opinions of experts, on science, art, foreign law, handwriting or fingerprints.
Character, which is relevant in narrow and different circumstances in civil and criminal cases.

body.text: **Relevancy** is the gate, then, and a fact is admissible only because some section of the Act makes it relevant.
Hearsay deserves a note, because the Act handles it differently from English law. **Hearsay** is a statement made outside court, offered to prove that what it said was true.

There is no single hearsay rule here with a list of exceptions hanging off it. Statements by absent persons are simply not made relevant, except where a section makes them so, which reaches a similar place by a different route.

sections.keypoint: Whoever asserts must prove — and the legal burden does not shift the way the evidential one does.

body.text: Puan Rosnah sues her former tenant for RM2,400 of unpaid rent. He says that he paid her in cash and never got a receipt for it. Who has to prove what here?
Part II of the Act deals with proof, and the burden provisions are the ones you will use most often of everything in it.
Whoever desires any court to give judgment as to any legal right or liability, dependent on the existence of facts which he asserts, must prove that those facts exist.

Put simply: if you want the court to decide something in your favour, and it turns on a fact, then you prove that fact. So Rosnah has to prove that the rent fell due, and the tenant has to prove that he paid it.
The burden of proof in a suit or proceeding lies on that person who would fail if no evidence at all were given on either side.

Section 103 puts the burden on any particular fact on the person who wants the court to believe that fact exists. Section 106 puts on a person the burden of proving a fact that is especially within their own knowledge.
That last one comes up constantly in criminal cases, and it is regularly pushed further by prosecutors than it will actually go.

Keep the two kinds of burden apart in your mind. The **legal burden** is the risk of losing if a fact is not proved, and it does not shift. The **evidential burden** is the burden of putting enough evidence on a point to make it a live issue, and that one does shift. Saying that the burden shifted to the accused, without saying which burden, is the standard error here — the legal burden in a criminal case stays with the prosecution throughout.

body.q: Puan Rosnah sues for RM2,400 of unpaid rent. Her former tenant says he paid her in cash. Who has to prove the payment?
options: The tenant — payment is the fact he is asserting
Puan Rosnah — she started the case, so every fact in it is hers to prove
Neither — the court simply decides whose account is more likely
body.why: The burden on a particular fact sits on whoever wants the court to believe that fact. Rosnah proves the rent fell due, and the tenant proves he paid it. The first answer confuses carrying the case with carrying every fact inside it. The third skips the burden provisions altogether, and they are the part of the Act you will reach for most often.

sections.keypoint: Illustration (g) lets a court presume withheld evidence would have been unfavourable, but not automatically.

body.text: The Act separates facts a court **shall** presume from facts it **may** presume. A **presumption** is a direction about what the court may or must infer from something.
The discretionary ones in section 114 are argued most often, and one of its illustrations has taken on a life of its own.
Section 114 illustration (g): the court may presume that evidence which could be and is not produced would, if produced, be unfavourable to the person who withholds it.
Put simply: if you could have produced a witness or a document and you did not, the court is allowed to conclude that it would not have helped you.

A landlord sues over damage to a rented room and relies on his own account of it. The handyman who inspected the room the next morning is available to give evidence, and is never called. The court may hold that gap against the landlord.

The presumption is permissive rather than automatic, which matters a great deal in argument. The court asks whether the missing witness was genuinely material and genuinely available before drawing anything at all from the gap.

body.title: When illustration (g) actually bites
body.caption: The presumption is permissive, not automatic. An answer that treats the inference as following from absence alone has skipped both questions the court actually asks.
body.alt: A question — was the missing evidence both available to that party and material? — branching two ways. Available and material: the court may presume it would have been unfavourable, though it is never bound to. Merely cumulative of what is already proved, or not that party's to call: no inference arises.
body.question: Was the missing evidence available to that party, and material?

branches.label: The court may presume against them
branches.note: may, not must — s 114 is discretionary

branches.cond: cumulative, or not theirs to call
branches.label: No inference arises

body.text: Failing to call a witness whose evidence would merely repeat what is already proved does not attract the inference. The provision is about evidence that was withheld, not about evidence that was simply incomplete.

sections.keypoint: Confessions are a distinct class of admission with conditions of their own.

body.text: Confessions are admissions made in criminal cases, and the Act treats them as a distinct class with conditions of their own.

A confession is irrelevant if it appears to have been caused by an inducement, a threat or a promise. That must come from a person in authority, and must be enough to give the accused grounds for supposing he would gain an advantage or escape something bad.
This is one of the most heavily litigated parts of the Act and the case law is enormous. Read the sections themselves before any commentary, and be careful with older authority.

sections.keypoint: Take a fact you want to prove and go and find the section that lets you prove it.

body.text: There are no flashcards or problems for this module yet. The single most useful exercise is to take a fact you would want to prove, and go and find the section that makes it relevant.
Doing that ten times teaches the Act better than reading a chapter about it. Start with the neighbour who wants to talk about the accused's temper.

lessons.title: How a civil action is shaped
lessons.summary: Choosing how to start an action, setting out a case in a pleading, and the interlocutory steps that dispose of most disputes before trial.

sections.keypoint: RM18,000 of unpaid work and a man who wants his day in court — which he may never get.
sections.h: The case that never reaches trial

body.text: Encik Rahim did RM18,000 of renovation work on a shophouse and was never paid. He wants his day in court. He may well never get one.
Most civil disputes are never tried. They are decided by a limitation point, a striking out, an application for summary judgment, or a settlement that one of those made likely.
Procedure is where the outcome is usually decided, so treating it as the boring administrative part is a mistake people make exactly once.
The Rules of Court 2012 govern, and they brought together what used to be separate sets of rules for the High Court and the subordinate courts.

body.title: Where a civil action can stop
body.caption: Only the last box is a trial. Each of the earlier ones ends cases outright, which is why procedure decides more outcomes than the substantive law does.
body.alt: Five stages, each of which can end the action. Limitation: out of time ends it here. Mode: writ, or originating summons. Pleadings, which fix what the trial can be about. Applications: striking out, and summary judgment. Then trial, reached by a minority of disputes.

steps.label: Limitation
steps.note: out of time ends it here

steps.label: Pleadings
steps.note: they fix what the trial can be about

steps.label: Trial
steps.note: reached by a minority of disputes

sections.keypoint: Six years for contract and tort, twelve to recover land, running from accrual rather than from the wrong.
sections.h: First: is it already too late?

body.text: The first question on any set of facts is whether the claim is already out of time. If it is, nothing else about the case matters at all.

body.prompt: Encik Rahim finished the renovation seven years ago and was never paid. Before you read on — what happens to his claim now?
options: He is out of time, and the court will not hear it
He can still sue — a debt does not stop being owed
It depends on when he last chased the shophouse owner for the money
body.reveal: Out of time. If you chose the first, you are not wrong about the money. The debt is still owed and it never stops being owed. What runs out is the court. A contract claim has to be brought within six years, counted from the breach, and chasing somebody for payment does not restart that clock. It is the first thing to check on any facts, because nothing else matters if the answer is no.

body.text: Actions founded on contract or on tort must generally be brought within six years of the date on which the cause of action accrued; actions to recover land, within twelve.
Put simply: six years for a contract or tort claim, twelve to recover land, counted from the moment the claim arose.

Accrual is not the same thing as the wrongful act. In contract the cause of action accrues on breach. In tort it generally accrues when damage occurs, which may be a good deal later. Getting accrual wrong is how a claim ends up filed a year out of time.

sections.keypoint: Writ where the facts are disputed; originating summons where the question is one of construction.

body.text: There are two main ways to begin an action, and the choice between them is not a matter of taste.

items: **Writ** — the mode where there is likely to be a real dispute about the facts. Evidence is given aloud in court and tested by cross-examination.
**Originating summons** — the mode for a question of law on undisputed facts, or about what a document or statute means. Evidence goes in by affidavit, which is a written statement sworn to be true.

body.text: A dispute about what a clause in a lease means, where nobody disagrees about what was signed, is an originating summons. A dispute about whether a promise was made at a meeting is a writ.
Choosing wrongly is not usually fatal, because the court can order the proceedings to carry on as if they had begun the other way. But it wastes time and it costs money.

body.title: Which mode, and why it is not a matter of taste
body.caption: Choosing wrongly is rarely fatal: the court can order the action to continue as if it had begun the other way. But it costs time the choice never needed to cost.
body.alt: A question — is the real dispute about the facts? — branching two ways. Yes: issue a writ, where evidence is given aloud and tested by cross-examination. No, it is a question of law on undisputed facts or about the meaning of a document: an originating summons, decided on affidavit.
body.question: Is the real dispute about the facts?

sections.keypoint: Plead material facts, not the evidence and not the law.

body.text: **Pleadings** are the documents setting out each side's case in material facts. They are what define the issues the trial will be about.
The statement of claim sets out the material facts the plaintiff relies on. The defence answers them, and a reply may follow after that.
Plead material facts, not evidence and not law. A pleading states what happened, in the facts that give rise to the right claimed.
Put simply: say what happened. Do not say how you will prove it, and do not argue the law.
Two consequences follow, and both of them bite. A party is bound by their pleadings, and cannot run a case at trial that was never pleaded.
And an allegation that is not answered in the defence is generally taken as admitted. So a bare denial of everything is not a defence, and a silence is an admission.

Some matters must be pleaded specifically and with particulars: fraud, misrepresentation, breach of trust, and anything else that would take the other side by surprise. Pleading fraud without particulars is worse than not pleading it at all.

sections.keypoint: Default judgment, summary judgment, striking out and discovery are where most cases actually end.

items: Judgment in default, where the defendant fails to enter an appearance or to serve a defence in time.
Summary judgment, where there is no defence with a real prospect of success and no other reason for a trial.
Striking out, where a pleading discloses no reasonable cause of action or defence, is scandalous or vexatious, or is an abuse of process.
Discovery, where each side must disclose the documents relevant to the matters in question, including the documents that hurt them.

body.text: Summary judgment and striking out decide the most cases, and the threshold for both of them is deliberately high. The court is taking a trial away from a party, so the applicant must show the case is clear, and any genuinely triable issue defeats the application.

Do not confuse the two. Striking out attacks the pleading as a document: assume every pleaded fact is true, and ask whether together they disclose a case. Summary judgment looks at the evidence and asks whether the defence is real.

Rahim's claim is properly pleaded, so an application to strike it out would fail. But if the only answer to it is a bare denial, with no invoice, no witness and no explanation, summary judgment may well succeed.

body.q: A statement of claim is carefully drafted, but even if every word of it were true it would still not be a claim the law recognises. Which application fits?
options: Striking out — the pleading discloses no reasonable cause of action
Summary judgment — there is no defence with a real prospect of success
Judgment in default — the claim is a bad one
body.why: Striking out attacks the pleading as a document. You assume every pleaded fact is true and ask whether together they add up to a case, which is exactly what fails here. Summary judgment looks at the evidence, and the evidence is not the problem. Default judgment has nothing to do with the merits at all. It is for a defendant who missed a deadline.

sections.keypoint: A judgment is a piece of paper; enforcement is a separate exercise.
sections.h: Winning is not the same as being paid

body.text: A judgment is a piece of paper rather than money. Enforcement is a separate exercise with procedures of its own.

They include execution against goods, garnishment of debts owed to the judgment debtor, charging orders over land, and winding up or bankruptcy where those fit. **Garnishment** means intercepting money that somebody else owes to the debtor.
Telling a client that they have won is incomplete advice if the defendant has nothing to take.
Appeals run up through the hierarchy under the Courts of Judicature Act 1964, with leave required at certain stages. The time limits for appealing are short and they are applied strictly.

sections.keypoint: Take a simple set of facts and write out the sequence from letter to payment.

body.text: There are no flashcards or problems for this module yet. The exercise that teaches it fastest is to take a simple set of facts and write out the sequence.
Limitation, then mode of commencement, then the pleading, then the application the other side would make, and finally what you would need to defeat it.

lessons.title: Judicial review: the grounds, and how far a court may go
lessons.summary: Illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety — and the Malaysian decision that let courts look at the substance of a decision, not only the process.

sections.keypoint: Eleven years of a licence, cancelled by letter with no reason given.

body.text: Puan Latifah has sold nasi lemak from the same stall for eleven years. One morning the council cancels her licence by letter. It gives no reason, and nobody asked her for her side of it.
The Act that set up the council gives her no appeal. What she can do instead is ask the High Court to look at how the decision was made. That is **judicial review**.

body.prompt: Puan Latifah asks the High Court to look at the council's decision. Before you read on — what will the court be deciding?
options: Whether cancelling her licence was the right thing to do
Whether the decision was lawfully made, including whether she was heard
Whether the council should be running a licensing system at all
body.reveal: How the decision was made. The first answer is the question Latifah actually wants answered, and it is the one a court on review traditionally refuses. The power to decide about licences was given to the council and not to a judge. Later in this lesson you will meet a Malaysian case that pushes hard on that line.

sections.keypoint: Review needs leave and an applicant adversely affected, and it examines the process rather than the merits.

body.text: Judicial review is the supervising power of the High Court over the exercise of public power. It is not an appeal, and that difference is the first thing to fix in your mind.
On an appeal the question is whether the decision was right. On review the traditional question is whether the decision was lawfully made.
So the court asks how the council reached its decision. It does not ask whether cancelling Latifah's licence was a good idea.
Review runs against public bodies exercising public functions. The remedies are the old prerogative orders, along with declarations and injunctions.

items: **Certiorari** — an order quashing a decision, which wipes it out as if it had never been made.
**Prohibition** — an order forbidding a body from doing something it is about to do.
**Mandamus** — an order compelling a public body to perform a public duty.
An **injunction** is a court order to stop doing something, and a **declaration** is the court stating what the legal position is.

body.text: Judicial review is commenced by an application for leave, and an applicant must be adversely affected by the decision complained of.
Put simply: you need the court's permission to bring the claim at all, and you have to show that the decision actually affected you.
The standing requirement was for many years read narrowly, and later authority has tended to relax it. Check the current position rather than assuming either extreme.

body.title: The route an application actually takes
body.caption: Leave comes first, and it is where applications stop most often. A good ground with no standing behind it never reaches a judge who can rule on it.
body.alt: Four steps. Apply for leave, which is permission to bring the claim at all. Show you are adversely affected: standing, long read narrowly and since relaxed. Establish one of the three grounds — illegality, irrationality, procedural impropriety. Then ask for a remedy, such as certiorari, mandamus or a declaration.

steps.label: Leave
steps.note: permission to bring the claim at all

steps.label: Adversely affected
steps.note: standing; long read narrowly, since relaxed

sections.keypoint: Illegality, irrationality, procedural impropriety — with proportionality argued as a fourth.

body.text: There is a standard way of sorting the grounds, which the Malaysian courts use, and it comes from the GCHQ case. It is the frame for almost every answer.
Illegality, irrationality, and procedural impropriety.
body.source: Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister for the Civil Service [1985] AC 374 (GCHQ)

items: **Illegality** — the decision-maker got the law wrong, went beyond its powers, or used a power for an improper purpose. It also covers taking irrelevant things into account, ignoring relevant ones, or tying its own hands in advance.
**Irrationality** — the decision is so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have reached it. That is the Wednesbury standard, and it is deliberately demanding.
**Procedural impropriety** — the body failed to follow the procedure laid down, or broke the rules of natural justice.

body.text: Going beyond your powers has a Latin name that gets used constantly. **Ultra vires** means beyond the powers, and therefore invalid.
**Natural justice** is two rules. *Audi alteram partem* means hear the other side. *Nemo judex in causa sua* means that nobody may be a judge in his own cause.
The test for bias is generally an objective one. It asks how the situation would look to a fair-minded observer, rather than demanding proof that the decision-maker was actually partial.

Latifah was never asked for her side, so the first rule of natural justice was broken. And if the councillor who voted to cancel her licence has a cousin applying for that same pitch, the second rule is in play too.

**Legitimate expectation** sits alongside these three grounds. It arises where a public body has promised a benefit or a procedure, or has consistently followed a settled practice. The person may then be entitled to expect it to carry on, or at least to be heard before it is taken away.

body.q: The council adopts a blanket policy of never renewing a licence for a stall older than ten years. It hears each stall holder, then applies the policy anyway. Which ground fits best?
options: Irrationality — no reasonable council would adopt such a policy
Illegality — the council has tied its own hands in advance
Procedural impropriety — the stall holders were not heard
body.why: A body given a discretion has to keep it. Settling the answer in advance and refusing to exercise the power is a form of illegality. The second answer is the reflex to watch. Irrationality gets reached for whenever a decision looks unfair, and the Wednesbury standard is set far higher than that. The third is ruled out on the facts, because the council did hear them.

sections.keypoint: Rama Chandran let a court reach the substance and substitute its own decision in an appropriate case.
sections.h: How far the court may go

body.text: This is the question on which Malaysian administrative law departs from the orthodox English position. If you take one thing away from this module, take this.
The traditional view confines review to the decision-making process. The court quashes an unlawful decision and sends it back to be taken again.
It does not put its own view of the merits in place of the decision-maker's, because the power was given to that body and not to a judge.

R Rama Chandran: on judicial review the court may in appropriate cases examine the substance or merits of a decision, and may grant relief that includes substituting its own decision rather than merely quashing and remitting.
body.source: R Rama Chandran v The Industrial Court of Malaysia [1997] 1 MLJ 145 (FC)

body.text: Put simply: in an appropriate case a Malaysian court may look at whether the decision itself was right, and may substitute its own decision instead of sending the matter back.
The reasoning is practical as well as doctrinal. Sending a matter back to a tribunal that has already made up its mind can leave a successful applicant with nothing except delay.
The decision has been applied, qualified and debated ever since, and the boundaries of when substitution is appropriate are not fixed.

body.title: How far a court will go, and where Malaysia sits
body.caption: Rama Chandran moved Malaysian law along this line without carrying it to the end. Citing it for the proposition that review has become an appeal overstates it, and later authority has been careful about the limits.
body.alt: A scale running from asking only how a decision was made to asking whether it was right. Orthodox review sits near the process end. Rama Chandran sits past the middle: in an appropriate case the court may examine substance and grant substituted relief. A full appeal sits at the far end, and review has not become one.

marks.label: appeal — what review is still not

body.text: Do not overstate it. Rama Chandran did not turn judicial review into an appeal, and later authority has been careful about its limits. Cite it for the proposition that merits review is available in appropriate cases, and then argue whether this is such a case.

sections.keypoint: An ouster clause cannot shut the court out entirely, because review is inherent in the civil courts.
sections.h: Clauses that try to shut the court out

body.text: Legislation sometimes says that a decision shall be final, or shall not be questioned in any court. A provision like that is called an **ouster clause**.

Whether one defeats review is an old question with a settled direction of travel. The courts read ouster clauses narrowly, and a decision made outside jurisdiction is treated as no decision at all, so there is nothing left for the clause to protect.

In Malaysia this connects to the constitutional material in the legal system module. Two Federal Court decisions matter here. The first is *Semenyih Jaya Sdn Bhd v Pentadbir Tanah Daerah Hulu Langat* [2017] 3 MLJ 561. It treats judicial power and judicial review as part of the **basic structure** of the Constitution, and *Indira Gandhi* followed it.
Judicial review of administrative action is inherent in the civil courts and forms part of the basic structure of the Constitution.
body.source: Indira Gandhi a/p Mutho v Pengarah Jabatan Agama Islam Perak [2018] 1 MLJ 545 (FC)

body.text: Put simply: the courts' power to check how public decisions are made is built into the Constitution. A clause in an ordinary Act cannot simply take it away.

lessons.title: How legal reasoning is actually done
lessons.summary: Rules and standards, reasoning by analogy, and why the answer is often genuinely open without being arbitrary.

sections.keypoint: Two competent lawyers read the same section and the same cases and disagree. Why that is not a scandal.

body.text: Two lawyers read the same section and the same three cases, and they reach opposite conclusions. Neither of them is lying, and neither of them is incompetent. So how can that happen?
Everything in this course up to this point has taught you rules. This module asks a different question: what kind of thinking is legal reasoning, and why does it produce so much honest disagreement?

The answer is that the materials leave the outcome genuinely open far more often than a textbook's confident prose suggests. Knowing where that happens is what separates an argument from a recitation.

sections.keypoint: Rules buy predictability and misfire on the odd case; standards fit every case and predict none.

body.text: Legal directives come in two shapes, and choosing between them is a real design decision with costs on both sides.

items: A **rule** fixes its trigger in advance: drive no faster than 90 km/h. It is predictable and cheap to apply, and it will sometimes give a result nobody wanted — the ambulance, or the empty road at three in the morning.
A **standard** states the goal and leaves the application open: drive at a speed that is reasonable for the conditions. It fits every case, and tells you nothing at all until a court has ruled.

body.text: Rules buy predictability at the cost of occasionally getting the individual case wrong. Standards buy accuracy in the individual case at the cost of predictability.
Put simply: a rule is easy to obey and occasionally unfair. A standard is fair in principle and very hard to plan around.
Noticing which of the two you are dealing with tells you what kind of argument is going to work.
Against a rule you argue that the trigger is not satisfied, or that this is not a case the rule was ever meant to reach. Against a standard you argue the factors instead.

Section 300(c) of the Penal Code is close to a rule: did you intend the injury, and would an injury like that normally kill? The reasonable person test in negligence is a standard rather than a rule. The argument that works against each of them is a different shape.

body.title: Two shapes, and the argument each one invites

left.h: Rule — the trigger is fixed in advance
items: Predictable, and cheap to apply.
Occasionally gets the individual case wrong.
Easy to obey, and easy to plan around.
**To argue against it:** the trigger is not satisfied, or this is not a case the rule was ever meant to reach.

right.h: Standard — the goal is stated, the application left open
items: Accurate in the individual case.
Very hard to plan around in advance.
Fair in principle, and expensive to apply.
**To argue against it:** the facts do not meet the goal the standard states, or the considerations point the other way.

sections.keypoint: Analogy is not mechanical: two cases are never identical, so the work is deciding which differences matter.

body.text: Precedent works by analogy, and analogy is not a mechanical operation at all. Two cases are never quite identical to each other.
So the question is always whether they are alike in the respects that matter. And what matters is decided by the rule you take the earlier case to stand for.
That is why the argument about how generally a **ratio** is stated is not a technicality. The ratio decidendi is the rule a decision actually rests on, and it is the binding part.

body.prompt: A decided case holds that a landlord owed his tenant a duty to repair a broken stair. This year a visitor to the same house falls on that stair. Before you read on — does the earlier case govern it?
options: Yes — the danger is identical, and so is the stair
It depends on how broadly the earlier case's rule is stated
No — that case was about tenants, and a visitor is not a tenant
body.reveal: The middle one. The other two are the arguments each side is going to run, and both can be taken honestly out of the same judgment. Read the earlier case as a rule about landlords and tenants, and it does not reach the visitor. Read it as a rule about anyone in control of a dangerous stair, and it does. Nothing in the judgment settles which reading is the right one.

body.text: State it narrowly and the earlier case can be distinguished away. State it broadly and the earlier case governs this one. Both statements can be defended honestly from the very same judgment.

A case holds that a bus company owed a duty to a passenger hurt by a sudden stop. Read narrowly, it is a case about buses and their passengers. Read broadly, it is about anybody in charge of a vehicle and anybody riding in one. Which side wants which reading depends entirely on the next set of facts.

This is not a licence to say that precedent means whatever you want. The range of defensible statements is real but bounded, and an argument outside it will simply lose. The skill lies in knowing where those edges actually are.

sections.keypoint: Words have a settled core and a doubtful edge, and litigated cases come from the edge.

body.text: Rules are made of words, and words have a settled core and an uncertain edge.
Hart's example is a by-law prohibiting vehicles in a public park. A car is plainly caught by it, and a bicycle is arguable. A war memorial tank on a plinth is the sort of case that makes the point.
Legal language has a core of settled meaning and a penumbra of doubt. Most cases are decided in the core and never litigated; the cases you read are disproportionately from the penumbra.
body.source: Hart, on the open texture of legal language

body.text: Put simply: most of the time everybody agrees what a word covers. The cases that reach a courtroom are the ones sitting out on the fuzzy edge.
This explains something about your reading that is otherwise quite disorienting. The law reports contain the hard cases, because the easy ones settle or never start at all.
So reading only reported cases gives a systematically distorted impression of how uncertain the law really is.

body.q: Why do the cases in the law reports make the law look less settled than it really is?
options: Because judges disagree with one another more than they used to
Because the cases that reach a court are the ones out on the fuzzy edge
Because the reports leave out the reasoning that made each case easy
body.why: Most words have a settled core, and disputes in the core get obeyed, settled or never brought at all. What is litigated and reported comes from the penumbra. The trap is to treat your reading list as a fair sample of the law, and then conclude that everything is arguable. Most of it is not.

sections.keypoint: Formalism and realism are worth being able to state, because most arguments reduce to one of them.

body.text: Two positions are worth being able to state, because arguments about how judges decide usually reduce to a version of one or the other.
**Formalism** holds that legal outcomes follow from the legal materials themselves. The rules, applied to the facts, give the answer, and the judge's job is to find it.
**Realism** holds that outcomes are substantially driven by other things, and that the legal reasoning is a justification constructed afterwards.
Neither of those extremes survives contact with practice. Most cases really are determined by the materials, but some really are not, and in those the judge is choosing.
The useful question is not which of the two camps is right. It is which kind of case you are in, because that decides whether your best argument is doctrinal or consequential.
Do not deploy realism as a way of avoiding doctrine. An answer that says the judge will decide as they please is not a legal argument, and it is wrong about the great majority of cases.

sections.keypoint: Take a case you have briefed and write its ratio twice, at two levels of generality.

body.text: There are no flashcards or problems for this module yet. The exercise that pays here is to take a case you have already briefed and write its ratio twice.
Write it once as narrowly as the judgment honestly allows, and once as broadly as it allows. Then say which side would argue for which version, and why. That is the whole module on a single page.

lessons.title: Reading a statute
lessons.summary: Malaysia has made the purposive approach statutory, and that changes what the traditional rules of interpretation are for.

sections.keypoint: No vehicle may enter the park. A father wheels in a child's scooter. Has he broken it?
sections.h: What does the word mean here?

body.text: A by-law says that no vehicle may enter the park. A father wheels his three-year-old in on a scooter. Has he broken it?
Working out what a written law means is a job with rules of its own. In Malaysia those rules start in a place that will surprise you if you have read an English textbook first.

sections.keypoint: Section 17A directs the purposive approach and is where Malaysian interpretation starts.
sections.h: The provision that changes the subject

body.text: Most treatments of statutory interpretation begin with three common law rules — literal, golden and mischief — and work towards the purposive approach as a modern development.

body.prompt: A Malaysian judge has a section that the words allow to be read two ways. Before you read on — where does the law tell her to begin?
options: With the ordinary meaning of the words, moving on only if that fails
With the purpose the Act was passed to serve
With whichever of the old common law rules gives the fairer result
body.reveal: With the purpose, and not because a judge chose to work that way. If you picked the first, that is the order almost every textbook teaches, and it is the order that makes English cases readable. Malaysia wrote its answer into an Act instead. The third answer is the one to let go of altogether. The old rules were never a menu to pick from.

body.text: In Malaysia that ordering is misleading. The purposive approach here is not a judicial preference that grew over time. It is enacted.

In the interpretation of a provision of an Act, a construction that would promote the purpose or object underlying the Act shall be preferred to a construction that would not promote that purpose or object.
Put simply: where a section can be read in two ways, prefer the reading that helps the Act do what it was passed to do.
Read the words of the section again: *shall be preferred*. That is a direction to the court, not one option among several approaches.
So an answer that works through the three common law rules and arrives at purposive construction as a possible modern alternative has the structure backwards.
This is the single most common error in this module, and it comes straight from using English or older textbooks. Start from section 17A.

body.title: The order construction actually goes in

items.text: Including any proviso, the definitions section, and the sub-sections that qualify the one you came for.

items.h: Establish that the words can bear two readings.
items.text: This is the step that makes s 17A applicable at all. Where the language admits one meaning only, purpose does not displace it.
The long title, the preamble where there is one, the mischief the Act addressed.

items.h: Prefer the reading that promotes it.

items.text: Against retrospectivity, in favour of mens rea, against ousting the courts, and strict construction of a penal provision.

sections.keypoint: The literal, golden and mischief rules are moves inside that framework, not rivals to it.
sections.h: What the older rules are still for

body.text: They are not obsolete. They describe recurring moves inside a purposive framework, rather than rival methods competing for the same job.

items: The **literal rule** — give the words their ordinary meaning. Still the starting point, because purpose does not licence ignoring the text, and a reading the words cannot bear is not available however desirable it looks.

The **golden rule** — depart from the literal meaning where it produces an absurdity. Now largely absorbed, since an absurd result is strong evidence that a reading does not promote the Act's purpose.

The **mischief rule** — ask what defect in the earlier law the Act was passed to cure. This is the closest ancestor of section 17A, and still a good way to find the purpose the section directs you to serve.

body.text: So a good answer moves in three steps. What do the words naturally mean, what is the purpose of the Act, and does the natural meaning promote that purpose?
Where the answer to that last question is no, section 17A tells you which reading to prefer.

Go back to the by-law about the park. The mischief was noise, fumes and danger from traffic, and a three-year-old's scooter causes none of them. The purposive reading keeps the father out of trouble, even though a scooter is arguably a vehicle.

sections.keypoint: The Interpretation Acts supply general aids — singular includes plural, unless a contrary intention appears.

body.text: **Internal aids** are parts of the Act itself. They include the long title, the preamble where there is one, headings, marginal notes, the interpretation section, provisos, explanations and schedules.
A **proviso** is a qualification attached to the provision it sits under, and it usually begins with the words *provided that*.
The interpretation section is the one people skip and should not. A defined term means exactly what the Act says it means, whatever it might mean anywhere else.
**External aids** sit outside the Act: dictionaries, earlier legislation on the same subject, international conventions the Act implements, and parliamentary material.
The use of Hansard, which is the record of what was said in Parliament, is the contested one. Check the current Malaysian position rather than assuming that the English rule applies here.
Words in the singular include the plural and words in the plural include the singular, unless a contrary intention appears.
Put simply: an Act that says “parent” usually covers “parents” as well, unless it plainly means otherwise.

That looks trivial and is not. Applied to the word *parent* in Article 12(4), it is the provision that decided the conversion question in Indira Gandhi. A rule of interpretation carried a constitutional case.

sections.keypoint: Presumptions are defaults the legislature is taken to have intended until it says otherwise.

body.text: A **presumption** is a default position that the legislature is taken to have intended, unless it says otherwise.

items: Against retrospective operation, particularly for provisions affecting substantive rights.
Against ousting the jurisdiction of the courts.
In favour of a mental element in a criminal offence, so that strict liability is not lightly inferred.
That penal provisions are construed strictly, with any ambiguity resolved in favour of the accused.

body.text: The linguistic canons are narrower tools, and they carry Latin names.

items: *Ejusdem generis* — general words following a list of specific items are read as limited to the same class.
*Noscitur a sociis* — a word takes its colour from the words around it.
*Expressio unius est exclusio alterius* — expressing one thing implies the exclusion of others. This is the weakest of the three, and the easiest to over-apply.

body.text: A provision applying to “cars, vans, lorries and other vehicles” will probably not reach a bicycle under ejusdem generis. The specific items share a class, and the general words are read within it.

body.q: A new Act creates an offence and says nothing at all about intention. What does a court presume?
options: That no intention is needed, since the section does not ask for one
That the section is too uncertain to be enforced
That a mental element is required, unless the Act shows otherwise
body.why: Strict liability is not lightly inferred, so silence leaves the ordinary requirement standing. The first answer reads silence as abolition, which is the usual mistake and an expensive one for whoever is charged. The third is not a presumption at all. An unclear penal provision is construed strictly in the accused's favour, not struck out.

sections.keypoint: A constitution is read more generously than an ordinary statute, and not by the same rules.

body.text: A constitution is not an ordinary statute and it is not read like one.

The Malaysian courts have said repeatedly that fundamental liberties are to be construed generously, and not with the narrowness that suits a penal provision. A constitution is read as a living document rather than as a conveyance of land.
The Eleventh Schedule applies certain provisions of the Interpretation Acts to the Constitution, and that is how the singular-includes-plural rule reached Article 12(4).
The interpretive posture is still different. Importing the strict approach that suits a taxing statute into Part II is an error.

sections.keypoint: Read section 17A itself. It is one sentence long.

body.text: There are no flashcards or problems for this module yet. Read section 17A itself, which is one sentence long.
Then take any section you have already worked with and build the argument both ways: the literal reading, the purposive reading, and which one section 17A directs you to prefer.

lessons.title: When someone else pays: vicarious liability
lessons.summary: An employer can be liable for a wrong they did not commit, forbade, and knew nothing about. The doctrine is strict, and the argument is about its limits.

sections.keypoint: Vicarious liability makes one person answer for another's tort without any wrongdoing of their own.

body.text: Almost everything else in tort asks what the defendant did wrong. This does not.
An employer may be liable for an employee's tort even though the employer was careful, gave clear instructions, and forbade the very thing that happened.
That is not a loophole. It is the doctrine working as intended, and the first thing to be clear about is that no fault of the employer is required.
So an answer arguing that the employer took every precaution has argued the wrong point. Precautions matter to primary liability in negligence, not to this.

sections.keypoint: The employer sets the enterprise in motion, profits from it, and can insure and spread the loss.

body.text: It is worth being able to say why, because the reasons decide the hard cases at the edges.
The enterprise creates the risk. The employer directs the activity and takes the profit from it.
And there is a blunt practical reason: an injured claimant recovers nothing from an employee with no money, and the employer can insure and price the risk.

body.prompt: Is vicarious liability best justified by fault, by risk-creation, or by who can pay?
options: Fault — the employer chose the employee
Risk-creation and loss-spreading, with the ability to pay as a practical reinforcement
body.reveal: Choosing the employee is a fault-based idea, and it cannot explain liability for a wrong the employer expressly prohibited. The enterprise account can: the employer created the situation in which the wrong became possible. Which justification you accept changes how widely you would extend the doctrine.

sections.keypoint: First, is the relationship one that attracts the doctrine; second, was the wrong closely enough connected to it.

body.text: The analysis has two stages and they must be taken in order.
Stage one is the relationship. Employment is the paradigm, and the employee or independent contractor distinction does most of the work here.
Stage two is connection. Not every wrong an employee commits is the employer's problem; the wrong has to be sufficiently connected to what they were employed to do.

items: Was the act a wrongful way of doing something authorised, or something wholly outside the job?
Did the employment create the opportunity, or merely the occasion?
Was the employee pursuing the employer's business at all?

body.text: Stage two is where the modern arguments are. Doing an authorised task badly is the easy case; deliberate wrongdoing is not.

sections.h: The frolic, and the deliberate wrong
sections.keypoint: An employee on a personal detour may take themselves outside the doctrine, but deliberate wrongdoing does not automatically do so.

body.text: Two edges are worth knowing because problems are built on them.
The first is the personal detour. An employee who abandons the job for their own purposes may put themselves outside it, and the question is one of degree rather than a bright line.

The second is deliberate wrongdoing. It is tempting to say an intentional wrong can never be part of the job. That is too quick: the doctrine can reach a deliberate act where the employment created more than a mere opportunity for it.

body.q: An employee deliberately assaults a customer during a dispute about the employer's business. Is the employer automatically outside the doctrine?
options: No — deliberateness does not end the question; the connection to the employment still has to be assessed
Yes — a deliberate crime cannot be in the course of employment
body.why: Treating intention as automatically decisive would make the doctrine easy to escape and would not match how the connection question is asked. The analysis is about the closeness of the tie to the employment, not about the employee's state of mind.

quiz.q: What must a claimant show at the first stage of a vicarious liability claim?
options: That the relationship between wrongdoer and defendant is one the doctrine attaches to
That the employer was careless in supervising
That the employee cannot pay
That the employer authorised the wrong
quiz.why: Stage one is about the relationship. Carelessness in supervision is a primary negligence claim against the employer, which is a different action with a different test.

quiz.q: Why does the enterprise justification explain the doctrine better than a fault-based one?
options: Because employers are usually insured
Because liability arises even where the employer expressly prohibited the act
Because employees are rarely careless
Because it is easier to prove
quiz.why: A fault account cannot explain liability for something the employer forbade. The risk-creation account can, because the employer set up the activity in which the wrong became possible.

lessons.title: Living next to someone: nuisance
lessons.summary: Negligence asks whether the defendant took care. Nuisance asks whether what the claimant is putting up with is unreasonable. That is a different question with a different answer.

sections.keypoint: Nuisance protects the use and enjoyment of land, which is why the claimant's connection to the land matters.

body.text: Nuisance is not a tort about carelessness. It is a tort about land.
What it protects is the use and enjoyment of land, which is why the first question is what interest the claimant has in the land affected.
Someone with no interest in the land may be genuinely inconvenienced and still have no claim in private nuisance.
This catches people out constantly. The instinct is that anyone harmed should be able to sue, and this tort is not built that way.

sections.keypoint: The test is whether the interference is unreasonable, judged by locality, duration, intensity and any malice.

body.text: Every neighbour is occasionally irritating. The tort catches interference that goes beyond what one must put up with.
Reasonableness here is assessed by the circumstances, and the factors recur.

items: Locality — what is normal for this kind of area
Duration and frequency — a one-off event is rarely enough
Intensity — how bad, at what times
Any malice — deliberate interference is harder to justify
Whether the claimant is unusually sensitive

body.text: Note what is missing from that list. The defendant's care is not on it. A carefully run activity can still be a nuisance.

body.prompt: A factory operates to the highest standards and still makes its residential neighbours' lives difficult. Is that a defence?
options: Yes — the defendant took all reasonable care
No — the question is the effect on the claimant, not the defendant's diligence
body.reveal: This is the sharpest difference between nuisance and negligence, and it is where a candidate who has only learned negligence goes wrong. Care answers a question nuisance does not ask.

sections.h: Public nuisance is a different thing
sections.keypoint: Public nuisance affects a class of the public, and a private claimant must show damage over and above the rest.

body.text: The name suggests a bigger version of the same tort. It is not.
Public nuisance concerns interference affecting a class of the public rather than one occupier's land.
An individual suing on it must show they suffered damage beyond that suffered by the public generally. Without that, the complaint is a public matter rather than their action.

body.q: A road is blocked, inconveniencing a whole neighbourhood including your client. Can your client sue in public nuisance?
options: Yes — they were inconvenienced
Only if they can show damage over and above what the public generally suffered
body.why: Shared inconvenience is what makes it public. The special damage requirement is what separates an individual's action from a matter for public enforcement.

sections.h: Remedies, and what a claimant actually wants
sections.keypoint: Damages compensate for what has happened; an injunction is usually what stops it, and it is discretionary.

body.text: Ask what the client wants. Usually it is not money.
Damages address past interference. They do nothing about tomorrow.
An injunction is the remedy that changes the position, and because it is equitable it is discretionary — conduct, delay and proportionality all bear on it.
So a nuisance advice that establishes liability and stops has answered half the question.

quiz.q: Why is the defendant's care not a defence to private nuisance?
options: Because the tort asks whether the interference with the claimant's land is unreasonable, not whether the defendant was careful
Because nuisance is a criminal offence
Because care is presumed
Because only intentional acts are actionable
quiz.why: Nuisance and negligence protect different things and ask different questions. An impeccably run operation can still impose an unreasonable interference on a neighbour.

quiz.q: What must an individual show to sue in public nuisance?
options: That they suffered damage over and above the public generally
That they own affected land
That the defendant acted maliciously
That an injunction is available
quiz.why: Special damage is what converts a public matter into an individual's cause of action. Sharing the general inconvenience is not enough.

lessons.title: Dangerous premises, and who answers for them
lessons.summary: Someone is hurt on land. The question is not who owns it but who controlled it, and what they owed to the person who came on.

sections.keypoint: The duty attaches to whoever has sufficient control of the premises, which need not be the owner.

body.text: Start with the wrong question and the whole analysis goes wrong. It is not who owns the land.
The duty attaches to the occupier, and occupation is a matter of control over the premises.
A tenant may be the occupier. So may a contractor in possession of a site. There can be more than one occupier at once.
A landlord who has let premises and retained no control may not be the occupier of them, while the tenant running a business there is.

sections.h: What is owed, and to whom
sections.keypoint: The duty is to take reasonable care that a visitor is reasonably safe for the purpose they were invited for.

body.text: The duty is a duty of reasonable care, not a guarantee of safety.
And it is tied to purpose. A visitor is owed safety for the purpose for which they were permitted to be there, not for whatever they choose to do.
Someone who enters without permission is in a different category, and what is owed to them is less. That category still attracts some duty; it is not a licence to injure.

body.prompt: A shop customer wanders into a plainly marked staff-only area and is hurt. Does the shop owe them the visitor duty there?
options: Not for that area — permission defines where and for what purpose they were a visitor
Yes — they were lawfully in the shop
body.reveal: Permission has boundaries in space and in purpose. Exceeding them can change a person's category, which changes what is owed. The marking matters because it is what fixes the boundary.

sections.keypoint: A warning helps only if it actually enables safety; children and independent contractors are treated separately.

body.text: Three qualifications do most of the work in problems.
A warning does not automatically discharge the duty. The question is whether it was enough to enable the visitor to be reasonably safe.
Children are owed more, because what is obvious to an adult may not be to them, and an allurement may draw them in.
Where the danger was created by an independent contractor's work, the occupier's position depends on whether it was reasonable to entrust the work and to check it.

sections.h: Where this sits in the corpus
sections.keypoint: This topic has been taught inside a property lesson, which is the wrong module for a tort duty.

body.text: Until now this material appeared only inside a land ownership lesson.
That is the wrong home. The question is a tort duty owed to an entrant, not an incident of title, and a reader looking for it in tort found nothing.

body.q: Your client was hurt on premises. What is the first thing to establish?
options: Who had sufficient control of the premises at the time
Who owns the land
body.why: Ownership and occupation come apart routinely, and suing the owner of premises they had let and did not control is a claim against the wrong defendant.

quiz.q: Who owes the occupier's duty?
options: The registered owner
The insurer
The person who built the premises
Whoever has sufficient control of the premises
quiz.why: Control is the test, and it can rest with a tenant or a contractor in possession. There may also be more than one occupier at the same time.

quiz.q: Does a warning notice discharge the occupier's duty?
options: Always, if it is visible
Never
Only if it was enough to enable the visitor to be reasonably safe
Only for adults
quiz.why: The duty is to make the visitor reasonably safe. A warning that does not achieve that has not discharged it, which is why the content and placement of the notice matter.

lessons.title: Dangerous things that escape
lessons.summary: A rule that makes a defendant liable for damage caused by something they brought onto land, without proof of negligence. Its conditions are narrow and its survival is contested.

sections.keypoint: The rule imposes liability for damage from an escape without requiring proof that the defendant was careless.

body.text: This rule exists because negligence sometimes cannot reach an obvious injustice.

Someone brings something dangerous onto their land. It escapes. It causes damage. Proving carelessness may be impossible, because the claimant has no idea what happened inside the defendant's operation.
The rule answers that by making the defendant liable for the escape itself, on stated conditions.
Strict does not mean absolute. There are conditions to satisfy and defences available, and most claims fail on the conditions rather than on the defences.

sections.h: The conditions, each a place to fail
sections.keypoint: Bringing and accumulating, a non-natural use, an escape, and damage of a foreseeable kind.

body.text: Take the conditions one at a time, because a claim can die at any of them.

items: The defendant brought the thing onto the land and accumulated it there
The use of the land was non-natural, in the sense of special rather than ordinary
The thing escaped from the defendant's land
Damage of a foreseeable kind resulted

body.text: The first condition excludes things naturally present. The second is the one that swallows most claims, and its meaning has narrowed over time.
The third requires an actual escape. Damage confined to the defendant's own land is not within the rule.

body.prompt: Water accumulates naturally on the defendant's land and flows onto the claimant's. Does the rule apply?
options: Yes — water escaped and caused damage
No — nothing was brought and accumulated, so the first condition fails
body.reveal: The rule is about things a defendant chose to bring and keep. Naturally occurring accumulation is outside it, which is why the first condition is worth stating explicitly rather than assuming.

sections.h: How much of it is left
sections.keypoint: As negligence and nuisance expanded, the rule's practical scope narrowed, and its independence is argued about.

body.text: This is where the topic becomes interesting rather than merely technical.
When the rule was formulated, negligence was undeveloped. It has since grown enormously, and so has nuisance.
So one view treats the rule as a species of nuisance dealing with isolated escapes. Another treats it as a distinct principle that still has work to do.

body.q: Why does it matter whether the rule is independent or a branch of nuisance?
options: Because the requirements differ, including whose interest in land is protected and what must be proved
It does not — the outcome is the same
body.why: If it is a branch of nuisance, nuisance's requirements come with it — including who may sue. Classification here decides what a claimant has to establish.

sections.keypoint: Received doctrine applies here subject to local circumstances, which is a live qualification for a rule about land use.

body.text: This rule comes into Malaysian law as received doctrine, and the reception provision carries a qualification about local circumstances.
That qualification is not decoration. A rule about what counts as a non-natural use of land is exactly the kind that might be applied differently in a different setting.
So an answer should reach the reception point rather than assume the English position transplants whole.

quiz.q: Which condition most often defeats a claim under the rule?
options: That the use of land was non-natural
That there was an escape
That damage occurred
That the defendant owned the land
quiz.why: The non-natural use requirement has narrowed over time and is where most claims fail. Ordinary use of land, however capable of causing harm, falls outside the rule.

quiz.q: Why does 'strict' not mean 'absolute' here?
options: Because damages are capped
Because it only applies to water
Because conditions must still be satisfied and defences remain available
Because negligence must still be proved
quiz.why: Strictness removes the need to prove carelessness. It does not remove the conditions of the rule, and those conditions are where the argument usually is.

lessons.title: Offences against the person short of death
lessons.summary: The Penal Code grades harm rather than treating all injury alike. The grading decides the offence, and the offence decides almost everything else.

sections.keypoint: The Code sorts injury by seriousness, so identifying the grade is the first analytical step.

body.text: The homicide lesson showed a structure: a wide category, a narrower one inside it, exceptions pushing a case back down.
Offences short of death are organised on a similar principle. Harm is graded, and the grade you are on decides which offence is charged.
So the first question is not whether the accused did something wrong. It is how serious the harm was, in the Code's own terms.
The Code's categories are defined terms, not ordinary English. A word like hurt has a definition in the statute, and reasoning from the everyday meaning will put you on the wrong rung.

sections.keypoint: Offences are aggravated by the means used, the intention behind them, and the circumstances of the act.

body.text: Above the base grade the Code adds aggravating features, and they are worth knowing as categories.

items: The seriousness of the injury itself
The means used — whether a weapon or dangerous instrument was involved
The intention or knowledge with which it was done
The circumstances, including who the victim was and why

body.text: Each feature typically has its own provision, so an accurate answer names the offence that matches the features present rather than the most serious one available.

body.prompt: Two accused cause identical injuries; one used a weapon. Same offence?
options: Yes — the harm is what matters
No — the means used is a separate aggravating feature with its own provision
body.reveal: Grading by outcome alone would make the Code much shorter and much blunter. The separate provisions exist precisely so that identical harm caused in different ways can be charged differently.

sections.h: The mental element still has to be found
sections.keypoint: Serious injury does not by itself establish the intention or knowledge the offence requires.

body.text: It is tempting to reason backwards from a bad injury to a guilty mind. The Code does not permit it.
Each offence states its own mental element, and it has to be established on the evidence like anything else.
So an answer must identify the mental element for the specific provision it is relying on, and apply it to the facts rather than inferring it from the harm.
The general exceptions in Chapter IV apply here as they do elsewhere, and the burden on them sits with the accused.

sections.keypoint: This lesson names no section numbers, because this corpus has not verified them.

body.text: You will have noticed that no section number appears above.
That is deliberate. This project's rule is that a provision is cited only where someone has checked it against the published Act, and nobody here has checked the provisions on hurt.
So the instruction is to open the Penal Code, find the chapter dealing with offences affecting the human body, and read the definitions and the grading provisions in order.

body.q: Why does this lesson give you a structure but no section numbers?
options: Because nobody working on this corpus has verified them against the published Act, and an unchecked citation is worse than none
Because the numbers change too often to be useful
body.why: A wrong section number on a law site looks exactly like a right one and survives every automated check. Naming the chapter and sending you to read it is the honest version, and it also builds the habit the whole reading tier exists for.

quiz.q: What decides which offence against the person is charged?
options: The victim's opinion
The length of the trial
The grade of harm, together with aggravating features such as means and intention
Whether the accused has previous convictions
quiz.why: The Code grades harm and then adds separate provisions for aggravating features. Matching the facts to the right combination is the analysis.

quiz.q: Why can the mental element not be inferred from the seriousness of the injury?
options: Because injuries are hard to assess
Because each offence states its own mental element, which must be established on the evidence
Because intention is presumed in all cases
Because the burden lies on the accused
quiz.why: Reasoning backwards from harm to state of mind skips the element the provision actually requires. Serious harm can be caused with a mental state the charged offence does not cover.
