lessons.title: Reaching people who did not do it themselves
lessons.summary: Criminal liability extends to those who tried, those who helped, and those who acted together. Each is a different route and they are not interchangeable.

sections.keypoint: Attempt, abetment and common intention extend liability in different directions and require different things.

body.text: Most offences describe someone doing something. The Code also reaches people who did not.
There are three distinct routes and they are commonly muddled.

items: Attempt — the offence was not completed
Abetment — someone helped, instigated or conspired
Common intention — several acted together in furtherance of a shared intention

body.text: They are not degrees of the same thing. An answer that says the accused was involved without naming the route has not identified the offence.

sections.keypoint: An attempt requires an act beyond mere preparation, together with the intention for the full offence.

body.text: Attempt asks how far along the accused had got.
Thinking about an offence is not an attempt. Buying what you need is usually still preparation.
Somewhere after that the conduct becomes an attempt, and the line is the hard part — it is a question of fact argued on the specifics.
The mental element is demanding: an attempt generally requires the intention to commit the full offence, even where the full offence could be committed with something less.

body.prompt: Why might attempt require a higher mental element than the completed offence?
options: It does not — the elements are always identical
Because without the result, intention is what identifies the conduct as criminal at all
body.reveal: When the harm has not happened, the act on its own may be entirely innocent. What makes buying an ordinary object into an attempt is the purpose behind it, so intention carries more weight than it does when a result has occurred.

sections.h: Abetment and common intention are different
sections.keypoint: Abetment is about helping or instigating another's offence; common intention is about acting together on a shared plan.

body.text: These two are confused more than any other pair in this area.
Abetment looks at what one person did in relation to another's offence — instigating it, helping it, agreeing to it.
Common intention looks at a group acting in furtherance of an intention they shared, and can make each liable for what was done in furtherance of it.
The practical difference is what you must prove. For abetment, the act of assistance or instigation. For common intention, the shared intention and participation in furtherance of it.

body.q: Your accused drove others to a location knowing what they planned. Which route do you analyse?
options: Both — driving may be an act of assistance, and there may also be a shared intention; they require different proof
Common intention only
body.why: The same facts can support either or both, and they are established differently. Choosing one without considering the other risks running the route the evidence supports least.

sections.keypoint: The provisions are in the Penal Code; this lesson names none, for the same reason as the last.

body.text: As with the previous lesson, no section numbers appear here.
The Code deals with abetment and with common intention in their own places, and attempt both generally and within particular offences.
Find them, read them, and write the numbers down with the date you checked.

quiz.q: What distinguishes an attempt from preparation?
options: The time elapsed
Whether a weapon was bought
Whether anyone was harmed
An act going beyond preparation towards commission, with the intention to commit the full offence
quiz.why: Preparation is not criminal as an attempt. The question is whether conduct has moved beyond it, and that is argued on the specific facts rather than settled by a formula.

quiz.q: How does abetment differ from common intention?
options: Abetment concerns helping or instigating another's offence; common intention concerns acting together in furtherance of a shared intention
They are the same offence
Abetment applies only to property offences
Common intention requires a written agreement
quiz.why: They reach different conduct and require different proof. The same facts may support both, which is why each has to be analysed rather than assumed.

lessons.title: After conviction: what a court may impose
lessons.summary: Conviction settles liability, not consequence. Sentencing is a separate exercise with its own purposes, its own material and its own arguments.

sections.keypoint: Sentencing follows conviction as a distinct exercise, argued on different material.

body.text: A criminal case does not end at conviction. It moves to a stage with its own rules.
The material differs. Evidence of the offence is settled; what matters now is the offender, the circumstances, and anything urged in mitigation.
So the advocacy differs too. An argument that the accused did not do it has no place here, and running it wastes the one opportunity to affect the outcome.
Students routinely treat sentencing as an afterthought. For a convicted client it is the entire remaining question.

sections.h: Purposes that pull in different directions
sections.keypoint: Punishment, deterrence, protection and rehabilitation can point to different sentences on the same facts.

body.text: Sentencing serves several purposes at once and they do not agree.

items: Retribution — a penalty proportionate to what was done
Deterrence — of this offender, and of others
Protection of the public
Rehabilitation of the offender

body.text: On the same facts, deterrence may argue for a heavier sentence than retribution would allow, and rehabilitation for a lighter one than protection would permit.

body.prompt: A first offender commits an offence that is becoming common in the area. Which purposes conflict?
options: Deterrence argues for severity to address prevalence; rehabilitation and proportionality argue against punishing this individual for a trend
None — they all point the same way
body.reveal: This is the sharpest recurring conflict in sentencing, and it is where general deterrence is most criticised: it uses one offender to send a message to others. Naming the conflict is a better answer than pretending the purposes align.

sections.keypoint: Factors are grouped around the offence and the offender, and the second is where mitigation usually lies.

body.text: Factors sort into two families and it helps to keep them apart.
Those concerning the offence: planning, the harm caused, the victim's vulnerability, the use of a weapon, the offender's role.
Those concerning the offender: previous record or its absence, age, a plea and when it was entered, cooperation, personal circumstances.
A plea in mitigation that only asserts the offence was not serious is arguing against the conviction. The stronger material is usually in the second family.

sections.keypoint: A court sentences within limits set by statute, and this lesson states none of them.

body.text: A court is not at large. Statute sets what may be imposed for an offence, and sometimes fixes a minimum.
Those limits are in the Penal Code and the Criminal Procedure Code, and this lesson names no section and no penalty.

body.q: Before advising a convicted client on likely sentence, what must you establish first?
options: The purposes of sentencing
What the statute permits for this offence, including any minimum
body.why: Purposes shape an argument within a range. The range itself comes from the statute, and advice given without checking it can promise something the court has no power to give.

quiz.q: Which sentencing purposes most often conflict?
options: Retribution and protection
Rehabilitation and protection
General deterrence and proportionality to this offender's conduct
None conflict
quiz.why: General deterrence looks outward to other potential offenders, while proportionality looks at what this offender did. Prevalence of an offence is the situation where the tension is sharpest.

quiz.q: What is the weakest form of plea in mitigation?
options: One relying on the offender's personal circumstances
One that in substance disputes the conviction
One mentioning an early plea
One raising the offender's age
quiz.why: Liability is settled by then. Re-arguing it spends the one chance to influence sentence on a question the court has already decided.

lessons.title: Who decides what happened
lessons.summary: A trial answers two different kinds of question. Knowing which one you are arguing, and who decides it, changes how you argue.

sections.keypoint: What happened is a question of fact; what follows legally is a question of law, and they are decided differently.

body.text: Every contested trial contains two kinds of question and they behave differently.
Questions of fact: what happened, who did it, what was said.
Questions of law: what the provision means, whether the established facts satisfy it.
The distinction matters most on appeal, where an appellate court will interfere far more readily with the second than with the first.

sections.h: Why findings of fact are hard to disturb
sections.keypoint: The trial court saw the witnesses, and an appellate court reading a transcript is not better placed to assess them.

body.text: The reason is practical rather than deferential.
The trial court watched the witnesses give evidence and be cross-examined. An appellate court has a transcript.
A transcript does not record hesitation, or the answer that arrived too quickly, so a court reading one is not better placed to decide who was telling the truth.

body.prompt: An appellant says the judge believed the wrong witness. How promising is that ground?
options: Weak on its own — it asks the appellate court to redo an assessment it is worse placed to make
Strong — appellate courts review the whole case afresh
body.reveal: It is not impossible, but it needs more: an inconsistency with undisputed documents, or a reason the assessment could not stand on the evidence. Simply preferring the other witness is the ground least likely to succeed, and knowing that redirects effort towards questions of law.

sections.keypoint: In a Malaysian trial both questions are decided by the judge, which shapes how each is argued.

body.text: In some systems fact and law are split between different decision-makers, with lay fact-finders deciding what happened and a judge ruling on law.
In a Malaysian trial the judge decides both.
That has a consequence for advocacy. Where the same person rules on admissibility and then decides the facts, they have necessarily seen material they may have excluded.
It also means reasons are given. A fact-finder who must explain a finding in writing is subject to a check that an unexplained verdict is not.
This lesson does not describe the history of lay participation in Malaysian trials or when it changed, because that has not been verified in this corpus. Check it before asserting anything about it.

sections.keypoint: Identify whether your point is one of fact or law before choosing how to make it.

body.text: The practical payoff is in how you spend your time.
A point of fact is argued from the evidence — inconsistencies, documents, what is inherently likely.
A point of law is argued from the provision and the authorities, and it is the one that travels on appeal.

body.q: You have a weak factual case and an arguable point of construction. Where should the effort go?
options: The facts, because they decide the case
The point of construction, which is also the ground most likely to survive an appeal
body.why: Effort should follow where it can actually change an outcome. A construction point can be decided in your favour on the material as it stands, and it is reviewable if it goes the other way.

quiz.q: Why are findings of fact rarely disturbed on appeal?
options: Appeals are discouraged
Facts are not appealable at all
Only the prosecution may appeal facts
The trial court saw the witnesses and an appellate court reading a transcript is not better placed to assess them
quiz.why: The reason is about who is better placed. A transcript loses everything about how evidence was given, which is much of what a credibility assessment rests on.

quiz.q: What follows from the same judge deciding both admissibility and the facts?
options: Nothing of significance
They will have seen material they may have ruled inadmissible, and they must give reasons for their findings
Admissibility is never argued
The trial must be split in two
quiz.why: Both consequences are real and they pull in opposite directions. Exposure to excluded material is a risk. The duty to give written reasons is a safeguard, and an unexplained verdict carries no such thing.

reading.where: the provisions governing the conduct of a trial and the recording of findings — read them for who decides what, and note the sections yourself
on the structure of a trial and on appeals against findings of fact

lessons.source: The distinction between questions of fact and law, and the standard on appeal against findings of fact, are general common law doctrine. No section of the Criminal Procedure Code is stated, and nothing is asserted about the history of lay participation in Malaysian trials, because neither has been verified here.

lessons.title: When the ordinary rules bend: emergency power
lessons.summary: A proclamation of emergency lets the government do things no ordinary law allows. This lesson shows where that power sits, how far it reaches, and which limits stay in place throughout.

sections.keypoint: An emergency is a legal state declared under the Constitution, not just a bad week for the country.
sections.h: A roadblock on a Tuesday morning

body.text: Encik Faizal drives a lorry between Ipoh and Butterworth. On Tuesday he is turned back at a roadblock. A curfew is in force, and he is told to go home.
He asks which Act allows that. The answer may be that no ordinary Act does. A proclamation of emergency was made, and the rules changed.
An emergency in this sense is a legal state. It is declared, it is written down, and it has a beginning and an end. It is not simply a description of a bad situation.
This Constitution is the supreme law of the Federation and any law passed after Merdeka Day which is inconsistent with this Constitution shall, to the extent of the inconsistency, be void.
Hold that rule in mind while you read on. Emergency power is the one place where the Constitution loosens its own grip. It does that on its own terms, and the terms are the whole subject.

This lesson gives no Article number for the emergency provisions, on purpose. That is not shyness. A wrong number here would be copied by every reader who trusted it. Look the Part up yourself in the current text before you write a number down.

sections.keypoint: A proclamation hands the executive powers that the ordinary constitutional scheme deliberately keeps away from it.

body.text: A proclamation of emergency is made by the Yang di-Pertuan Agong. He acts on the advice of the government of the day.
The trigger is a serious threat. Security, economic life and public order are the recognised grounds. A proclamation may cover the whole country or only one part of it.
Once it is in force, three things become possible that were not possible the day before.

items: **Parliament may legislate more widely.** It may make laws on subjects it could not normally touch, and laws that would otherwise be inconsistent with the Constitution.
**The Yang di-Pertuan Agong may make ordinances.** Where Parliament is not sitting, he may make emergency ordinances, and an ordinance has the force of an Act.
**The centre may direct a State.** The federal government may give directions on matters that would normally belong to the State alone.

body.text: Read that list again and ask who holds each power. Almost all of it sits on the executive side. Very little of it passes through a court.

body.prompt: Encik Faizal's curfew comes from an emergency ordinance, not from an Act of Parliament. Before you read on — does that make it weaker in law?
options: Yes — an ordinance is only a rule, so an Act would beat it
No — while the emergency lasts it has the force of an Act
Yes — only a court can restrict a person's movement
body.reveal: The second. An emergency ordinance is not a lesser thing than an Act, and that is exactly what makes this power large. If you picked the first, you were reasoning from the ordinary hierarchy of laws, where an instrument made by the executive ranks below a statute. That hierarchy is one of the things a proclamation suspends.

sections.keypoint: Emergency laws expire with the proclamation, and a short list of subjects stays out of reach throughout.
sections.h: The limits that stay in place

body.text: The power is wide. It is not unlimited, and the limits are the part worth learning precisely.

items: **Some subjects are out of reach.** A short list of matters cannot be touched even during an emergency. Religion, citizenship and language are on it, along with Malay custom.
**Parliament keeps a say.** The proclamation and any ordinance made under it must be laid before both Houses, and Parliament may annul them.
**Everything expires.** When a proclamation is revoked or lapses, the laws made under it cease to have effect. They do not quietly stay on the books.

body.text: Each of those three limits carries a time period and a procedure. The periods are short and specific, and they have been amended. Take them from the current text of the Constitution rather than from any summary, including this one.
The third limit does more work than people expect. An emergency law does not become an ordinary law by lasting a long time. It lives and dies with the proclamation that carried it.

sections.keypoint: Attack the scope and the expiry date, not the government's judgment that a crisis existed.
sections.h: How far can a court look behind it?

body.text: Encik Faizal wants to challenge the curfew. The useful question is not whether a court can help him. It is which question he should put.

body.caption: Four ways to attack an emergency measure, and how much traction each has
columns: How far a court will go with it
rows: Was there really an emergency?
Not far. The judgment that a threat exists is treated as one for the executive.
Did the ordinance stay within the proclamation?
Further. A court can read the ordinance against the power that produced it.
Is the proclamation still in force?
All the way. Revocation and lapse are plain questions of fact and law.
Does the measure touch an excluded subject?
All the way. That limit is written into the Constitution and a court applies it.
body.alt: Four questions about an emergency measure, and how far a court will go with each. Whether an emergency really existed: not far, because that judgment is treated as the executive's. Whether the ordinance stayed within the proclamation: further, because a court can read the ordinance against the power that produced it. Whether the proclamation is still in force: all the way, since revocation and lapse are plain questions of fact and law. Whether the measure touches an excluded subject: all the way, because the limit is written into the Constitution.

body.text: So the strongest arguments are rarely about whether the crisis was genuine. They are about scope, about time, and about the excluded subjects.

body.q: An emergency ordinance is still being enforced two years after the proclamation was revoked. What is the best first argument?
options: That the ordinance has no force left, because emergency law expires with the proclamation
That the emergency was never genuine in the first place
That the ordinance is unfair to lorry drivers
body.why: Expiry is the argument a court can actually decide, and it wins outright. The first answer asks a court to second-guess the executive's judgment about a threat, which is the weakest ground available. The third is not a legal argument at all.

lessons.source: Federal Constitution Art 4(1), and the Part of the Federal Constitution dealing with special powers and emergency, cited generally and without an Article number on purpose.

lessons.title: Equality, and the difference the Constitution permits
lessons.summary: The Constitution guarantees equality before the law, then allows a great deal of difference in how people are treated. This lesson shows how a court sorts a lawful classification from an unlawful one.

sections.keypoint: Unequal treatment and unlawful treatment are two different findings, and the gap between them is the subject.

body.text: Puan Kalsom and Encik Ravi both apply for a hawker licence in the same town. Hers is granted for a stall selling nasi lemak. His is refused.
The council tells him that licences go only to people who have lived in the district for five years. Ravi moved there last year.
Is that unequal treatment? Plainly. Is it unlawful? Not necessarily. The distance between those two answers is what this lesson is about.
All persons are equal before the law and entitled to the equal protection of the law.
body.source: Federal Constitution, Part II — the equality guarantee. This lesson deliberately does not state its Article number; see the verify note.

body.text: Notice the word **persons**. This right does not belong to citizens alone. Anybody in the country may rely on it, which is not true of every liberty in Part II.

sections.keypoint: A real difference between the groups, and a sensible link between that difference and the law's purpose.
sections.h: Why equality cannot mean treating everyone the same

body.text: Law sorts people constantly. Children cannot vote. A doctor needs a licence and a hawker does not. An undischarged bankrupt cannot be a company director.
If equality meant identical treatment, every one of those rules would be void. Nobody thinks that is the law, so the guarantee must mean something narrower.
It does. It forbids treating like cases unalike, and unlike cases alike, without a good reason. Courts test that with a two-part question.

items: **Is the group real?** The law must sort people by something that actually distinguishes those inside the group from those outside it.
**Does the sorting fit the purpose?** That difference must have a sensible connection to what the law is trying to achieve.

body.text: Lawyers call this the **reasonable classification** test. A classification is just a way of dividing people into groups; a reasonable one is a division the law can justify.
Both halves must be satisfied. A genuine difference that has nothing to do with the law's purpose fails, and so does a purpose served by an imaginary difference.

A scheme pays fuel subsidies only to registered fishermen. The group is real, and the link to a policy about fishing costs is obvious. It stands. A scheme paying subsidies only to people born in January would fail the second half at once.

sections.keypoint: Concede the obvious difference and put all your weight on the missing link to the law's purpose.
sections.h: Working the test on Ravi's facts

body.prompt: Ravi is refused because he has lived in the district for under five years. Before you read on — which half of the test is his stronger attack?
options: The first — length of residence is not a real difference between people
Neither — a licence is a privilege, so equality does not apply to it
The second — the link between years of residence and hawking is weak
body.reveal: The second. Length of residence is plainly a real difference, and arguing otherwise burns your credibility on a point you cannot win. All the pressure goes on the connection. Ask what the licensing scheme is actually for. If it is about food hygiene, or about how many stalls a street can hold, five years of residence does no work at all.

body.text: That is the ordinary shape of an equality argument. The first half is usually conceded in a sentence. The second half is where the case is won or lost.
Do not stop at showing that a rule hurts your client. Every rule hurts somebody, and a court knows it. You must show that the sorting itself has no sensible link to what the rule was made to do.

sections.keypoint: One part of the Constitution cannot be used to strike down another part of the same Constitution.

body.text: Some unequal treatment is not merely tolerated. It is written into the Constitution itself, and three examples come up constantly.

items: **The special position.** The special position of the Malays and of the natives of Sabah and Sarawak, together with the legitimate interests of other communities, has an Article of its own.
**Personal law.** Marriage and divorce follow different rules for Muslims and non-Muslims. The Constitution's own division of law-making power is what produces that.
**Citizen-only rights.** Some liberties are given to citizens alone. A non-citizen simply cannot claim them, and no equality argument repairs that.

body.text: Where the Constitution itself provides for a difference, the equality guarantee cannot be used to attack it. One part of a document does not strike down another part of the same document.

The Articles behind those three examples are not numbered here on purpose. This is the area where a wrong Article number does the most damage, because the sentence reads perfectly well either way. Look each one up before you write it down.

body.q: A federal Act treats Muslim and non-Muslim spouses differently on divorce. What is the best answer to an equality challenge?
options: The difference is unconstitutional, because all persons are equal before the law
The Constitution itself provides for separate personal law, so this is a difference it permits
Equality protects citizens only, and both spouses here are citizens
body.why: The equality guarantee is read alongside the rest of the Constitution, not against it. The first answer treats the guarantee as absolute, which no court does. The third is wrong twice over: the guarantee speaks of persons, and citizenship would not matter even if it did not.

lessons.source: Federal Constitution, Part II — the equality guarantee; the Article on the special position of the Malays and the natives of Sabah and Sarawak. The reasonable classification test as applied by the Malaysian courts.

lessons.title: Who decides a child's religion
lessons.summary: Article 12(4) says the religion of a person under eighteen is decided by a parent or guardian. One word in that clause, read with the Eleventh Schedule, sits at the centre of some of the hardest cases in Malaysian law.

sections.keypoint: A single word in Article 12(4) decides whether one parent alone can change a child's religion.
sections.h: A conversion the other parent knew nothing about

body.text: Encik Suresh and Puan Devi married in Ipoh and have two young children. The marriage breaks down and Suresh moves out.
He converts to Islam. He then takes the two children to a religious office and has them registered as Muslims. Devi learns of it three weeks later.
She wants the registration undone. Her whole argument turns on one word, in one clause, of the Constitution.
The religion of a person under the age of eighteen years shall be decided by his parent or guardian.
Read it again, slowly. It says *parent*, in the singular. Suresh says one parent is therefore enough. Devi says it must mean both.
That looks like a squabble about grammar. It is not. Whole families have turned on it.

sections.keypoint: The Constitution carries its own reading rules, and one of them lets a singular word cover the plural.
sections.h: The Eleventh Schedule turns one into many

body.text: The Constitution does not leave singular and plural to guesswork. It carries its own interpretation rules, and they sit in a Schedule at the back.
The Eleventh Schedule applies specified interpretation provisions to the Constitution, including the rule that words in the singular include the plural and words in the plural include the singular.
So *parent* in Article 12(4) can be read as *parents*. That is not a clever lawyer's trick. It is the Constitution's own instruction on how to read itself.
On that reading, the decision belongs to both parents together. A conversion arranged by one of them alone would not satisfy the clause at all.

The singular-includes-plural rule is a default, not a command. It applies unless the context requires otherwise. So the argument is real and it is strong, but it is not automatic. Expect the other side to argue that the context here does require otherwise.

body.prompt: Suppose the court reads *parent* as *parents*. Before you read on — what happens when the two parents disagree?
options: The father decides, as the head of the household
The child decides, whatever the parents want
Neither may act alone, so the disagreement has to go to a court
body.reveal: Nobody gets to act unilaterally. The clause stops being a power one parent holds and becomes a decision the two must reach together. When they cannot, someone has to resolve it, and that is a court's work. Notice how much a rule about singular and plural just changed.

sections.keypoint: Frame the question as constitutional compliance, or Article 121(1A) closes the civil court's door.
sections.h: Why the fight moves to which court

body.text: Suppose Devi is right about the words. She still has to find a court willing to say so.
The courts referred to in Clause (1) shall have no jurisdiction in respect of any matter within the jurisdiction of the Syariah courts.
Suresh will say a conversion to Islam is exactly such a matter, so the civil courts must keep out. Devi will say she is asking a different question.
Her question is whether a clause of the Constitution was complied with. That is a constitutional question, and Syariah courts do not decide those.
She has a second point too. She is not a Muslim, so a Syariah court has no jurisdiction over her at all. Sending her there gives her no forum.

How the question is characterised decides these cases more often than the merits do. State the issue as compliance with Article 12(4), not as the validity of a conversion. The second framing hands the case away before it starts.

sections.keypoint: Age, then who decided, then whether one parent is enough, then the forum — worked in that order.
sections.h: The pieces, in the order they come

body.caption: Four questions in a child conversion problem, and where each answer comes from
rows: Is the child under eighteen?
Article 12(4) applies only below that age.
Who made the decision?
The clause names a parent or guardian, and nobody else.
Does parent mean both parents?
The Eleventh Schedule, unless the context requires otherwise.
Which court hears it?
Article 121(1A), and how the question is characterised.
body.alt: The four questions in order. First, is the child under eighteen, because Article 12(4) applies only below that age. Second, who made the decision, since the clause names a parent or guardian and nobody else. Third, does the word parent mean both parents, which the Eleventh Schedule allows unless the context requires otherwise. Fourth, which court hears it, which turns on Article 121(1A) and on how the question is characterised.

body.text: Work them in that order. Most answers start at step four, and starting there concedes the argument on the words without ever making it.

Devi's affidavit opens by stating the children's ages and naming who signed the registration forms. Only then does it reach the Eleventh Schedule. That order is not decoration. It builds the constitutional question the civil court needs before it can take the case at all.

body.q: A father converts his fifteen-year-old alone, and the mother objects. What is the strongest opening point?
options: That the child is old enough to choose for herself
That Article 12(4) says parent, and the Eleventh Schedule lets that be read as both parents
That any conversion to Islam is always a matter for the Syariah courts
body.why: Article 12(4) draws its line at eighteen, so the first answer argues against the clause rather than with it. The third is the other side's case, not hers. The second is the point that both fits the words and keeps the matter in a civil court.

lessons.source: Federal Constitution Art 12(4), the Eleventh Schedule, and Art 121(1A).

Find the current Federal Court position before relying on the reading given here. Confirm the text of Article 12(4), the Eleventh Schedule and Article 121(1A) in the Federal Constitution as published by the Attorney General's Chambers. Record the date you checked.

lessons.title: Who decides to prosecute, and who may question it
lessons.summary: The choice to charge somebody, or to stop a charge, belongs to the Attorney General and to nobody else. Article 145(3) says so, and the separation of powers is the reason it is drawn that way.

sections.keypoint: Starting, running and stopping a prosecution are one power, held by one office, at that office's discretion.
sections.h: The police report that went nowhere

body.text: Encik Gopal is knocked off his motorcycle on the way to work. His leg is broken and the bike is a write-off. He makes a police report.
The police investigate and send the file on. Six months later Gopal is told there will be no charge. Nobody explains why.
He wants a court to order a prosecution. Before asking whether he can get one, find out who actually holds the decision.

The Attorney General shall have power, exercisable at his discretion, to institute, conduct or discontinue any proceedings for an offence, other than proceedings before a Syariah court, a native court or a court-martial.
Three verbs carry that clause. To **institute** is to start proceedings. To **conduct** is to run them. To **discontinue** is to stop them part-way through.
All three sit in one office. And the Article says the power is exercisable at his discretion.

sections.keypoint: A discretion given by name to one office cannot be exercised by a court on that office's behalf.
sections.h: What the words at his discretion are doing

body.text: Those four words are the heart of the clause. A **discretion** is a choice the law gives you without telling you how to make it.
The Article gives that choice to the Attorney General by name. Three consequences follow, and each of them surprises somebody.

items: **The police do not decide.** They investigate and hand over a file. A strong file is not a charge.
**A victim cannot start a prosecution as of right.** The offence is against the public, and the public's choice is made by one office.
**A withdrawal is not a mistake.** Discontinuing a charge on the morning of trial is the power being used, not a failure of it.

body.text: The Attorney General is also the Public Prosecutor, and different statutes use different titles for the same person. Deputy Public Prosecutors act on his behalf. So when a report says the Public Prosecutor has decided something, this is the power being exercised.

body.prompt: Gopal asks the High Court to order that the driver be charged. Before you read on — what is the likely answer?
options: The court will order the charge if the evidence is strong enough
The court will send the file back to the police to investigate again
The court will not order it, because the choice belongs to the Attorney General
body.reveal: The second. The strength of the evidence is not the issue, which is the part that feels wrong. A court that ordered a charge would be exercising a power the Constitution handed to a different branch of government. Gopal is not without a remedy — but it is a civil one, and he has to bring it himself.

sections.keypoint: Five decisions in a criminal case belong to four different bodies, and most complaints aim at the wrong one.
sections.h: Separation of powers, in one clause

body.text: This is a good place to watch the separation of powers do real work. The phrase names a plain idea.
Parliament makes law. The executive administers and enforces it. The courts decide disputes and say what the law means.
Article 145(3) puts the choice to prosecute firmly on the executive side of that line. A court that refuses to order a charge is not being timid. It is staying on its own side of the line.

body.caption: Five decisions in a criminal case, and who owns each one
rows: Whether this conduct should be a crime at all
Parliament, when it passes the law
Whether to investigate
The police
Whether to charge, continue or stop
The Attorney General, under Article 145(3)
Whether the charge is proved
The court
What sentence follows a conviction
The court, within the range the law sets
body.alt: Five decisions in a criminal case and who owns each. Whether conduct should be a crime at all belongs to Parliament, when it passes the law. Whether to investigate belongs to the police. Whether to charge, continue or stop belongs to the Attorney General under Article 145(3). Whether the charge is proved belongs to the court. What sentence follows a conviction belongs to the court, within the range the law sets.

body.text: Read down that second column. Almost every complaint about a criminal case is really aimed at the wrong row, and naming the right row is half the advice.

sections.keypoint: The power stops at Syariah, native and court-martial proceedings — and a civil claim was always the victim's own.

body.text: The discretion is wide. It is not a wall with no door in it, and two openings are worth knowing.

items: **It has an edge.** The power covers proceedings for an offence. It does not reach proceedings before a Syariah court, a native court or a court-martial. The Article says so in terms.
**A discretion is given for a purpose.** An exercise of it on a plainly improper basis is arguable. The argument is hard, it rarely succeeds, and it needs authority you have read yourself.

body.text: Gopal has a better route in any case. A criminal charge is not the only way to make somebody answer for a collision.

He sues the driver in the civil courts for negligence. He controls that case himself, and no discretion stands between him and the court. The standard of proof is lower, and the remedy is money for the bike, the hospital bills and the lost wages.

body.q: Which of these falls outside the power in Article 145(3)?
options: A charge of theft in the Magistrates' Court
An appeal by the prosecution against an acquittal
Proceedings before a Syariah court
body.why: The Article carves out proceedings before a Syariah court, a native court and a court-martial. Those run under their own systems. The other two are ordinary criminal proceedings and sit squarely inside the power.

lessons.source: Federal Constitution Art 145(3); the separation of powers as it operates in Malaysian criminal procedure.

lessons.title: What is lost when the speaker is absent
lessons.summary: Hearsay is not kept out because second-hand accounts are always false. It is kept out because the person who actually saw the thing is not there to be tested.

sections.keypoint: A sergeant wants to repeat what a bystander told him. The bystander is not in the room.
sections.h: The officer who was not there

body.text: Encik Firdaus is on trial in Ipoh for snatch theft. The only witness the prosecution has is Sergeant Lim.
Sergeant Lim reached the scene four minutes after the snatch. He did not see it. He wants to tell the court what a bystander told him there.

body.prompt: Sergeant Lim wants to repeat what the bystander said, to prove that Firdaus did it. Will the court take that?
options: Generally not, because the bystander is the one who saw it
Yes, the sergeant is a police officer and is under oath
Yes, but only if the bystander has since died
body.reveal: Generally not. Nobody is calling Sergeant Lim a liar. The problem is that the bystander cannot be asked a single question. Death does not open the door by itself either. It matters only where a section makes such a statement relevant.

body.text: The sergeant is honest. That is not the difficulty. The difficulty is that the person who saw the theft is not in the room.

sections.keypoint: Cross-examination attacks perception, memory, honesty and wording. An absent speaker escapes all four.
sections.h: The four things you cannot test

body.text: Put a witness in the box and there are four separate things you can attack. An absent speaker is safe from every one of them.

body.caption: What cross-examination reaches, and what an absent speaker escapes
columns: Why the absent speaker escapes it
rows: Perception
How far away were you? Was it dark?
Nobody can ask the bystander where he was standing.
Memory
When did you first tell anyone this?
The gap between seeing and speaking goes untested.
Honesty
Do you know the accused? Do you owe anyone a favour?
No oath was taken and no motive is exposed.
Choice of words
You said he grabbed it. Do you mean he pulled, or took?
An ambiguous phrase is passed on as if it were plain.
body.alt: A table of four risks in second-hand evidence. Perception: nobody can ask the absent speaker where he stood or how dark it was. Memory: the gap between seeing and speaking goes untested. Honesty: no oath was taken and no motive is exposed. Choice of words: an ambiguous phrase is passed on as though it were plain.

body.text: A witness in the box also takes an oath. The judge watches how the answers come out. None of that reaches the bystander.
So the objection is not that the report is false. The objection is that it cannot be checked.
This is why an offer to prove the bystander was reliable does not help. The rule is not about that speaker. It is about the machinery that is missing.

sections.keypoint: Words repeated to show they were said are ordinary evidence. Words repeated to show they were true are hearsay.
sections.h: Ask what the statement is offered to prove

body.text: The same sentence can be hearsay in one case and ordinary evidence in the next. It depends on why you want it in.
Ask one question. Are you asking the court to believe what the words said, or only that the words were said?
Cik Suria sues a builder. She says she warned him about a leaking pipe on 3 March. Repeating the warning to prove she gave notice is fine. Repeating it to prove the pipe was leaking is hearsay.

items: **Words as the act itself.** An offer, an acceptance, a threat, a defamatory sentence. The words are the event the case is about.
**Words to show notice.** What matters is that the hearer was told, not that the message was true.
**Words to show a state of mind.** What a person said about their own fear or intention can show the state they were in.

body.q: A guard says he opened the gate because the driver told him the manager had approved it. It is offered to explain why he opened it. Is that hearsay?
options: No, because it explains the guard's conduct rather than proving approval
Yes, because the driver is not in court
Only if the manager denies approving anything
body.why: The court is not being asked to believe that the manager approved anything. It is being asked to see why the guard acted. Offer the same words to prove approval and they become hearsay at once.

sections.keypoint: There is no single hearsay rule here with exceptions hanging off it, only a closed list of what a section makes relevant.

body.text: English law states a rule against hearsay and then hangs a long list of exceptions on it. The Act does not work that way.
Evidence may be given in any suit or proceeding of the existence or non-existence of every fact in issue and of such other facts as are declared to be relevant by this Act, and of no others.
So a statement made out of court is not pushed back out by an exclusionary rule. It simply never becomes relevant, unless a section makes it relevant.
Several sections do. The Act makes certain statements relevant where the maker cannot be called, and it has its own regime for records and documents.
That route reaches roughly where the English exceptions reach. It arrives by the opposite road, and the difference shows up in how you write the answer.
Never write that hearsay is never admissible. Write that it does not come in unless a provision lets it in. Then go and name the provision.
This lesson gives you no section numbers for those routes on purpose. Look them up in the current Act and write the numbers into your own notes.

lessons.title: A confession, and what must be true before it counts
lessons.summary: A confession is the strongest thing a prosecution can hold, which is why the Act puts conditions on using it. The first question is never what the accused said, but how it came to be said.

sections.keypoint: Encik Hafiz signed a statement after an officer told him things would go easier. That sentence is the whole issue.
sections.h: Three in the morning at the station

body.text: Encik Hafiz is arrested in Seremban over a house-breaking. He is taken to the station at eleven at night.
At three in the morning he signs a statement admitting he was inside the house. An officer had told him things would go easier if he cooperated.

body.prompt: The prosecution wants the signed statement before the court. What does the court ask first?
options: Whether the statement was made voluntarily
Whether what Hafiz wrote is true
Whether Hafiz had a lawyer with him
body.reveal: Voluntariness comes first. Truth is not the entry test. An induced statement is kept out even if every word of it turns out to be accurate. The lawyer question matters a great deal, and it is a separate one, taken up later in this lesson.

body.text: Notice the order. The court does not begin with whether the statement is true. It begins with how it was obtained.

sections.keypoint: Not every damaging sentence is a confession, and the conditions in this lesson attach only to confessions.

body.text: An admission is any statement by a party pointing to a fact against their own interest. A confession is narrower than that.
A confession is a statement made by an accused person which suggests the inference that he committed the offence charged.
body.source: Evidence Act 1950, the provisions on admissions and confessions in Part I. No section number is stated here; see the verify note for this lesson.

body.text: So the statement has to point at guilt. A statement that admits one small damaging fact is an admission and nothing more.
Hafiz says he was on that street at midnight. That places him nearby and it hurts him. It is not a confession, because being on a street is not the offence.
The line matters because of what follows from it. The conditions in the next section attach to confessions. An ordinary admission does not carry them.
A mixed statement causes trouble. A man may admit taking the goods and add that he believed they were his. Courts do not simply keep the damaging half and drop the rest.

sections.keypoint: An inducement, threat or promise from a person in authority spoils a confession, whether or not it is true.
sections.h: Voluntariness, and who can spoil it

body.text: The Act makes a confession irrelevant where it appears to have been caused by an inducement, a threat or a promise.
Three things have to line up before that bites.

items: **An inducement, threat or promise.** Something offered or held over the accused, not merely a long and unpleasant night.
**From a person in authority.** A police officer or a prosecutor is one. A friend in the next cell usually is not.
**Enough to give grounds for supposing an advantage.** The accused must reasonably suppose he gains something, or escapes something, in the proceedings against him.

body.text: The word appears is doing real work there. The court asks how the confession looks on the material before it. The accused does not have to prove a threat.
Telling Hafiz that things go easier if he cooperates is a promise of advantage from a person in authority. That is the classic shape of the objection.
Where voluntariness is disputed, the court holds a trial within a trial. It hears evidence about how the statement was taken, before deciding whether to admit the statement itself.
This is one of the most heavily litigated parts of the Act, and older authority has been overtaken. Read the sections themselves before any commentary. Check the date of anything you rely on.

sections.keypoint: Section 28A of the Criminal Procedure Code sets out the rights on arrest, and section 117 controls how long detention may run.
sections.h: What the Code gives a person in custody

body.text: Voluntariness is not argued in the abstract. It is argued against what happened in the hours after arrest. The Criminal Procedure Code governs those hours.
A person arrested shall be informed as soon as may be of the grounds of his arrest. He shall be allowed to communicate with a relative or friend, and to consult a legal practitioner of his choice.
The section also restricts questioning until the arrested person has had that consultation. The exceptions to that are set out in the section itself.
A police officer who wants to detain an arrested person beyond twenty-four hours must produce him before a Magistrate and apply for a remand order.

body.caption: Where to look when a confession is challenged
rows: Whether the statement was voluntary
The confession provisions of the Evidence Act 1950
Whether he was told why he was arrested
Criminal Procedure Code, s 28A
Whether he was allowed to call a lawyer
Criminal Procedure Code, s 28A
Whether the detention itself was lawful
Criminal Procedure Code, s 117
Whether a statement to a police officer may be used at all
A separate provision of the Code, amended more than once
body.alt: A table pairing each line of attack on a confession with where the rule sits. Voluntariness sits in the confession provisions of the Evidence Act 1950. Being told the grounds of arrest and being allowed a lawyer both sit in section 28A of the Criminal Procedure Code. The lawfulness of detention beyond a day sits in section 117. Whether a statement made to a police officer may be used at all sits in a separate provision of the Code.

body.q: Hafiz's statement turns out to be accurate in every detail. He was still promised leniency by the investigating officer. What follows?
options: The statement goes in, because accuracy cures the promise
The judge admits it and gives it less weight
The statement may still be shut out, because voluntariness is the entry test
body.why: Truth is not the test for getting a confession in. One caused by a promise of advantage from a person in authority is kept out, however accurate it later proves. Giving evidence less weight happens after admission, and that stage is never reached.

body.text: A retracted confession is a separate problem. The accused says in court that he never meant it, and the court then decides what the retraction is worth.

lessons.title: When the court will listen to an opinion
lessons.summary: A witness is there to say what happened, not what they think it means. Expert opinion is the exception to that, and it is narrower than most people expect.

sections.keypoint: Puan Latifah says the signature on the transfer is not hers. Nobody in court can settle that by looking.

body.text: Puan Latifah's land in Alor Setar has been transferred to her nephew. She says she never signed the transfer form.
The signature on the form looks like hers. It also looks like three others in the same file. The judge cannot settle this by staring at it.

body.prompt: Who may tell the court whether that signature is genuine?
options: Only a document examiner with the relevant skill
Any witness who has an honest view about it
Only Puan Latifah, because it is her own signature
body.reveal: A qualified document examiner, and that is the main route. Latifah may of course say the signature is not hers, but she is a party with an interest. The Act also allows a person genuinely familiar with someone's handwriting to speak to it, which is a narrow second route.

body.text: That is the shape of the subject. Most witnesses may not offer a view at all. A few may.

sections.keypoint: The court draws the conclusions, and a witness who offers one is doing the judge's job with less information.
sections.h: Why opinions are usually kept out

body.text: The ordinary rule is short. A witness states the facts they perceived. Drawing conclusions from those facts is the court's work.
There are two reasons for that, and both are practical.

items: **The judge decides the case.** Letting witnesses vote on the outcome does not make the decision better, only louder.
**An opinion cannot be tested the way a fact can.** You can ask a witness where she stood. You cannot cross-examine a hunch.

body.text: So a neighbour may say she saw the car swerve across the line. She may not say the driver was negligent.

The line is thinner than it looks. Ordinary witnesses give compressed judgments constantly, about speed, about age, about whether someone seemed drunk. Those are treated as shorthand for what was observed.

sections.keypoint: Skill in a listed field, proved to the court, on a question the court cannot answer without help.
sections.h: What makes a witness an expert

body.text: The Act makes relevant the opinions of persons specially skilled in certain matters. The listed fields are where you start.

items: Foreign law.
Science.
Art.
The identity of handwriting.
Finger impressions.

body.text: Skill is proved, not assumed. The party calling the expert has to show the court where that skill came from.
It can come from a degree, from a professional qualification, or from years of doing the work. Experience on its own can be enough.

Latifah calls a document examiner with fifteen years in a government laboratory. The nephew objects that she holds no university degree. That objection is weak, because skill can be built by practice.
An expert is an expert only on their own field. A fire investigator asked to give a view on a company's accounts is a lay witness with an impressive title.

sections.keypoint: Admitting an opinion is not accepting it, and an opinion with no stated reasoning is worth very little.
sections.h: Getting it in is only half the job

body.text: Getting an expert's evidence in is the first half. What the court does with it is the second, and answers usually skip that part.
The court is not bound to accept the opinion. It weighs the opinion like any other piece of evidence.
What gives an expert weight is the reasoning behind the conclusion. An expert who states a conclusion and no grounds has given the court nothing to check.
The Act treats the grounds of an opinion as relevant as well. That is the statutory expression of the same idea.

body.caption: What separates a strong expert opinion from a weak one
rows: Sets out the method used, step by step
States a conclusion and stops
Names the material actually examined
Relies on documents nobody produced
Says how confident the conclusion is
Speaks in flat certainties
Answers the technical question only
Tells the court who should win
body.alt: A table contrasting strong and weak expert opinion. A strong opinion sets out its method step by step, names the material actually examined, says how confident it is, and answers only the technical question. A weak one states a bare conclusion, relies on documents nobody produced, speaks in flat certainties, and tells the court who should win.

body.q: Two document examiners reach opposite conclusions about Latifah's signature. What should the judge do?
options: Prefer whichever expert has more years of experience
Examine the reasoning each gave and decide which holds up
Treat the point as unproved and put both aside
body.why: The court weighs expert evidence like any other evidence, and reasoning is what makes it weighable. Length of service is one factor and never the deciding one. Putting both aside would leave a fact in issue undecided when material to decide it was given.

body.text: Watch for an expert who answers the very question the court has to decide. That is where an opinion stops helping the judgment and starts replacing it.

lessons.title: Three turns at a witness, and what a witness may refuse
lessons.summary: A witness is questioned three times over, and each turn has its own rules about what may be asked. A witness may also refuse some questions outright, and the widest refusal protects what a client told a lawyer.

sections.keypoint: Cik Nurul is questioned by three people in turn, under three different sets of rules.

body.text: Cik Nurul saw a car crash on Jalan Tun Abdul Razak. She is called by the plaintiff in the Sessions Court in Johor Bahru.
Her time in the box has three parts. The plaintiff's lawyer asks first. Then the defendant's lawyer. Then the plaintiff's lawyer again, briefly.

body.prompt: The plaintiff's lawyer opens with: the blue car ran the red light, didn't it? Is that allowed?
options: Yes, he called her, so he may lead her
No, you may not lead your own witness on a disputed point
Only if the defendant's lawyer does not object
body.reveal: Not allowed. A leading question suggests the answer, and you may not feed answers to your own witness on the disputed part of the case. Leading is fine for uncontested background, and it is the normal way to cross-examine. Objection matters in practice, but it is not the reason.

body.text: Each turn has its own name and its own limits. Running them together is the most visible mistake in a moot.

sections.keypoint: Examination-in-chief, cross-examination, re-examination, in that order, and only the middle one lets you lead.

body.text: The three stages run in a fixed order. Each one is limited by what came before it.

body.caption: The three stages of questioning a witness
rows: Examination-in-chief
The party who called the witness
Not on disputed matters
The witness's own account
Cross-examination
The opposing party
Allowed
Anything relevant, including credit
Re-examination
The party who called the witness
Not on disputed matters
Explaining what came out in cross-examination
body.alt: A table of the three stages of questioning a witness. Examination-in-chief is taken by the party who called the witness, may not lead on disputed matters, and covers the witness's own account. Cross-examination is taken by the opposing party, may lead, and covers anything relevant including credit. Re-examination returns to the party who called the witness, may not lead, and is confined to explaining what came out in cross-examination.

body.text: A **leading question** is one that suggests the answer wanted. Did you see the broken bottle is leading. What did you see is not.
Re-examination is the narrowest stage. It exists to repair damage done in cross-examination. It may not open new ground without leave of the court.
Re-examination is not a second chance to make your case. A question there with no root in the cross-examination is objectionable, and it will be stopped.

sections.keypoint: If you never challenge a witness's account, you cannot later ask the court to disbelieve it.
sections.h: Cross-examination, and the duty to put your case

body.text: Cross-examination is where the four risks tested in the hearsay lesson are actually attacked. Perception, memory, honesty, and choice of words.
It has a second job that answers often miss. You have to put your own case to the witness.
That means telling the witness what your client says happened. It means giving them the chance to accept it or deny it.
The defendant's case is that Nurul stood behind a bus and saw nothing. His lawyer must put that to her. Saying it for the first time in closing submissions is too late.
Failing to put your case invites the court to treat that witness's account as unchallenged. It is a common and expensive mistake, and it cannot be repaired afterwards.
When the prosecution has finished with all its witnesses, a criminal trial reaches a fixed checkpoint.

At the close of the case for the prosecution the court shall consider whether the prosecution has made out a prima facie case. If it has not, the court shall record an order of acquittal. If it has, the court shall call upon the accused to enter his defence.
So the value of cross-examination is tested there first. A case taken apart in cross-examination may never reach a defence at all.

sections.keypoint: What a client told a lawyer is protected, and the protection belongs to the client rather than to the lawyer.
sections.h: What a witness may refuse to answer

body.text: A witness generally answers. Privilege is the narrow set of questions a witness may refuse, and the widest of them covers legal advice.

An advocate shall not be permitted to disclose any communication made to him in the course and for the purpose of his employment as an advocate, or the contents of any document he became acquainted with in that course, or any advice given by him to his client.
Two things escape that protection. Both are set out in the proviso to the same section.

items: A communication made in furtherance of an illegal purpose.
A fact observed by the advocate in the course of the employment, showing that a crime or fraud has been committed since the employment began.

body.text: The protection in section 126 extends to interpreters and to the clerks and servants of an advocate.
No one shall be compelled to disclose to the court any confidential communication between himself and his legal professional adviser, unless he offers himself as a witness.

body.caption: Where each of the four privilege provisions bites
rows: Stops the advocate disclosing what the client told him
Extends that to interpreters, clerks and servants
Says when a party is taken to have consented to disclosure
Stops the client being compelled to disclose the same material
body.alt: A table of the four privilege provisions. Section 126 stops the advocate disclosing what the client told him. Section 127 extends that protection to interpreters, clerks and servants. Section 128 says when a party is taken to have consented to disclosure. Section 129 stops the client being compelled to disclose the same material.

body.text: The privilege belongs to the client, not to the lawyer. A lawyer cannot waive it to be helpful. A client who simply gives evidence in the case has not waived it either.

body.q: A client tells his advocate how he plans to forge a receipt he will rely on at trial. Is that communication protected?
options: Yes, because everything said to an advocate is protected
Yes, unless the advocate reports it to someone
No, because the proviso removes a communication made in furtherance of an illegal purpose
body.why: The proviso to section 126 takes out communications made in furtherance of an illegal purpose. The protection exists for getting legal advice, not for arranging a fraud. Whether the advocate must report anything is a separate professional question.

lessons.title: Terms and representations: what actually got into the contract
lessons.summary: Not everything said before signing becomes part of the contract. Which side of that line a statement falls on decides whether you sue for breach or attack the agreement itself.

sections.keypoint: The salesman said it and the paper did not, and that gap decides which claim Faizal has.

body.text: Encik Faizal buys a used Proton from a dealer in Ipoh for RM28,000. The salesman tells him the engine was rebuilt last year. The signed agreement says nothing about the engine.
Three months later the engine seizes. It was never rebuilt. Faizal wants his money back.
Everything turns on one question. Was that sentence part of the contract? Or was it only something said to get him to sign?
A **term** is a promise inside the contract. A **representation** is a statement of fact that led you into it. Both were spoken aloud. Only one was promised.

The law separates a promise that forms part of the agreement from a statement of fact that merely induced a party to enter into it. That distinction comes from the received common law, which applies in Malaysia subject to local circumstances and to any written law.
body.source: General principle of contract law as received under the Civil Law Act 1956, s 3.

body.text: The Contracts Act 1950 does not sort statements for you. It says what a contract needs. It leaves this question to the case law.
That is why the topic feels different from formation and consideration. There you reach for a section. Here you reach for the facts, and argue.

sections.keypoint: No single test settles it: timing, importance, special knowledge and writing all pull at once.

body.text: There is no single test. A court weighs several things together, and the weight shifts with the facts.

body.caption: What pushes a spoken statement towards being a term
rows: Timing
Said at or close to the moment of signing
Said weeks earlier, with much talk in between
Importance
The buyer showed he would not sign without it
Nobody treated it as decisive
Special knowledge
The speaker knew the subject and the listener did not
The listener knew more than the speaker
Put in writing
The statement went into the signed document
The document stayed silent about it
body.alt: Four things a court weighs. Timing: said at signing points to a term, said weeks earlier points to a representation. Importance: a buyer who showed he would not sign without it points to a term, and general talk points away. Special knowledge: a speaker who knew the subject and a listener who did not points to a term. Writing: a statement put into the signed document points to a term, and a silent document points away from one.

body.text: The last row is the strongest of the four. It is still not conclusive. A signed document that stays silent can be attacked as an incomplete record of the deal.
Notice what the whole list is doing. It asks who was in a position to know, and who was relying on whom.

Faizal knows nothing about engines. The salesman services these cars every week. Faizal asked twice about the engine before he signed. Three of the four pointers favour a term, even though the paper says nothing.
Do not settle this by asking whether the statement mattered to the buyer. Almost every statement did. The question is what the two of them showed each other at the time.

sections.keypoint: Some terms are in the contract without being spoken, put there by fact, by statute or by trade custom.

body.text: Not every term is written or spoken. Some are read into the contract by law.
There are three ordinary routes in, and they work differently.

items: **By fact.** The term is so obvious that both sides would have agreed at once had anyone raised it. Courts use this sparingly, and only to make the contract work.
**By statute.** Parliament writes terms into certain contracts. Sale of goods and hire purchase are the familiar examples, and those terms are harder to bargain away.
**By custom.** A settled practice, well known in a particular trade, can be read into an agreement made in that trade.

body.text: A term implied by fact is the hardest to win. You are asking a court to add words the parties never used.
Faizal's agreement says nothing about the car being fit to drive. He may not need it to. Terms about goods sold can be implied into a contract of sale by statute, whatever the paper says.
Look those statutory terms up before you cite them. They live in the Sale of Goods Act 1957, not in the Contracts Act 1950, and this lesson gives no section number for them.
So the map has three layers. What the parties wrote, what they said, and what the law puts in without being asked.

sections.keypoint: A broken term is a breach measured by section 74; a false representation attacks consent under section 14.

body.text: Now the payoff. The two labels lead to two different claims.
Say the sentence was a term. The contract stands, and one promise inside it was broken. Faizal claims the money the breach cost him.

When a contract has been broken, the party who suffers by the breach is entitled to receive compensation for any loss or damage caused to him which naturally arose in the usual course of things from the breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach.
Put simply: he recovers the loss that ordinarily follows. He also recovers unusual loss the dealer knew about when the deal was struck.
Say instead the sentence stayed outside the contract. Nothing inside it was broken. The attack is on his consent, and section 14 is the section that lists what spoils consent.
When consent to an agreement is caused by coercion, fraud or misrepresentation, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused.
Put simply: a misrepresentation does not end the contract by itself. It hands Faizal a choice, and he has to make it.
He may rescind and unwind the sale. Or he may affirm it and insist on being put in the position he would have been in, had the statement been true.

body.prompt: The engine sentence was typed into the signed agreement, and the engine was never rebuilt. Which route should Faizal take?
options: Sue for breach of a term, because the promise sits inside the contract
Rescind the sale, because he was told something untrue
Neither, because he had a chance to inspect the car before buying
body.reveal: The second one. Once the sentence is in the signed document it is a promise, not an inducement. Breaking a promise inside a contract is breach, and section 74 measures what he gets. Rescission is the route for a statement that stayed outside. Reaching for it here throws away the easier claim.

body.text: One more step after the label. Some terms go to the root of the deal, and breaking one lets the innocent side end the contract. Breaking a minor term gives damages and nothing more.
Naming the statement a term wins nothing on its own. Say how serious the breach was, and say what your client can actually do about it. That is where the marks are.

lessons.source: Contracts Act 1950 (Act 136) ss 14, 19(1) and 74; Civil Law Act 1956 s 3. The term and representation distinction, and the routes by which a term is implied, are received common law rather than statute.

lessons.title: Exclusion clauses: getting in, and getting past the words
lessons.summary: A clause that takes liability away has to clear three hurdles before it protects anybody. It must get into the contract, cover what actually went wrong, and survive the limits the law imposes from outside.

sections.keypoint: Three hurdles stand between the operator and his clause, and most answers argue only the last one.
sections.h: The ticket in the car park

body.text: Puan Nurul parks at a car park in Johor Bahru. The machine prints a ticket. On the back, in small type, it says the operator is not liable for loss or damage howsoever caused.
She comes back to a dented door and a missing wing mirror. The attendant points at the ticket.
An **exclusion clause** takes away a liability that would otherwise exist. A **limitation clause** caps it at a figure instead of removing it. The analysis below fits both.
That clause has to clear three hurdles before it helps the operator at all.

items: **Did it get in?** A clause binds nobody unless it became part of the contract.
**Does it cover this?** The words have to reach the thing that actually went wrong.
**Does the law allow it?** Some clauses fail even when they are in and on point.

body.text: Take them in that order. Arguing that a clause is unfair is wasted work if it never got into the contract in the first place.

sections.keypoint: Signature, notice given before the deal is struck, or a long course of dealing between the same parties.

body.text: A clause becomes part of a contract in one of three ordinary ways.

items: **Signature.** A person who signs a document is normally bound by what is in it, read or not.
**Notice.** An unsigned clause binds only if reasonable steps were taken to bring it to the other side's attention. Those steps must come before or at the moment the contract is made.
**Course of dealing.** Where the same two parties have dealt on the same terms many times, those terms may carry into the next deal.

body.text: The timing point does the most work of the three. A clause handed over after the deal is struck has arrived too late to be part of it.

Nurul's contract was made when she took the ticket and the barrier lifted. Words printed on the back of that ticket reached her at that same moment, or later. The operator has to show she had reasonable notice by then.
The more unusual the clause, the more the law expects it to have been pointed out. A sweeping clause buried in small print is the hardest of all to bring in.
A signature is strong but it is not magic. It can be attacked where the signer was misled about what the document contained, and section 14 of the Contracts Act 1950 is where that argument starts.

sections.keypoint: Ambiguity is read against the party relying on the clause, and excluding your own negligence needs clear words.

body.text: Suppose the clause got in. The next question is whether it covers what happened.
Courts read these clauses strictly. Any real ambiguity is resolved against the party who is relying on it.
That rule has a name worth knowing: contra proferentem. It means against the one who put the words forward.

An exclusion clause is construed strictly, and any ambiguity in it is resolved against the party seeking to rely on it. Clear words are required before such a clause is read as excluding liability for that party's own negligence.
body.source: Received rules of construction, applied in Malaysia under the Civil Law Act 1956, s 3.

body.text: So sweeping words like howsoever caused are weaker than they look. A court asks what the clause plainly covers, not what it could be stretched to reach.
Say the dent came from an attendant reversing a van into Nurul's car. The operator is then asking the clause to cover his own carelessness. He needs words that say so.

body.q: A clause says the operator is not liable for any loss howsoever caused. An attendant damages the car through carelessness. Is the operator covered?
options: Yes, because howsoever caused covers everything
No, because a clause can never cover negligence
Not without clearer words, because excluding your own negligence requires them
body.why: General words are read strictly, and against the person relying on them. The third option overstates it, since negligence can be excluded where the clause plainly says so. The first option adopts the drafter's sweep as if it were the court's reading.

sections.keypoint: Section 24 and the consumer legislation set an outer limit that careful drafting cannot get past.

body.text: The third hurdle is the law's own limit. Two sources matter here, and they work differently.
The first is the Contracts Act itself. Where the object or the consideration of an agreement is unlawful, the agreement is void.

The consideration or object of an agreement is unlawful if it is forbidden by law, or would defeat any law, or is fraudulent, or involves injury to the person or property of another, or the court regards it as immoral or opposed to public policy. Every agreement of which the object or consideration is unlawful is void.
Put simply: a clause that exists to defeat a law, or that offends public policy, is not rescued by careful drafting.
The second source is consumer protection legislation. Malaysia has a statute dealing with unfair terms in consumer contracts, and it works outside the Contracts Act.
This lesson gives no section number for those unfair terms provisions. Find them in the current Consumer Protection Act 1999, and write down the date you checked.
Notice who that statute helps. It reaches consumer dealings. A contract between two businesses is usually fought on the first two hurdles instead.
So the order matters once more. Incorporation, then construction, then control. An answer that opens on unfairness has skipped the two hurdles the operator is likeliest to fail.
