lessons.title: Privity: who can actually sue on the promise
lessons.summary: Consideration in Malaysia may come from a stranger, but a stranger still cannot sue on the contract. That gap catches the person who paid for work done for somebody else.

sections.keypoint: Ganesan signed and paid, and his mother got the bad workmanship. Only one of them is in the contract.
sections.h: The son paid, the mother lives there

body.text: Encik Ganesan pays a contractor RM40,000 to rewire his mother's house in Klang. He signs the agreement. He pays every instalment himself.
The work is bad. Sockets spark. His mother, Puan Letchumi, is the one living with it.
She wants to sue the contractor. She has the loss, the damage and the inconvenience. What she does not have is a contract.
That single fact is the whole problem, and it has a name.
Only a party to a contract may sue upon it. A person who is not a party acquires no right to enforce the promise, even where the promise was made for that person's benefit.
body.source: The doctrine of privity of contract, received in Malaysia under the Civil Law Act 1956, s 3.

body.text: **Privity of contract** means being one of the parties to the deal. Letchumi is not, however plainly the work was meant for her.

sections.keypoint: Who supplied the consideration and who may sue are two different questions with two different answers.
sections.h: Why section 2(d) does not rescue her

body.text: Malaysian consideration is wider than the English kind. Section 2(d) of the Contracts Act 1950 says so in plain words.

When, at the desire of the promisor, the promisee or any other person has done or abstained from doing, or does or abstains from doing, or promises to do or to abstain from doing, something, such act or abstinence or promise is called a consideration for the promise.
Read the phrase the promisee or any other person. Consideration may move from somebody who is not the promisee at all.
It is tempting to run that straight into privity. If a stranger's money can be the price, why can a stranger not sue?
Because the section answers a different question. It says what counts as consideration. It says nothing about who may bring the action.

body.prompt: Letchumi's neighbour pays one instalment as a favour. Does that give the neighbour a claim against the contractor?
options: Yes, because she supplied consideration under section 2(d)
No, because supplying consideration is not the same as being a party
Only if the contractor knew where the money had come from
body.reveal: The second one. Section 2(d) widens what can count as the price of a promise. It does not widen the list of people who may sue on it. If you picked the first answer, you have made the mistake this topic is built around. Keep the two questions apart and the case law stays straight.

body.text: Kepong Prospecting Ltd v Schmidt is the decision usually cited here. It gets cited for consideration and for privity, and running the two together is the standard error.
Do not write that Malaysia has abolished privity. It has not. Section 2(d) changed where consideration may come from, and it changed nothing else.

sections.keypoint: Agency, a trust of the promise, assignment, statute and a collateral contract each get the third party in by a different door.

body.text: The rule is real, and so are the routes around it. None of them breaks privity. Each one finds the third party a contract of their own, or a right of some other kind.

items: **Agency.** If Ganesan contracted as his mother's agent, she is the real party and the difficulty disappears.
**Trust of a promise.** Where the promisee holds the benefit of the promise on trust for the third party, that party can be brought before the court.
**Assignment.** A contracting party may transfer the benefit of the contract to somebody else, who then sues in their own name.
**Statute.** Some statutes give a named person a direct claim. Insurance is the familiar example.
**Collateral contract.** A separate small contract between the promisor and the third party, supported by its own consideration.

body.text: Test agency first. It is often true on the facts and rarely argued. Ask who was named, and ask who was really doing the dealing.
Say Letchumi asked her son to arrange the rewiring, gave him the money and told him to sign for her. The argument is agency. She is then a party, and privity never bites at all.
This lesson gives no section numbers for agency. The Contracts Act 1950 deals with agency in a Part of its own, and that numbering must be checked before you cite it.
Tort is the other exit, and it is not an exception to privity. A person injured by careless work may have a claim that never depended on a contract.

sections.keypoint: Ganesan can sue, but section 74 measures the loss caused to him, and the loss was his mother's.
sections.h: What the party with the contract can recover

body.text: Turn the problem around. Ganesan has the contract, so he can sue. His trouble is the measure of what he gets.

When a contract has been broken, the party who suffers by the breach is entitled to receive compensation for any loss or damage caused to him which naturally arose in the usual course of things from the breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach.
Read the words caused to him. The section measures the loss of the party who suffers by the breach.
The contractor will say Ganesan lost nothing. He does not live in the house. The sparking sockets are not his to complain of.
The answer runs through what Ganesan actually bargained for. He paid for a sound installation in that house, and he did not get one.

body.q: Letchumi sues the contractor in her own name over the wiring. What is the first answer she will meet?
options: That the work was reasonable in the circumstances
That she is not a party to the contract and cannot sue on it
That she paid nothing towards the price
body.why: Privity is the threshold point and it is taken first. The third option confuses consideration with standing, because under section 2(d) consideration can come from anyone and still not make her a party. The first option is the trial she never reaches.

body.text: So the practical lesson here is about drafting, not litigation. Name the person who will suffer the loss as a party, and the problem never arises.
Check whether Parliament has since legislated on the rights of third parties. Several jurisdictions have done so, and a statute of that kind would move the starting point of this lesson.

lessons.source: Contracts Act 1950 (Act 136) ss 2(d) and 74; Civil Law Act 1956 s 3; Kepong Prospecting Ltd v Schmidt. Privity itself is received common law, not a provision of the Act.

Check as well whether any Malaysian statute now gives a third party a direct right to enforce a contract made for their benefit.

lessons.title: Unlawful object: how section 24 kills an agreement
lessons.summary: Section 24 lists five ways the purpose or the price of a deal can be unlawful. Any one of them makes the whole agreement void, and getting your money back afterwards is a separate fight.

sections.keypoint: Zulkifli's agreement was written, signed and witnessed, and it was worth nothing the moment it was made.
sections.h: Paying a man to arrange a licence

body.text: Encik Zulkifli wants a licence for a food stall. A man tells him he knows the right officer. For RM15,000 he will arrange it.
They write it down. Zulkifli pays RM8,000 up front. No licence ever arrives.
He wants the licence, or the RM8,000 back. He has a signed agreement, a witness and a receipt.
None of that helps him. A court will not enforce this agreement, and the reason has nothing to do with how it was made.

All agreements are contracts if they are made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and are not hereby expressly declared to be void.
Read the phrase lawful object. Formation, consent and consideration can all be perfect. If the object is unlawful the agreement fails anyway.
This is the one contract defect that a careful drafter cannot design around. It is about what the parties are doing, not how they wrote it.

sections.keypoint: Forbidden by law, defeating a law, fraudulent, injurious, or against public policy — one limb is enough.
sections.h: The five ways to be unlawful

body.text: Section 24 is a list. Read it as five separate limbs. An argument in a real case is about which limb is engaged.

The consideration or object of an agreement is unlawful if it is forbidden by law, or is of such a nature that, if permitted, it would defeat any law, or is fraudulent, or involves or implies injury to the person or property of another, or the court regards it as immoral or opposed to public policy. Every agreement of which the object or consideration is unlawful is void.

body.caption: The five limbs of section 24, with the everyday shape of each
rows: Forbidden by law
A deal to do the very thing a statute makes an offence
Would defeat any law
A deal lawful on its face, arranged to get around a statute
Fraudulent
A deal whose purpose is to cheat somebody, inside the deal or outside it
Injury to person or property
A deal to hurt somebody, or to damage what belongs to them
Immoral or against public policy
A deal the court will not lend its help to, such as one corrupting a public duty
body.alt: The five limbs of section 24. Forbidden by law catches a deal to do the very thing a statute makes an offence. Defeating a law catches a deal that is lawful on its face but arranged to get around a statute. Fraudulent catches a deal whose purpose is to cheat. Injury to person or property catches a deal to hurt someone or damage their belongings. Immoral or against public policy catches a deal the court will not help, such as one corrupting a public duty.

body.text: Zulkifli's agreement fits more than one limb. Paying for the exercise of a public duty corrupts it, and the second limb reaches an arrangement built to work around a licensing scheme.
Name the limb. An answer that says the deal is illegal, without saying which limb, has not started.
Public policy is the widest limb and the most abused. It is not a place to put an argument that would not fit anywhere else, and a court will want the policy named.

sections.keypoint: Void means there was never a contract, so the claim for the RM8,000 has to come from somewhere else.
sections.h: Void, and getting the money back

body.text: Section 24 makes the agreement void. Void means it had no legal effect from the very start.
So Zulkifli cannot sue on it. There is no promise to enforce, and no breach to complain of.
His RM8,000 is a separate question. The Act deals with restoring what somebody received under an agreement that turns out to be void.

When an agreement is discovered to be void, or when a contract becomes void, any person who has received any advantage under the agreement or contract is bound to restore it, or to make compensation for it, to the person from whom he received it.
Put simply: money paid under a void agreement normally has to go back.
Now read the opening words again. Section 66 speaks of an agreement discovered to be void.
Zulkifli knew from the beginning what he was paying for. The other side will argue that nothing was discovered, because nothing had been hidden from him.

body.prompt: Zulkifli sues for his RM8,000 back under section 66. What is the strongest answer against him?
options: That the agreement was in writing, so he is bound by its terms
That section 66 applies only to dealings in land
That he knew the object was unlawful, so nothing was discovered to be void
body.reveal: The second. Section 66 turns on an agreement discovered to be void, and a party who knew all along has trouble with that word. Do not assert this as a settled rule. It is the argument you have to meet, and it needs current authority. The first option gets it backwards, because writing does not rescue an unlawful object.

body.text: This is the contested part of the topic. Do not write that a party to an unlawful deal always recovers, or never does. Set out the argument on both sides and say which you prefer.

sections.keypoint: Part of an agreement can be unlawful without killing all of it, and restraint of trade has a provision of its own.

body.text: Two things sit just outside section 24. Both turn up in the same problem questions.
The first is an agreement that is only partly unlawful. One clause offends, and the rest is ordinary commerce.
The Contracts Act deals with that case in a provision of its own. Whether the good part survives depends on whether the unlawful part can be cut out cleanly.

This lesson gives no section number for the partly unlawful agreement, or for agreements in restraint of trade. Both have their own provisions, and both numbers must be checked in the current text before you cite them.
The second is restraint of trade. That means a promise not to compete, not to work in a trade, or not to deal with certain customers.
Malaysia treats these by statute, and the statutory position is not the English one. Do not import the English test of reasonableness without reading the Act.

A shop in Melaka is sold, and the seller promises not to open a similar shop nearby. That promise is dealt with by the Act's own provision, which carries its own exceptions. It is not settled by asking whether the promise was reasonable.
So an illegality answer ends with two checks. Is the whole agreement gone, or only part of it? And is the clause you are attacking one the Act treats separately?
Public policy moves. A judgment from thirty years ago may not describe what offends it today. This is a topic where the date of your authority matters.

lessons.source: Contracts Act 1950 (Act 136) ss 10(1), 24 and 66. The provisions on a partly unlawful agreement and on restraint of trade are referred to without section numbers on purpose.

lessons.title: Shares, capital, and what a shareholder actually owns
lessons.summary: Buying shares in a company does not buy you a slice of its lorries or its bank account. It buys a bundle of rights against the company, and the law is strict about when the company may hand money back.

sections.keypoint: Buying shares buys rights against the company, not a share of the vans in its yard.

body.text: Hafiz pays RM60,000 for 3,000 shares in Kedai Perabot Mawar Sdn Bhd. That is thirty per cent of the shares on issue. The company owns two delivery vans and a warehouse of furniture.
A year later he falls out with the other two shareholders. He wants one of the vans. He reasons that thirty per cent of the company must be thirty per cent of everything in it.

body.prompt: Hafiz holds thirty per cent of the shares. Can he take one of the company's two vans, or force the company to sell him one?
options: No, because the vans belong to the company and he owns shares in it
Yes, because he owns thirty per cent of every asset
Only if the other two shareholders agree in writing
body.reveal: The vans belong to the company. Hafiz owns shares. Those are two different kinds of property, and holding the second does not carry a slice of the first. If you picked the first answer, you reasoned the way most new shareholders do.

body.text: The company is a person in law. It owns the vans. Hafiz owns shares in that person, and a share is a different thing altogether.

A share is personal property of the member. It carries rights against the company: to vote at meetings, to be paid a dividend when one is properly declared, and to share in any surplus when the company is wound up. It does not give the member any legal or beneficial interest in the property of the company.
body.source: Companies Act 2016 (Act 777), the provisions on the nature and transferability of shares, read with the separate legal personality principle in Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd [1897] AC 22.

body.text: So ask two questions, in this order. What does the company own? And what does the member hold against the company?

sections.keypoint: Under the 2016 Act shares have no par value, so the figure on an old certificate values nothing.

body.text: Older Malaysian share certificates carry a figure. RM1 per share, usually. People read that as what the share is worth.
It never was. Par value was a floor for issuing, not a valuation. The Companies Act 2016 removed the concept.

Shares issued by a company incorporated under the Companies Act 2016 have no par or nominal value. The whole of what a subscriber pays for a share forms part of the company's share capital. The share premium account, the capital redemption reserve and the ceiling formerly called authorised capital went with par value.
body.source: Companies Act 2016 (Act 777), the share capital provisions abolishing par value, together with the transitional provisions for companies incorporated under the repealed Companies Act 1965.

body.caption: Share capital before and after the Companies Act 2016
rows: Par or nominal value printed on each share
Gone. A share has an issue price and no face value.
Authorised capital, a ceiling written into the constitution
Gone. The company issues what the members allow it to issue.
Share premium account
Merged into share capital.
Capital redemption reserve
Merged into share capital.
body.alt: A table of four old share capital concepts and what became of each. Par value and authorised capital were abolished outright. The share premium account and the capital redemption reserve were both merged into ordinary share capital.

body.text: This matters when you read an old document. A constitution drafted in 2010 may still speak of authorised capital. That clause now describes nothing.
Do not tell a client their shares are worth RM1 each because the certificate says so. Value comes from what the company is worth and from the rights the share carries.

sections.keypoint: A company pays dividends out of profits, and only while its directors are sure it stays solvent.
sections.h: Taking money out of the company

body.text: Hafiz wants a return on his RM60,000. Money moves lawfully from a company to a shareholder in only a few ways.

items: **A dividend**, declared out of profits available for distribution.
**Salary or fees**, if the shareholder also works for the company and the payment was properly approved.
**Repayment of a loan** the shareholder made to the company.
**A share of the surplus** on a winding up, once every creditor has been paid in full.

body.text: A company may only make a distribution to its shareholders out of profits available for distribution, and only if the company is solvent. The directors must be satisfied that the company will be able to pay its debts as they become due within twelve months after the distribution. A director who authorises a distribution knowing the company is not solvent may be ordered to repay the amount to the company.
body.source: Companies Act 2016 (Act 777), the provisions on distributions to shareholders and on the liability of directors for improper distributions.

body.text: Drawing cash through the year and calling it a dividend at audit time is not a dividend. With no distributable profit behind it, the payment is a return of capital and it can be clawed back.

Reducing share capital is a separate exercise with its own procedure. A company does it either on a solvency statement signed by the directors, or with the confirmation of the court. Neither is a matter of writing a cheque.

sections.keypoint: The register of members decides who is a member; a signed transfer form on its own does not.
sections.h: Becoming a member, and getting out

body.text: Hafiz signs a transfer form selling his shares to his cousin. He assumes the cousin is now a shareholder.
Not yet. The register of members is what makes a person a member. Until the company enters the cousin's name, Hafiz is still on the register and still the member.

A person becomes a member of a company limited by shares when their name is entered in the register of members. Shares are transferred by a proper instrument of transfer delivered to the company, and the transferee becomes a member when that transfer is registered.
body.source: Companies Act 2016 (Act 777), the provisions on the register of members and on the transfer and transmission of shares.

items: **Transfer** is a sale or a gift. It needs an instrument, and in a private company the directors may hold a power to refuse to register it.
**Transmission** happens by operation of law, on death or on bankruptcy. The personal representative or the trustee steps into the entitlement without a transfer form.
**A private company** restricts the right to transfer its shares, caps how many members it may have, and may not offer its shares to the public.

body.q: Rosnah dies holding shares in a private company. Her son is her sole beneficiary. What is his position?
options: The entitlement passes by transmission, and he becomes a member when the company registers him
He must buy the shares back from the company
He is a member as soon as the will is read
body.why: Transmission moves the entitlement by operation of law. It still does not put a name on the register, and the register is what decides membership.

lessons.source: Companies Act 2016 (Act 777), the Parts on share capital, on distributions to shareholders, and on the register and transfer of shares.

lessons.title: Directors: appointment, removal, and being barred from the job
lessons.summary: Members appoint directors and can usually remove them, though a private company's constitution can make removal harder. The Act also decides who may hold the job at all, and it treats some people as directors who were never appointed.

sections.keypoint: Votes remove a director in a private company only if the constitution has not set up something else.
sections.h: Norhayati wants her brother-in-law off the board

body.text: Norhayati holds sixty per cent of Perabot Seri Muda Sdn Bhd. Her brother-in-law Rajan holds forty per cent and sits on the board. He has stopped turning up and stopped answering.
She wants him removed. She has the votes. The question is whether votes alone are enough.

body.prompt: Norhayati holds sixty per cent of a private company. Can she remove a director by calling a meeting and voting him out?
options: Yes, always — a majority of members can remove any director
Usually, unless the company's own constitution provides otherwise
No, only a court can remove a director
body.reveal: Read the constitution first. A private company may remove a director by ordinary resolution unless its constitution says otherwise, and some constitutions say exactly that. A shareholders' agreement can add a further hurdle on top.

body.text: In a private company, the members may remove a director before the end of that director's term by ordinary resolution, unless the constitution provides otherwise. In a public company, the members may remove a director by ordinary resolution despite anything in the constitution or in any agreement, and special notice of the resolution must be given.
body.source: Companies Act 2016 (Act 777), the provisions on the removal of directors of private and public companies.

body.text: Removal ends the office. It does not end a service contract. If Rajan is also an employee under a written contract, removing him may cost the company damages.
The two limbs are not the same rule. A public company constitution cannot contract out of removal by the members; a private company constitution can shape it.

sections.keypoint: A director must be a living adult, not disqualified, and ordinarily resident in Malaysia.
sections.h: Who is allowed to hold the job

body.text: Not everyone may be a director. The Act sets a short list, and a company that ignores it has a hole in its board.

items: **A natural person.** A company cannot be a director of a Malaysian company.
**At least eighteen years of age**, and of sound mind.
**Not an undischarged bankrupt**, unless leave is given by the court or by the Director General of Insolvency.
**Not disqualified**, whether by a conviction the Act names or by an order of the court.
**Ordinarily resident in Malaysia**, by having a principal place of residence here.

body.text: A private company must have at least one director and a public company at least two. Every director counted towards that minimum must be a natural person who is at least eighteen years of age, is not disqualified, and ordinarily resides in Malaysia by having a principal place of residence in Malaysia.
body.source: Companies Act 2016 (Act 777), the provisions on the qualification of directors and on the minimum number of directors.

body.text: Residence is about where a person actually lives, not about citizenship. A Malaysian who has moved abroad for good may not count towards the minimum, and a foreigner living here may.
The first directors are named in the application to incorporate. After that the members appoint, by ordinary resolution, unless the constitution provides another way.
One extra rule applies to public companies. Each director must be voted on individually, so a single resolution appointing a whole slate is void unless the meeting first agrees to it without dissent.

sections.keypoint: You cannot resign your way out if that would leave the company below its minimum number of directors.

body.text: Rajan reads the constitution, sees that Norhayati can remove him, and resigns first. Norhayati stays on the board, so the company still has a director. His notice takes effect.
Change one fact. Suppose Rajan were the company's only director. His notice would leave the company with none, and the Act does not allow that.

A director may resign by giving written notice to the company at its registered office. A resignation is ineffective if it would leave the company without the minimum number of directors required by the Act, and the director remains in office despite having given notice.
body.source: Companies Act 2016 (Act 777), the provisions on the resignation of directors and on vacation of office.

body.caption: How a directorship ends, and what each way leaves behind
rows: Resignation
The director, by written notice to the registered office
Liability for everything done while in office.
Removal
The members, by resolution
A possible claim by the director for breach of a service contract.
Vacation of office
The Act itself, on bankruptcy or on disqualification
Liability, and an offence if the person carries on acting.
Disqualification
A court, after a conviction or an insolvent liquidation
A bar on acting as a director for the period fixed.
body.alt: A table of four ways a directorship ends. Resignation is the director's own act and leaves past liability intact. Removal is the members' act and may leave the company owing damages under a service contract. Vacation of office happens automatically on bankruptcy or disqualification. A court may also disqualify a person after a conviction or an insolvent liquidation, barring them for a fixed period.

body.text: Acting as a director while disqualified is an offence. Resigning does not wash off what you did while you held the post, and a liquidator can still come after you for it.

sections.keypoint: Duties follow the job as it is actually done, not the title on a company search.

body.text: Encik Faizal is not on the company search. He is not in the register of directors. He is at every meeting, and the two registered directors do what he tells them.

The Act reaches him anyway. It defines a director to include a person occupying the position of director, whatever the person is called. It also reaches a person on whose instructions the directors are accustomed to act.
So Faizal carries a director's duties without ever having been appointed to anything.

A director of a company shall at all times exercise his powers in accordance with the Act, for a proper purpose and in good faith in the best interest of the company. A director shall exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence.

A director or officer shall not, without the consent or ratification of a general meeting, use the property of the company, any information acquired by virtue of his position, his position itself, any opportunity of the company, or engage in business in competition with the company, so as to gain directly or indirectly a benefit for himself or any other person, or to cause detriment to the company.

body.q: Faizal was never appointed a director, but the board follows his instructions. He diverts a supply contract to a firm he owns. What is his position?
options: He may be treated as a director, so the duties in sections 213 and 218 reach him
Nothing follows, because he was never appointed
Only the two registered directors can be liable for it
body.why: The Act defines a director by the position occupied and by the instructions the board is accustomed to follow. Appointment is evidence of the job, not the whole of it.

lessons.source: Companies Act 2016 (Act 777), sections 213 and 218, together with the Part on directors covering appointment, qualification, resignation, removal and disqualification.

lessons.title: Charges: what a lender takes when it lends to a company
lessons.summary: A company borrows by giving security over its assets, and a floating charge lets it go on trading with the very things it has pledged. Lodge the charge late and the debt survives while the security does not.

sections.keypoint: A fixed charge pins named assets; a floating charge hovers over a class that keeps changing.

body.text: Logistik Sinar Sdn Bhd borrows RM800,000. The bank takes security over two named lorries. It also takes security over all present and future stock and book debts.
Encik Sivam runs the company. He needs to know whether he can still sell stock on Monday morning without ringing the bank.

body.prompt: The bank holds security over two named lorries and over all present and future stock. Which of those can the company sell without asking the bank?
options: Neither, because both are pledged to the bank
Both, until the bank objects in writing
The stock, but not the lorries
body.reveal: The stock. Security over a shifting class of assets is a floating charge, and the company trades on as usual until it crystallises. The lorries are named, so that charge is fixed and the company cannot sell them free of it.

body.text: A fixed charge attaches to identified property at once, and the company cannot dispose of that property free of the charge without the consent of the chargee. A floating charge is taken over a class of assets that changes in the ordinary course of business, and the company may deal with those assets in that ordinary course until the charge crystallises.
body.source: The general law on fixed and floating charges as applied in Malaysia, read with the provisions of the Companies Act 2016 (Act 777) on charges created by a company.

body.text: The label in the debenture does not settle which it is. A court looks at how much freedom the company was actually left with.

sections.keypoint: Crystallisation freezes the class, and from that moment the charge behaves like a fixed one.
sections.h: When a floating charge stops floating

body.text: A floating charge is useful precisely because it does not interfere. That ends on a stated event.

items: The company defaults and the chargee steps in.
A receiver is appointed under the debenture.
The company goes into winding up.
The company stops carrying on business.
An event the debenture itself names as crystallising the charge.

body.text: The bank appoints a receiver on a Tuesday. The stock sitting in the warehouse that morning is caught by the charge. A customer who bought and collected goods on Monday took them free of it.
Debentures often carry a negative pledge: a promise not to grant a later charge ranking ahead of this one. Whether it binds a later lender turns on what that lender knew.
Crystallisation matters most on the day a company fails. Until then the two kinds of charge feel the same to whoever is running the business.

sections.keypoint: An unlodged charge leaves the lender unsecured, with the loan called in immediately on top.
sections.h: Lodging the charge, and the cost of being late

body.text: A charge created by a company must be lodged with the Registrar of Companies. There is a short window, counted in days from the day the charge is created.
Miss it and the consequence is severe. It falls on the lender, not on the borrower.

A charge created by a company over property of a class specified in the Act must be lodged with the Registrar within the period the Act allows. Where it is not lodged within that period, the charge is void against the liquidator and against any creditor of the company. The money secured by the charge does not cease to be owed; it becomes immediately payable.
body.source: Companies Act 2016 (Act 777), the provisions on the registration of charges created by a company and on the effect of failing to register.

body.caption: What lodging a charge on time protects, and what being late costs
rows: The security stands against the liquidator.
The security is void against the liquidator.
The lender takes its asset ahead of unsecured creditors.
The lender queues with the unsecured creditors.
Later lenders are on notice from the public register.
Later lenders find nothing, and may rank ahead.
The loan runs to its agreed term.
The loan becomes immediately payable.
body.alt: A table comparing a charge lodged in time with one that was not. Lodged in time, the security stands against the liquidator and the lender is paid ahead of unsecured creditors. Later lenders are put on notice, and the loan runs its agreed term. Not lodged in time, the security is void against the liquidator and the lender queues with unsecured creditors. Later lenders find nothing on the register, and the loan falls due at once.

body.text: This is also why you search before you lend. A company search at the Companies Commission of Malaysia shows the charges already registered against that company.
The debt survives an unregistered charge. Clients often hear that a late charge is void and assume the loan is gone. It is not, and it is now due at once.

sections.keypoint: Between two charges over one asset, kind, timing and registration together decide the order.

body.text: Two lenders can hold charges over the same asset. Three things sort them out.

items: **Kind.** A fixed charge over an asset generally beats a floating charge over the same asset, even one created earlier.
**Time.** As between charges of the same kind, the earlier one generally ranks first.
**Registration.** A charge not lodged in time is void against the liquidator and other creditors, so it ranks nowhere useful.

body.text: A receiver appointed under a debenture answers to the chargee who appointed them. The receiver is not there to look after the company, its directors, or its other creditors.
One more rule waits at the end of the story. In a winding up a floating charge is paid after the preferential debts, and employees' claims sit among those.

body.q: A bank holds a floating charge over stock and never lodged it with the Registrar. The company is now wound up. Where does the bank stand?
options: It takes the stock, because the charge was validly created
It ranks after the preferential debts but ahead of the unsecured creditors
The charge is void against the liquidator, so the bank claims as an unsecured creditor
body.why: Creation and registration are different steps. The charge was validly created and is still void against the liquidator, which leaves the bank in the unsecured queue with everyone else.

lessons.source: Companies Act 2016 (Act 777), the Division on the registration of charges created by a company; and the general law on fixed and floating charges as applied in Malaysia.

lessons.title: Winding up, and the queue for what is left
lessons.summary: When a company is wound up a liquidator gathers what it has and pays it out in a fixed order. Shareholders stand at the back of that queue, and the money usually runs out long before it reaches them.

sections.keypoint: Before asking what a creditor will be paid, work out who is standing in front of them.

body.text: Puan Chandra supplies packaging to Bina Kuat Sdn Bhd. She is owed RM40,000. The cheques have stopped.
The company owes a bank RM500,000 on a secured loan. Eleven staff are two months unpaid. There is a warehouse of stock and RM90,000 in the bank.

body.prompt: Bina Kuat is wound up. The cash and the stock are all there is. Where does Puan Chandra's RM40,000 stand?
options: She is behind the secured bank, the costs of the winding up and the employees, and shares what is left with other unsecured creditors
She shares the money equally with the bank and the staff
She is paid first, because the goods she supplied are still in the warehouse
body.reveal: An unsecured trade creditor stands near the back. Only the shareholders are behind her. That is the ordinary outcome, and it is why a supplier's credit terms are a legal decision as much as a commercial one.

body.text: A winding up asks three questions. Which route is being used? What is there to sell? And who stands ahead of you in the queue?
Selling goods that are still in the debtor's warehouse gives you nothing extra by itself. Ownership passed on delivery unless the contract kept title with you.

sections.keypoint: Whether the directors can honestly sign a declaration of solvency decides who controls the process.
sections.h: Three routes to the same end

body.text: There are two voluntary routes and one through the court. Which applies turns on whether the company can pay everyone in full.

body.caption: The three routes into a winding up
rows: Members' voluntary winding up
The members, by special resolution
The company can pay its debts in full, and the directors sign a declaration of solvency.
Creditors' voluntary winding up
The members resolve, but the creditors choose the liquidator
No declaration of solvency can honestly be made.
Winding up by the court
A petitioner, usually an unpaid creditor
The company is unable to pay its debts, or another ground the Act lists applies.
body.alt: A table of the three routes into a winding up. A members' voluntary winding up is begun by the members by special resolution, and needs a declaration of solvency from the directors. A creditors' voluntary winding up begins with a members' resolution too, but the creditors choose the liquidator. It is used when no declaration of solvency can honestly be made. A winding up by the court begins with a petition, usually from an unpaid creditor, on the ground that the company cannot pay its debts.

body.text: A company is deemed to be unable to pay its debts where a creditor to whom the company owes a sum exceeding the amount fixed by the Act serves a written demand at the registered office of the company, and the company for the period allowed by the Act neglects to pay the sum, or to secure or compound for it to the reasonable satisfaction of the creditor.
body.source: Companies Act 2016 (Act 777), the provisions on winding up by the court and on when a company is deemed unable to pay its debts.

body.text: A statutory demand is not a collection tool for a disputed debt. Petition on a debt the company genuinely disputes and the petition can be struck out, with costs against you.

One further ground is worth knowing. A member may petition to wind the company up on the just and equitable ground. That ground answers a breakdown between the people running the company, not an unpaid bill.

sections.keypoint: The liquidator displaces the board and can unwind payments the company made before it failed.

body.text: The liquidator takes control of the company's property. The directors' powers stop. The company itself carries on existing until it is dissolved.

items: Gets in the company's assets and sells them.
Investigates why the company failed, and reports on it.
Disclaims onerous property, such as a lease nobody wants.
Challenges transactions made before the winding up that put one creditor ahead of the rest.
Distributes what is left, in the order the Act sets.

body.text: Paying a friendly supplier in full a month before the winding up is the classic problem. The liquidator can ask the court to undo it.
A director who kept the company trading on credit with intent to defraud creditors can be ordered to pay the company's debts personally. Separate legal personality does not survive that finding.

sections.keypoint: A fixed chargee takes its asset outside the queue; the members are last and usually get nothing.
sections.h: The order the money goes out in

body.text: Property subject to a valid fixed charge is applied to the secured creditor to the extent of the security. The remaining assets are applied first to the costs and expenses of the winding up, including the remuneration of the liquidator, then to the preferential debts listed in the Act, then to claims secured by a floating charge, then rateably among the unsecured creditors, and last of all to the members.
body.source: Companies Act 2016 (Act 777), the provisions on the priority of payments in a winding up and on preferential debts.

body.caption: The queue in a winding up
rows: Outside the queue
A creditor holding a valid fixed charge
The charged asset, up to the amount owed.
First
The winding up itself
The liquidator's remuneration, and the costs and expenses of the winding up.
Second
Preferential debts
Employees' wages, workers' compensation, provident fund contributions and taxes, in the order and up to the limits the Act sets.
Third
A creditor holding a floating charge
Whatever the charge catches, once the preferential debts are met.
Fourth
Unsecured creditors
A rateable share of whatever remains.
Last
The members
Any surplus, according to the rights attached to their shares.
body.alt: A six row table of the winding up queue. A fixed charge holder stands outside it and takes the charged asset. Then come the costs of the winding up, then the preferential debts such as employees' wages and provident fund contributions. Floating charge holders follow, then the unsecured creditors sharing rateably, and last of all the members.

body.text: Preferential debts are capped. A long serving employee may be preferential up to the limit the Act sets, and an ordinary unsecured creditor for everything above it.

body.q: After the bank takes its charged warehouse, RM120,000 is left. The liquidator's costs are RM70,000 and preferential wage claims come to RM60,000. What do the unsecured trade creditors receive?
options: A rateable share of the RM120,000
Nothing, because the costs and the preferential wages exhaust the fund
A rateable share of RM50,000
body.why: The costs of the winding up are paid first, which leaves RM50,000. Preferential wage claims of RM60,000 come next and take all of it. The queue ends before the trade creditors are reached.

lessons.source: Companies Act 2016 (Act 777), the Part on winding up: the modes of winding up, the powers of a liquidator, and the priority of payments and preferential debts.

lessons.glossaryDense: The rule block is the order of payment itself, and the order IS the lesson. Turning a queue into a paragraph loses the one property that matters about it — that it is a sequence, and each place in it is a different answer for a creditor asking where they stand.

lessons.title: Four grades of fault, from intention down to negligence
lessons.summary: The Penal Code does not use one test for a guilty mind. It uses four graded standards, and every offence names the one it needs.

sections.keypoint: Every offence names its own fault standard, so read the words before you argue about blame.
sections.h: One lorry, four states of mind

body.text: Encik Zainal drives a lorry along the Federal Highway. He clips a motorcyclist, who dies at the roadside.
Everyone agrees on what his lorry did. The whole argument is about what was in his head.
That argument has four possible answers here. They are not shades of one idea. They are separate standards, and the Penal Code names each of them.

items: **Intention** — he meant that result to happen.
**Knowledge** — he did not want it, but he saw it coming as likely.
**Rashness** — he saw the risk and ran it anyway.
**Negligence** — he never saw a risk that a careful driver would have seen.

body.text: The four sit in order, from the most demanding down to the least. Moving down the ladder makes the prosecution's job easier.
Do not start from how bad the conduct feels. Start from the words of the section, because the section has already picked its standard for you.

sections.keypoint: Intention is about what you wanted; knowledge is about what you saw coming.

body.text: The Penal Code, s 299, sets the top two rungs side by side. It is worth reading for that alone.
Section 299 reaches a person who causes death with the knowledge that the act is likely to cause death, as well as a person who intends death or intends an injury likely to cause it.
Notice what that knowledge limb does. It catches a person who never wanted anybody to die.
Knowledge asks what this accused actually foresaw. It is a real state of mind, and it has to be proved like any other.
Zainal overtakes on a blind bend at speed. He says he hoped nothing was coming the other way. If he in fact saw that a crash was likely, that is knowledge.

body.prompt: Zainal insists he never wanted anyone hurt. Does that answer a charge built on knowledge?
options: Yes — without a wish for the result there is no fault
Only if he also kept within the speed limit
No — knowledge asks what he foresaw, not what he wanted
body.reveal: Wanting a result and foreseeing one are different questions. The second answer is the everyday meaning of a guilty mind, and the Code does not use it. The third is the near miss, because keeping to a speed limit does not stop a driver foreseeing a crash.

sections.keypoint: Rashness runs a risk you actually saw; negligence misses a risk you ought to have seen.

body.text: Below knowledge sit rashness and negligence. The Penal Code uses both words, and they do not mean the same thing.
A rash person turns their mind to the risk. They see it, and they go ahead anyway, hoping it will not come off.
A negligent person never turns their mind to it at all. They simply fall short of the care a reasonable person would take.
The Penal Code creates separate offences for causing death, and for causing hurt, by an act done rashly or negligently, and it treats the rash act as the graver of the two.
body.source: Penal Code, the provisions on rash and negligent acts in the chapter on offences affecting the human body; section number deliberately not stated — see this lesson's verify note.

body.text: This lesson gives you no section number for those offences. Look them up in the Code yourself, and write down the date you checked.

sections.keypoint: Match the facts to the standard the section names, then argue the rung above and the rung below.

body.caption: The four standards, and the question each one asks
rows: Intention
Did he mean this result?
He meant something else entirely
Knowledge
Did he foresee it as likely?
He never turned his mind to it
Rashness
Did he see the risk and run it?
He never saw the risk at all
Negligence
Would a careful person have seen it?
A careful person would have done the same
body.alt: Four fault standards in a table. Intention asks whether he meant the result, and it fails if he meant something else. Knowledge asks whether he foresaw the result as likely, and it fails if he never turned his mind to it. Rashness asks whether he saw the risk and ran it, and it fails if he never saw the risk. Negligence asks whether a careful person would have seen the risk, and it fails if a careful person would have done the same.

body.text: In an answer, name the standard the section uses. Then test the facts against it, and say what the next rung down would need.

body.q: A charge requires knowledge. The evidence shows only that a careful person would have seen the danger. What follows?
options: The charge fails on that element, though an offence built on negligence may still fit
The charge is made out, because the danger was obvious
Knowledge is presumed once the danger is obvious
body.why: Obviousness supports negligence. It does not by itself show that this accused foresaw anything, and knowledge is about what he actually foresaw. The first and third answers both slide from what a reasonable person would see to what this person did see.

lessons.source: Penal Code (Act 574), s 299, for the intention and knowledge limbs. lessons.title: The Code defines its own words
lessons.summary: Ordinary English will not tell you what dishonestly or good faith mean in the Penal Code. The Code defines them itself, in a chapter near the front that governs every offence after it.

sections.keypoint: A word in the Code can look ordinary and still carry a meaning the Code has fixed for it.
sections.h: A bicycle, and an honest mistake

body.text: Puan Kalsom wheels a bicycle out of a rack at a flat in Cheras. It is not hers. It looks exactly like hers, and hers is missing.
Theft under the Penal Code, s 378, requires her to have acted dishonestly. So did she?
You cannot answer that from ordinary English. Dishonestly is a defined term, and the Code fixes what it means.
The same is true of a whole set of words. They sit together in the Code's chapter of general explanations, near the front.

sections.keypoint: Dishonesty here is tied to wrongful gain or wrongful loss, not to a general sense of bad character.

body.text: Start with the word that carries the most weight. It appears in theft, in criminal breach of trust and in cheating.

The Penal Code defines a person as acting dishonestly when the person acts with the intention of causing wrongful gain to one person, or wrongful loss to another. Wrongful gain and wrongful loss are themselves defined terms, turning on property a person is not entitled to get or is entitled to keep.
body.source: Penal Code, the chapter of general explanations, the definitions of dishonestly, wrongful gain and wrongful loss; section number deliberately not stated — see this lesson's verify note.

body.text: Put simply: dishonesty in this Code is about property moving where it should not.
Go back to Kalsom. She believed the bicycle was hers, so she intended no wrongful gain and no wrongful loss.
The element fails, and the charge fails with it. Her mistake did not make her careless. It made her not dishonest.
The same defined word does the same work in s 405 and in s 415 of that Code.
An honest claim of right answers all three of those property offences. It is an argument about an element, and not a plea for sympathy.

sections.keypoint: Three more defined words change results quietly, because each reads differently from its everyday twin.
sections.h: Good faith, voluntarily, and acts that are omissions

items: **Good faith** — the Penal Code ties it to due care and attention. A belief held carelessly is not held in good faith, however sincere it is.
**Voluntarily** — a person causes a result voluntarily if they cause it by means they knew, or had reason to believe, were likely to cause it.
**Act** — a single word can cover a series of acts, and an illegal omission can count as an act.
**Reason to believe** — a lower bar than knowing. It asks what a person had cause to think, given what was in front of them.

body.text: Encik Ravi signs a delivery note without reading it. He says he believed the goods had arrived. Sincerity will not carry him if he took no care at all.
Look at what the omission point does. A duty to act, broken by doing nothing, can put a person inside an offence written in terms of acts.

body.prompt: Does a sincere but careless belief count as good faith under the Penal Code?
options: Yes — sincerity is what good faith has always meant
No — the Code's own definition brings in due care and attention
Only where the offence carries a light sentence
body.reveal: The everyday meaning of good faith is honesty on its own. The Code adds care, so a belief nobody bothered to check can fail the test even when it is genuine. The third answer invents a rule about sentence that the definitions simply do not contain.

sections.keypoint: These provisions sit at the front of the Code because they run through everything that follows them.
sections.h: Why the front of the Code is worth reading first

body.text: General explanations are easy to skip. They read like a dictionary, and the offences look far more interesting.
Skipping them is how answers go wrong. A defined word decides an element, and an element decides the charge.
Section 6 of the Penal Code belongs to that same part of it. It tells you that every definition of an offence is read subject to the general exceptions, even where the section never mentions them.
So the front of the Code does two jobs at once. It fixes the vocabulary, and it attaches the exceptions.

body.q: Where should you look first when a section uses a familiar word such as dishonestly or good faith?
options: In a dictionary of ordinary English
In the Code's own chapter of general explanations
In a reported case on that offence
body.why: The Code defines these words for itself, and its definition beats both ordinary usage and your instinct. Cases still matter, but they are interpreting the defined term rather than replacing it.

lessons.title: Robbery and extortion: what force adds
lessons.summary: Force and fear turn an ordinary property offence into a graver one. Which offence you end up with depends on how the owner's will was overcome, and on when.

sections.keypoint: The same handbag can be taken in three ways, and each way carries a different offence.
sections.h: Three grabs at a night market

body.text: Encik Ganesan runs a stall at a night market in Ipoh. Three things happen near it on one evening.

items: A young man lifts a handbag off a stall and walks away before anybody notices.
He pulls a second bag from a woman's shoulder, shoving her hard to get it free.
He tells a trader that the stall will burn tonight unless RM500 is handed over, and the trader pays.

body.text: The property is the same kind in all three. The offences are not.
The earlier property lesson asked one question: how did the accused come to have the thing? This lesson adds a second question.
Was the owner's will overcome, and if so, by force or by fear? That is what separates the grave property offences from the plain ones.

sections.keypoint: In extortion the victim hands the property across, because a threat has put them in fear.

body.text: Take the trader who paid RM500. He was not robbed of it in the ordinary sense, because he handed it across himself.
He handed it across because he had been put in fear of injury. That fear is what the Penal Code aims at in extortion.

Extortion is committed by a person who intentionally puts another in fear of injury, and thereby dishonestly induces that person to deliver property, or to deliver anything signed or sealed that may be converted into a valuable security.
body.source: Penal Code, the provision defining extortion; section number deliberately not stated — see this lesson's verify note.

body.text: Now line that up against cheating, in s 415 of the same Code. There too the victim hands the property over willingly.
The difference is the lever. Cheating works by a lie, and extortion works by fear.

body.caption: Three ways an owner's will is overcome
rows: Theft, s 378
Taken out of possession
Nothing — consent was never given
Cheating, s 415
Handed over
A deception
Extortion
Handed over
Fear of injury
body.alt: Three offences compared. Theft under section 378: the property is taken out of possession, and consent was never given at all. Cheating under section 415: the property is handed over, and a deception is what overcame the will. Extortion, whose section number this lesson does not state: the property is handed over, and fear of injury is what overcame the will.

sections.keypoint: Robbery is not a fresh way of taking; it is theft or extortion done with force or fear at the time.
sections.h: Robbery is built on top of the others

body.text: Robbery in the Penal Code sits on top of the two offences above. You cannot reach it without finding one of them first.

Robbery is theft, or extortion, aggravated by the offender causing or attempting to cause death, hurt or wrongful restraint, or fear of any of these, in order to commit the offence or to carry away the property obtained by it.
body.source: Penal Code, the provision defining robbery; section number deliberately not stated — see this lesson's verify note.

body.text: Timing carries a lot of the weight. The force must be used in committing the taking, or in getting away with what was taken.
The shove that freed the second handbag was force used in order to take it. That is robbery, and not merely theft.
Force used long afterwards, for some unrelated reason, does not turn an earlier theft into robbery. Ask when the force was used, and what it was used for.

sections.keypoint: Name the base offence first, then say exactly what the force or the fear adds to it.

body.text: An answer that says robbery without identifying the theft underneath it has skipped a step. The grave offence borrows its elements from the plain one.
So work in order. Find the base offence, look for force or fear, then check when that force or fear was used.

body.q: A man snatches a phone from a table and runs. A bystander grabs him, and he punches the bystander to get away. Is that robbery?
options: No, never — the theft was complete the moment he picked the phone up
Yes, automatically — any violence after a theft makes it robbery
It is arguable, because force used to carry away the property is inside the definition
body.why: The definition reaches force used in carrying away the property, so the punch is capable of counting. The first answer seals the theft off at the moment of taking. The third goes too far the other way, because violence for some unrelated reason would not qualify.

body.text: This lesson names no section for robbery or for extortion. Find both in the Penal Code, and record the numbers with the date you checked.

lessons.title: Forgery: when the document itself lies
lessons.summary: Forgery is not simply writing something untrue on paper. It is making a document that lies about how it came to exist, and that difference decides the charge.

sections.keypoint: A false statement and a false document are different things, and only one of them is forgery.
sections.h: A letter that was never signed

body.text: Nurul is a clerk at a small firm in Johor Bahru. A client needs a letter of support from her employer.
She types the letter and signs her employer's name at the bottom. The letter goes out that afternoon.
Now change one detail. Suppose she signs her own name instead, and writes something untrue inside the letter.
Both letters mislead the person who reads them. Only the first one is a false document, and that is the distinction this lesson turns on.

sections.keypoint: A document is false when it lies about who made it, or when, or with whose authority.

body.text: Think about what a document tells a reader before anyone reads a word of it.
It says who made it. It says roughly when, and it often says on whose authority.
Forgery attacks that layer. The document tells a lie about its own making.

The Penal Code treats a document as false where a person dishonestly or fraudulently makes, signs, seals or executes it so that it appears to have been made by someone who did not make it, or at a time when it was not made, or where it is altered after execution without lawful authority.
body.source: Penal Code, the provision on making a false document; section number deliberately not stated — see this lesson's verify note.

body.text: Nurul's first letter fails on the first limb. It appears to have been signed by her employer, and he never signed anything.
Her second letter passes that test. It really was made by her, and it says so on its face.

body.prompt: The second letter contains a plain lie. Is that forgery?
options: No — the document is genuine, even though what it says is untrue
Yes — a document containing a lie is a false document
Yes, but only where somebody relied on it
body.reveal: A lie written into a genuine document is a lie in a document. Forgery needs the document itself to be false about its own making. The second answer is the natural reading of the word, and it is the mistake this area is famous for.

sections.keypoint: Making a false document is not enough on its own; the Code also asks what it was made for.

body.text: A false document made as a joke, or as a classroom exercise, is not yet forgery.
The Penal Code asks about purpose. It looks for an intention of a particular kind, and the list is short enough to learn.

items: To cause damage or injury to the public, or to any person
To support a claim or a title
To cause a person to part with property
To make a person enter into an express or implied contract
To commit fraud, or so that fraud may be committed

body.text: That list explains why forgery so often sits beside a property charge. The false document is the tool, and the gain is the point.

body.caption: Three things the Code keeps apart
rows: Signing another person's name to a letter
The document's own making
Forgery
Telling a lie so that money is handed over
The statement, not the document
Cheating, s 415
Putting a forged letter into use as genuine
The document, and the use made of it
Using a forged document
body.alt: Three offences kept apart. Signing another person's name to a letter makes the document's own making false, and that is forgery. Telling a lie so that money is handed over makes the statement false rather than the document, and that is cheating under section 415. Putting a forged letter into use as genuine involves both a false document and the use made of it. That is a separate offence, and this lesson does not state its number.

sections.keypoint: The person who makes a false document and the person who uses it need not be the same person.
sections.h: Using it is its own offence

body.text: Forgery is complete once the false document is made. Nobody has to be deceived by it, and nobody has to lose anything.
The Penal Code deals separately with a person who uses a forged document as genuine, knowing or having reason to believe that it is forged.
So two people can be charged out of one letter. One of them made it, and the other put it to work.

body.q: Nurul's client posts the letter to a bank, knowing whose signature is really on it. What is his position?
options: He is a witness only, because he made nothing himself
He may be liable for using a forged document as genuine
He may be liable for forgery, because he is the one who benefited
body.why: Using a forged document as genuine is a separate offence, and knowledge or reason to believe is what it turns on. He did not make the document, so the making offence does not fit him at all.

body.text: This lesson numbers nothing but the cheating provision. Open the Penal Code at the chapter dealing with documents, and write the rest down yourself.

lessons.source: Penal Code (Act 574), s 415, used only for the contrast with cheating. lessons.title: Assault, battery, and being shut in
lessons.summary: Three torts protect the body and its freedom, and none of them asks whether you were hurt. Trespass to the person is complete the moment the interference happens.

sections.keypoint: Trespass to the person is complete without proof of damage, which is what separates it from negligence.
sections.h: Three torts that need no injury

body.text: Encik Ravi is queuing at a bank in Klang. A guard grabs his arm, marches him to a back room, and locks the door. Nobody hits him. Nobody hurts him.
Ravi has a claim anyway. Three separate torts cover what happened to him, and not one of them requires an injury.
Negligence gives nobody a claim without damage. Trespass to the person is the opposite. The wrong is the interference itself.

Trespass to the person is committed by a direct and intentional interference with another person's body or liberty. It is actionable per se, meaning the claimant need prove no damage. The three forms are assault, battery and false imprisonment.
body.source: General principle of the law of tort, received in Malaysia under the Civil Law Act 1956, s 3.

items: **Assault** — making someone reasonably apprehend immediate unlawful contact.
**Battery** — actually applying unlawful force to another person.
**False imprisonment** — completely restraining someone's freedom of movement, without lawful justification.

body.text: Ravi may have all three. The grab is a battery. The march to the room may be an assault. The locked door is a false imprisonment.
These words also appear in the Penal Code, where they carry their own statutory meanings. Do not import a criminal definition into a civil claim.

sections.keypoint: Assault is about what the victim expects; battery is about what the defendant does to them.

body.text: These two are taught together and are constantly mixed up. Keep them apart by asking where the wrong happened.
Assault happens in the victim's mind. They must reasonably expect immediate unlawful contact. No touch is needed.
Battery happens on the victim's body. Any unlawful contact will do, and it need not hurt at all.
A man raises a parang at Puan Aishah across a coffee shop table. That is an assault. If he then shoves her shoulder, that is a battery as well.
Hostility in the everyday sense is not required. An unwanted touch can be a battery even when it is gentle.
But ordinary life involves contact. Being jostled at a Ramadan bazaar is not a battery, because that contact is generally accepted.

body.prompt: The guard swings a fist at Ravi from behind, and Ravi never sees it coming. It misses. Has the guard committed an assault?
options: No — Ravi never apprehended the contact
Yes — the guard meant to hit him
Yes — a swung fist is always an assault
body.reveal: Assault protects the victim from the fear of contact. A blow nobody sees coming produces no fear. The guard may have attempted a crime, and he commits a battery if he connects. But there is no assault, because the element this tort protects was never touched.

sections.keypoint: The restraint must be complete, but the victim need not know about it at the time.

body.text: False imprisonment does not need a prison. A locked room, a held arm, or a refusal to open a gate can each be enough.
Two things do the work. The restraint must be total, and it must be without lawful justification.
Total means there is no reasonable way out. A person who could simply walk away by another route is not imprisoned.
A reasonable escape route is not the same as any escape route. A window three floors up is not a way out.
The victim need not know at the time. Ravi would have a claim even if he had slept through the whole thing.

body.q: A mall guard tells Cik Farah she may not leave until a manager arrives. She stays. She could have walked out of an open door behind her. Is that false imprisonment?
options: No — the restraint was not total, because a reasonable way out was open
Yes — she was told she could not leave
Yes — a guard has no authority to detain anyone
body.why: Being told to stay is not the same as being prevented from leaving. Totality is the element doing the work. The third answer states a rule that is too wide, because lawful justification for detention does sometimes exist.

sections.keypoint: Consent and lawful authority answer most claims, and the award often marks the wrong rather than a loss.
sections.h: Defences, and what a claim is for

body.text: Most defendants do not deny the contact. They justify it.

body.caption: The four justifications that come up most often
rows: Consent
The claimant agreed to the contact — a patient to an operation, a player to a tackle.
Lawful authority
A power to detain or to use force, given by statute or by the common law.
Self-defence
Force used to protect themselves or another, in proportion to the threat.
Necessity
Action taken to prevent a greater harm, where there was no real alternative.
body.alt: Four defences in a table. Consent: the claimant agreed to the contact. Lawful authority: a power to detain or use force, given by statute or common law. Self-defence: proportionate force against a threat. Necessity: action to prevent a greater harm.

body.text: Powers of arrest and detention come from statute, and the officer must stay inside them. Detention that outlives its authority becomes false imprisonment.
Because these torts are actionable per se, a claimant with no measurable loss still recovers. The award marks the wrong rather than replacing money.
Where an official has abused a power, the manner of the wrong can be taken into account. Ask what your client wants, which is often an admission.

lessons.title: Trespass to land, and to goods
lessons.summary: Two torts protect what you possess rather than what you own. Both are complete on entry or interference, with no need to show that anything was harmed.

sections.keypoint: The claimant sues because they possessed the land, not because their name sits on the title.

body.text: Puan Maswati comes home to Rawang and finds an excavator parked on her land. The contractor says he has the wrong lot number.
She rents the house. Her landlord owns it. She can still sue, and the contractor's mistake makes no difference.

Trespass to land is committed by a direct and unjustified interference with land in the possession of another. It is actionable per se. What must be intentional is the act of entry; an intention to trespass is not required.
body.source: General principle of the law of tort, received in Malaysia under the Civil Law Act 1956, s 3.

body.text: Two points in that rule cause most of the trouble. The first is possession, and the second is the mistake.
Possession, not ownership, is the interest protected. A tenant can sue. An owner who has parted with possession usually cannot.
And an honest mistake is no defence. Believing the land was yours does not stop the entry being a trespass.

body.q: The contractor genuinely believed lot 41 was his employer's site. Does that defeat Maswati's claim?
options: No — he intended to enter that land, and that is the intention required
Yes — he had no intention to trespass
Yes — the mistake was a reasonable one
body.why: The tort asks whether the entry was deliberate, not whether the defendant knew he had no right to be there. A mistake may reduce what the court awards. It does not answer the claim.

sections.keypoint: Land is a volume, and permission that has run out turns a lawful visitor into a trespasser.

body.text: Land is not only the surface. It reaches upward and downward, within limits the law keeps sensible.

items: An overhanging signboard or crane jib can trespass into the airspace above.
Digging or piling under a neighbour's lot can trespass below the surface.
Leaving rubbish or a vehicle on the land is a trespass by placing a thing there.
Staying after permission ends is a trespass, even though the entry was lawful.

body.text: Aircraft at ordinary heights are a different matter. The law does not treat everyday overflight as a trespass.
Boundaries and title in Malaysia are governed by the National Land Code, not by this tort. Check the register before arguing about where a line runs.

sections.keypoint: Three separate wrongs cover goods, and choosing the wrong one changes what the court can order.

body.text: Goods are protected too, and by more than one tort. The differences matter, because the remedies differ.

body.caption: Three wrongs against goods, and what each one is for
rows: Trespass to goods
Directly interfered with goods in the claimant's possession.
Damages for the interference itself.
Conversion
Dealt with the goods in a way that denied the claimant's rights.
The value of the goods, as though they had been sold.
Detinue
Refused to return the goods after a proper demand.
The goods back, or their value.
body.alt: Three wrongs against goods. Trespass to goods is a direct interference, and the claim is for the interference itself. Conversion is dealing with goods in a way that denies the owner's rights, and the claim is for their value. Detinue is a refusal to return goods after a demand, and the claim is for the goods or their value.

body.text: A workshop in Cheras keeps Encik Zul's motorcycle after he refuses to pay a disputed bill. Zul demands it back and is refused. That refusal after demand is the classic detinue.
Conversion is the serious one. Selling someone's goods, or destroying them, denies the owner's rights completely.

body.prompt: A courier delivers Zul's parcel to the wrong address, and it is never seen again. Which wrong is that closest to?
options: Trespass to goods, because the parcel was handled
Conversion, because delivering goods to the wrong person denies the owner's rights
Nothing — the courier was merely careless
body.reveal: Handing goods to a person with no right to them is a classic act of conversion. The third answer is the tempting one, because carelessness is obviously present. But conversion does not ask whether the defendant meant harm. It asks whether the dealing was inconsistent with the owner's rights.

body.text: Detinue has been abolished in some jurisdictions and survives in others. Check the Malaysian position before pleading it as a separate cause of action.

sections.keypoint: Damages, an injunction, an order for possession, and a narrow right to act for yourself.
sections.h: Getting them off, and getting it back

body.text: Ask what the client needs. It is rarely only money.

items: **Damages** for the interference, even where nothing was harmed.
**An injunction** to stop a continuing trespass, granted at the court's discretion.
**An order for possession**, where someone has occupied land and will not leave.
**Self-help**, which the law allows narrowly and plainly distrusts.

body.text: Self-help means acting without a court. You may remove a trespasser, using no more force than is reasonable.
Self-help goes wrong easily. Excessive force turns the occupier into the defendant, facing a claim in trespass to the person.
Injunctions in Malaysia are governed by the Specific Relief Act 1950. That is statute, and a general account of equitable remedies does not replace it.

lessons.source: Trespass to land, trespass to goods, conversion and detinue are received English doctrine applying in Malaysia under the Civil Law Act 1956, s 3. No case is cited and none is relied on.
