lessons.title: Money lost when nobody was hurt
lessons.summary: Negligence pays readily for broken bodies and broken things. It is far more reluctant to pay for money lost on its own, and the reasons for that reluctance are the whole topic.

sections.keypoint: Money lost alongside injury or property damage is recoverable; money lost with neither is its own category.

body.text: Encik Hafiz buys a shophouse in Ipoh. He relies on a surveyor's report saying the structure is sound. It is not, and the building is worth RM180,000 less than he paid.
Nobody was injured. Nothing of Hafiz's was damaged. He has simply paid too much.
That is **pure economic loss**, which is financial loss suffered without injury to the person or damage to property. The law treats it as its own category.
Compare the loss that follows physical damage. A lorry damages a factory's machine, and the factory loses a week of production.
That lost production is **consequential economic loss**. It rides on physical damage, and negligence pays for it in the ordinary way.

A defendant who negligently causes physical injury or damage to property is liable for the financial loss consequent upon it. Financial loss suffered without any such injury or damage is treated as a distinct category, in which a duty of care is not readily imposed.
body.source: General principle of the law of negligence, received in Malaysia under the Civil Law Act 1956, s 3.

body.text: So the first move is always to classify the loss. Getting that wrong sends the whole answer down the wrong road.
The snail case, *Donoghue v Stevenson* [1932] AC 562, was about physical harm from a defective product. It decides nothing about money lost on its own.

sections.keypoint: Indeterminate liability, and the fact that money losses usually already have a home in contract.

body.text: The reluctance is not squeamishness. There are three reasons, and an answer that names them argues rather than asserts.

items: **Indeterminate liability.** One careless act can cost a very large number of people money, in amounts nobody can predict.
**Contract is the usual home.** Parties who deal with each other can allocate financial risk in their agreement.
**Ripple effects.** Physical damage stops somewhere. Financial loss spreads outward through everyone who dealt with the victim.

body.text: A contractor cuts a power cable in Shah Alam. Forty factories lose a day of output. None of them owns the cable, and none of their property is damaged.
Letting all forty recover would make one careless spade very expensive. That is the floodgates worry, stated concretely.
In Malaysia the Contracts Act 1950 governs the agreement route. Ask first whether your client has a contract, because it is usually the better claim.

sections.keypoint: A negligent statement can found a claim where the maker took responsibility and the reliance was reasonable.

body.text: There is one well-established route through. It is the negligent statement.
Hafiz's surveyor damaged nothing. He said something careless, and Hafiz relied on it.
The law allows recovery here where the relationship between the parties is a special one. Four things are usually asked.

items: Did the maker have, or claim to have, special skill or knowledge?
Did the maker know the statement would be passed to this claimant?
Did the maker know it would be relied on for this kind of decision?
Was the claimant's reliance reasonable in the circumstances?

body.text: Notice the third question. Purpose does a great deal of work in this area.
Where accounts are prepared for one statutory purpose, the maker does not thereby assume responsibility to a stranger who relies on them for a different purpose, such as deciding whether to invest.
body.source: Caparo Industries plc v Dickman [1990] 2 AC 605 (HL)

body.text: Put simply: a statement made for one job is not a promise to everybody who later reads it. Ask what the statement was for.

body.prompt: Hafiz's surveyor was engaged by the seller, not by Hafiz. Does that end Hafiz's claim?
options: Yes — only the person who paid for the report can complain about it
Yes — the claim belongs to the seller alone
Not necessarily — the question is whether the surveyor knew a buyer would rely on it
body.reveal: The absence of a contract is where this topic starts, not where it ends. The point of the negligent statement route is that it reaches a person who never engaged the maker. What matters is whether the surveyor knew a buyer would rely, and for what.

body.text: A disclaimer in the report changes the analysis. It bears directly on whether responsibility was assumed at all.

sections.keypoint: Cite a Malaysian decision, because recovery for pure economic loss here has not simply followed England.

body.text: This is not an area to answer out of an English textbook.
*Caparo Industries plc v Dickman* [1990] 2 AC 605 (HL) supplies the three-stage duty test used in novel situations. Malaysian courts have worked with it.
*Lok Kok Beng v Loh Chiak Eong* [2015] 4 MLJ 734 (FC) is the Federal Court decision to read on the duty owed by a professional. Read it in full rather than in summary.
Read the Malaysian cases for what they decided, and note their dates. The position has moved, and an old summary may describe a stage that has been superseded.

body.q: A client lost money relying on advice and has no contract with the adviser. What should your answer establish first?
options: That the adviser was careless
That the loss is pure economic loss, and so which route to a duty is in play
That the adviser was insured
body.why: Classifying the loss decides everything that follows. Carelessness matters only once you know a duty could exist, and the second answer is what tells you where to look for one.

lessons.source: Caparo Industries plc v Dickman [1990] 2 AC 605 (HL); Lok Kok Beng v Loh Chiak Eong [2015] 4 MLJ 734 (FC); Donoghue v Stevenson [1932] AC 562. The category of pure economic loss is received doctrine applying in Malaysia under the Civil Law Act 1956, s 3.

lessons.title: When more than one person is to blame
lessons.summary: Two careless people can produce one injury that cannot be divided, and the victim should not have to work out who did what. The law makes each of them answerable for the whole, then lets them argue among themselves.

sections.keypoint: Separate careless acts producing a single indivisible injury make each defendant answerable for all of it.

body.text: Cik Norlia is waiting at a junction in Seremban. A lorry runs the light and clips a van. The van mounts the kerb and breaks her hip.
Both drivers were careless. Her hip was not broken twice. There is one injury, and nobody can divide it.
Lawyers call defendants like these **concurrent tortfeasors**. Their wrongs are separate, but the damage they caused together is one thing.
That differs from **joint tortfeasors**, who are responsible for the same wrongful act. An employer held vicariously liable is the standard example.
Where the wrongs of two or more persons combine to cause one indivisible item of damage, each of them is liable to the claimant for the whole of that damage.
body.source: General principle of the law of tort, received in Malaysia under the Civil Law Act 1956, s 3.

body.text: Read that rule again, because it is counter-intuitive. Each defendant answers for the whole, and not for a share.
Do not confuse this with vicarious liability. There, one person answers for another's wrong. Here, each answers for their own.

sections.keypoint: She may sue either driver for the full sum, and she can be paid only once.

body.text: The practical consequences are large, and they are the reason the rule exists.
Norlia may sue both drivers. She may also sue only one, and recover the whole of her damages from that one.
She does not have to prove what proportion each driver contributed. That question is the defendants' problem, not hers.

body.prompt: The lorry driver has no insurance and no money. The van driver is fully insured. Who carries the risk of the lorry driver being worthless?
options: Norlia — she can recover only half from the van driver
It is shared out between all three of them
The van driver — Norlia can recover the whole sum from him
body.reveal: This is the point of the rule. An injured person should not go undercompensated because one wrongdoer turned out to have nothing. The van driver pays the whole sum, then tries to recover a share from the lorry driver. If that recovery fails, the loss stays with a wrongdoer rather than the victim.

body.text: One limit matters. Norlia is entitled to one satisfaction of her claim, and no more than one.
So she cannot collect the full award twice by suing each driver in turn. A judgment against one does not double her money.
Settling with one defendant can affect the claim against the other. Read the terms of any release with care before signing it.

sections.keypoint: A defendant who pays more than their share can claim contribution from the others, and that is statutory here.

body.text: The van driver has now paid for damage the lorry driver helped to cause. He is not left carrying it.
A defendant in that position may claim **contribution**, which is a payment from another wrongdoer towards what has been paid out.
The court fixes the amount at what is just and equitable, having regard to each wrongdoer's responsibility for the damage.
In Malaysia this is statutory rather than a matter of common law. It sits in the Civil Law Act 1956. Look the provision up rather than taking a number from a summary.
Procedure matters too. A defendant who wants contribution normally brings the other wrongdoer in as a third party.

body.q: The van driver has paid Norlia in full. What does he do next?
options: Claim contribution from the lorry driver, in a proportion the court thinks just and equitable
Nothing — he paid, and that is the end of it
Sue Norlia for the amount above his own share
body.why: Contribution is the mechanism that makes several liability fair to defendants. The third answer inverts the whole scheme, because the claimant is entitled to keep what she recovered.

sections.keypoint: Divisible damage is split at the start, and the claimant's own share is a different question again.

body.text: Not every case involves one indivisible injury. Sometimes the damage really does come apart.
Where each defendant caused a distinct part, each is liable for that part and no more. The claimant must then prove who caused what.
Two factories in Pasir Gudang discharge waste into the same river on different days. If the harm from each discharge can be identified, each pays for its own.
Do not mix this up with contributory negligence. Apportionment between defendants and apportionment against the claimant are separate exercises.

Where any person suffers damage as the result partly of his own fault and partly of the fault of any other person, a claim shall not be defeated by reason of the fault of the person suffering the damage, but the damages recoverable shall be reduced to such extent as the court thinks just and equitable having regard to the claimant's share in the responsibility for the damage.
That section is about Norlia's own carelessness. It is not the provision that shares liability out between the two drivers.

lessons.source: Joint and several liability for indivisible damage is received doctrine applying in Malaysia under the Civil Law Act 1956, s 3. Apportionment for the claimant's own fault is under the Civil Law Act 1956, s 12(1). No case is cited and none is relied on.

lessons.title: Getting the papers into the defendant's hands
lessons.summary: Filing a claim opens a file, but it does not bind anybody. Service is the step that does, and this lesson covers how it is done, how it is proved, and what to do when the defendant cannot be found.

sections.keypoint: Filing opens a file. Service is the step that binds a defendant to it.

body.text: Puan Mariam Zakaria supplies steel in Ipoh. Encik Danial owes her RM42,000 for three deliveries. She files a writ, pays the fee, and goes home satisfied.
Nothing has happened to Danial yet. The court has a file. He does not know it exists, and he is not bound by anything in it.
Service is the step that changes that. It is how the papers reach the defendant, in a way the court will accept as proof.

Originating process must be served on every defendant in a manner the Rules of Court 2012 permit, and service must be proved to the court before the court will act on a defendant's failure to respond.
Put simply: filing opens a file, and service starts the defendant's clock. Until then the case is a document sitting in a registry.

body.prompt: Mariam's writ is filed and sealed. It is still in her lawyer's drawer a month later. What can she do about Danial's silence?
options: Nothing yet. His time to answer has not started, because he has not been served
Ask for judgment in default, since he has not answered
Ask the court to serve it for her, since filing is complete
body.reveal: Nothing yet. The clock a defendant misses is the one that starts on service, not on filing. A default judgment against an unserved defendant is worth very little. He can come back and have it set aside, and the costs of that will usually be hers.

sections.keypoint: An individual, a company and a defendant with solicitors on the record are each reached differently.
sections.h: Who you are serving changes the route

body.text: The Rules set out the permitted modes of service. Which one fits depends on what kind of defendant you have.
Personal service means handing the document to the defendant himself. It is the safest route, and for some documents it is the required one.

body.caption: Who the defendant is, and what that changes
rows: An individual
Personal service, or another mode the Rules allow
He must actually receive it. A document left at an old address proves nothing.
A company
Service at its registered office
The registered office is often an accountant's address rather than where the company trades.
A defendant with solicitors
Service on the solicitors, where they have agreed to accept it
The agreement should be in writing. An oral assurance is not proof.
A defendant outside Malaysia
Service abroad, with the court's leave
Leave is granted only in the categories the Rules set out, and the exercise is slow.
body.alt: Four kinds of defendant and how each is reached. An individual is served personally or by another permitted mode, and must actually receive it. A company is served at its registered office, which is often an accountant's address rather than where it trades. A defendant with solicitors may be served on them where they have agreed in writing to accept service. A defendant outside Malaysia is served abroad with the court's leave, granted only in the categories the Rules set out.

body.text: Do not assume the address on a letterhead is good for service. Check the register for a company, and check the Rules for the mode, before you send anything.

sections.keypoint: Substituted service needs an order first, granted on evidence of the attempts that failed.

body.text: Mariam's process server attends Danial's house three times. The gate is locked each time. A neighbour says he moved to Penang months ago.
This is common, and the Rules have an answer for it. It is called substituted service.
Substituted service is service by some other means, ordered by the court, where the ordinary means cannot practicably be used.

Where personal service cannot practicably be effected, the court may order that service be effected by such other means as it thinks fit, on evidence of the attempts already made and of the likelihood that the substituted means will bring the document to the defendant's notice.
Two things are being asked for. First, proof that you genuinely tried. Second, a method that is actually likely to reach him.

The affidavit sets out three attendances, with dates, times and what the process server saw. The order sought is for the papers to be pasted on the gate and advertised once in a newspaper he is likely to read.
You need the order before you serve, not after. Pasting a writ on a gate without an order is not service, and everything built on it can fall.

body.q: A process server calls once, at 11am on a working day, finds nobody in, and applies for substituted service. What is the likely response?
options: The order will be granted, because one attempt shows service is impracticable
The court will want better evidence that personal service cannot practicably be effected
The application will be refused, because substituted service is only for defendants abroad
body.why: One visit in office hours shows very little. The court is being asked to accept something less than personal service, so it wants evidence of real attempts. Substituted service is not limited to defendants abroad. It is for defendants who cannot practicably be served in the ordinary way.

sections.keypoint: A defendant never properly served can return months later and have the judgment set aside.
sections.h: Service that fails, and what follows

body.text: Bad service is not a technicality. It is one of the grounds on which finished judgments are undone.

items: Keep the affidavit of service. It is the proof, and without it the court has only your word.
An irregularity in service can often be cured or waived. A fundamental defect may make the judgment a nullity instead.
A defendant who wants a judgment set aside must usually move promptly, and delay counts against him.
A defendant who takes a step in the action knowing of the defect may be treated as having accepted service.

body.text: So the question at the start is not only whether you can win. It is whether you can prove the defendant knew he was being sued.
Service abroad is a separate exercise and needs the court's leave. Treaty arrangements and the law of the receiving country both matter, and it is slow. Build the delay into your timetable.

lessons.title: Discovery, privilege, and the document you wish you had not written
lessons.summary: Each side must disclose the relevant documents it holds, including the ones that damage its own case. This lesson covers what relevance means, what privilege really protects, and what to do when the other side holds back.

sections.keypoint: You disclose a relevant document because it is relevant, not because it helps you.
sections.h: The site diary that ruins your own case

body.text: Encik Kumaran runs a contracting firm in Shah Alam. He is suing a developer for RM380,000 in unpaid progress claims.
His own site diary records two weeks when his crew never turned up. He asks whether he has to show it to the other side.
He does. This is the rule that surprises non-lawyers more than any other in civil procedure.

Each party must disclose the documents in its possession, custody or power which are relevant to the matters in question in the action, whether those documents support that party's case or damage it. Disclosure is made by list, and the other party may then inspect the listed documents which are not privileged.
Put simply: you list what you hold, including what hurts. The other side may then ask to look at it.

body.prompt: Kumaran's lawyer suggests leaving the site diary off the list, since the developer does not know it exists. What is wrong with that?
options: Nothing, so long as the diary is never referred to at trial
It breaks a duty owed to the court, and the consequences land on Kumaran as well as on his lawyer
Nothing, because a party never has to produce a document against itself
body.reveal: The first. Disclosure is a duty owed to the court, not a tactic. A claim can be struck out for a deliberate failure, and a document that surfaces later does far more damage than one disclosed at the start. The instinct behind the other two answers is natural. It is exactly what this rule overrides.

sections.keypoint: Narrow pleadings narrow discovery, which is why drafting and disclosure are really one skill.
sections.h: Relevance is fixed by the pleadings

body.text: Relevant to what? To the matters in question in the action. And those are set by the pleadings.

A pleading states the material facts relied on, not the evidence for them and not the law. Because the pleadings define the issues in the action, they also fix the boundary of what is relevant, and therefore of what must be disclosed.
So a claim pleaded wide invites wide discovery. A claim pleaded tightly keeps the exercise proportionate.
A document is not only paper. Emails, spreadsheets, messages and drafts are documents too, and so is the version you deleted but still hold in a backup.
Possession, custody or power is wider than possession. A file held by your accountant, or sitting on a server your company controls, may still be yours to produce.

sections.keypoint: Privilege is narrow, it belongs to the client, and confidentiality is not the same thing.

body.text: Some documents are listed and then withheld from inspection. That is privilege, and it is narrower than most people expect.

items: Legal advice privilege covers communications between a client and a lawyer for the purpose of giving or getting legal advice.
Litigation privilege covers documents created for the dominant purpose of litigation that is pending or reasonably anticipated.
Without prejudice communications are genuine settlement negotiations, and they are generally kept out on the question of who is right.

body.caption: Three documents people wrongly assume are protected
rows: Your solicitor's written advice on the claim
Yes
It is a communication made for the purpose of legal advice.
The site diary, sent to your solicitor after the dispute began
No
It existed already. Sending a document to a lawyer does not clothe it in privilege.
An internal email stamped strictly confidential
No
Confidentiality is not privilege, and a stamp does not create one.
body.alt: Three documents and whether privilege protects them. A solicitor's written advice on the claim is protected, because it is a communication made for the purpose of legal advice. A site diary that already existed and was later sent to the solicitor is not protected, because sending a document to a lawyer does not make it privileged. An internal email stamped strictly confidential is not protected either, because confidentiality is not privilege.

body.text: Privilege belongs to the client rather than the lawyer, and a client can lose it. Quoting the advice in order to justify your own conduct may waive it for the whole document.

body.q: A developer's insurer commissions an expert report after a wall collapses, at a point when a claim is clearly coming. Is the report likely to be protected?
options: No, because expert reports are always disclosable
Probably, if the dominant purpose of creating it was the anticipated litigation
No, because it was commissioned by an insurer rather than by a lawyer
body.why: Litigation privilege turns on the dominant purpose for which the document was created, not on who paid for it. A report made mainly to work out how to rebuild the wall would not be protected. Whether an expert report is later served for use at trial is a separate question from whether it must be disclosed now.

sections.keypoint: Name the document or the class you say is missing; a request that reads like a fishing trip is refused.
sections.h: When the other side holds back

body.text: Sometimes a list is obviously incomplete. There are ways to press, and they escalate.

items: Apply for specific discovery, identifying the document or the class of documents you say has been left out.
Serve interrogatories, which are written questions the other side must answer on oath.
Ask the court to compel a person who is not a party to produce documents that person holds.
Ask for sanctions where an order is ignored, which can extend to striking out the claim or the defence.

body.text: You must say what you are after and why you believe it exists. An application that asks to see everything and hopes something turns up will be refused as a fishing expedition.
Keep the duty in mind after the list has been served. A relevant document that comes to light later still has to be disclosed.

lessons.title: Who pays for the fight
lessons.summary: Costs usually follow the event, but a winner rarely recovers what the fight actually cost. This lesson covers the two separate bills, what moves the figure, and how the risk of costs shapes what parties really do.

sections.keypoint: What the loser pays is a contribution assessed by the court, not a refund of the winner's bill.
sections.h: Winning, and still being out of pocket

body.text: Puan Hasnah sues a renovation company over RM25,000 of defective work. After fourteen months, she wins.
Her own solicitor's bill is RM19,000. The court orders the defendant to pay her costs of RM10,000. She has won, and she is out of pocket.
This is normal rather than a mistake. Understanding why is the difference between advising a client and misleading one.

Costs are in the discretion of the court. The usual order is that costs follow the event, so that the unsuccessful party pays the successful party's costs; but the court may make a different order where the conduct of the parties, or the outcome on the individual issues, justifies it.

body.prompt: Hasnah asks why the defendant is not simply ordered to pay her RM19,000 bill. What is the answer?
options: The costs a loser pays are a contribution assessed by the court, not the winner's actual bill
The court has no power to order costs above the amount claimed
She should have agreed a fixed figure with her solicitor before starting
body.reveal: The second. There are two separate bills, and only one of them is the court's business. What her solicitor may charge her comes from her retainer with him. What the defendant must pay her is assessed by the court, and it is almost always the smaller number.

sections.keypoint: One bill comes from your retainer with your own solicitor; the other is assessed by the court.

body.caption: The two bills a winning party has to deal with
rows: Solicitor and client
Your retainer with your own solicitor, subject to the court's supervision
Everything your solicitor did on your instructions
Party and party
The court, either by fixing a sum or on taxation
A contribution towards costs properly incurred in the action
body.alt: Two bills. The solicitor and client bill is fixed by your retainer with your own solicitor, subject to the court's supervision. It covers everything the solicitor did on your instructions. The party and party bill is fixed by the court, either as a stated sum or on taxation. It covers only a contribution towards costs properly incurred in the action.

body.text: Taxation is the process of assessing a bill item by item. It has costs and delay of its own, which is why parties often ask the court to fix a sum instead.
The gap between the two bills is real, and it never closes entirely. Give the client that number before the case starts, not after it ends.

sections.keypoint: Conduct, the issues actually won, and offers to settle all pull the award away from the simple rule.

body.text: Costs follow the event is a starting point rather than a formula. Several things move it.

items: Conduct. A hopeless point run to the last day, or correspondence left unanswered, can cost a winner part of the award.
Issues. A party who wins overall but loses a substantial issue may not recover the costs of that issue.
Offers. A claimant who turns down an offer and then does no better may bear the costs incurred after it was made.
Interlocutory applications. Each one carries its own costs order, and those accumulate long before any trial.
Costs thrown away, where a hearing is wasted because one side turned up unready.

body.text: A costs order is a real order. It is enforceable in the same ways as any other money judgment.

body.q: A plaintiff wins RM8,000 on one of five pleaded claims, and loses the other four after a long trial spent mostly on them. What costs order is likely?
options: Something less than full costs, because he lost the issues the trial was actually spent on
Full costs, because costs follow the event and he is the successful party
No order as to costs, since each side won something
body.why: He is the successful party, so the starting point favours him. But the court looks at what the trial was actually spent on, and four of the five claims failed. Expect an award reduced by reference to the issues, or even a separate order against him on the claims he lost.

sections.keypoint: Most cases settle because of what losing would cost, not because anyone changed their mind on the merits.

body.text: Costs are the strongest pressure in civil litigation, and they work long before any judgment is delivered.

items: A defendant weighs the claim, plus the claimant's costs, plus its own. That total is often several times the sum in dispute.
A claimant of modest means faces a bill it cannot pay if it loses, which deters good claims as well as bad ones.
A defendant may apply for security for costs where there is reason to doubt that a plaintiff could pay an award against it.

body.text: Security for costs is not available against every plaintiff who looks poor. The grounds are set out in the Rules and they are limited, so read them before you threaten an application.
An advice on the merits that says nothing about costs exposure is half an advice. Give the client both numbers.

lessons.title: Who is on the record, and why it matters
lessons.summary: A good claim can be lost at the start by naming the wrong person as defendant. This lesson covers who can sue and be sued, how parties are joined or changed, and what happens when the mistake is found after time has run.

sections.keypoint: Only a person the law recognises can sue or be sued, and a trading name is often not one.

body.text: Encik Azman is hurt when scaffolding gives way at a site in Klang. The signboard on the hoarding says Sri Maju Construction.
He sues that name. It turns out to be a business name registered to one man, and the site was actually run by a company nobody had mentioned.
Naming the defendant is not clerical work. Get it wrong and there is nobody on the other side of the case.

A civil action must be brought by and against a person the law recognises: a natural person, a body corporate, or an entity which a statute or the Rules of Court 2012 permit to sue or be sued in a particular name.

items: A sole proprietorship is not a person. The defendant is the owner, and the trading name may be added to identify the business.
A partnership may generally be sued in the firm's name, but the partners remain personally liable on the judgment.
A company is a separate person, and a director is not a defendant merely for being a director.
A dead person cannot be sued. The claim lies against the estate, through the personal representatives.
A club or society that was never incorporated has no legal personality, so the right defendants are usually its officers.

body.prompt: Azman's lawyer then finds that the company which ran the site was struck off the register last year. What follows?
options: The claim can proceed, because a struck-off company is still a defendant
The claim must be brought against its directors personally instead
There is no company to sue until it is restored to the register, and restoration is a separate application
body.reveal: The third. A company that is off the register is not there to be sued, and a writ naming it is a writ against nobody. Restoring it takes its own application and its own time. That is why the identity of a corporate defendant is checked at the start, rather than after the limitation clock has run.

sections.keypoint: A common question and a common transaction are what let several parties share one action.
sections.h: Joinder: more than one on a side

body.text: Joinder means bringing more than one claimant, or more than one defendant, into the same action.
The test looks for a link. There must be a common question of law or fact, and rights arising out of the same transaction or series of transactions.
Azman and two other workers hurt in the same collapse can sue together. A worker injured at a different site the year before cannot join them.
The court may also add, substitute or strike out a party at any stage of the action, on application or of its own motion.
Joining every name on the site does not spread the risk. Defendants who should never have been sued get their costs, and it is your client who pays them.

sections.keypoint: An amendment that takes an accrued time bar away from a new defendant is the hardest one to obtain.
sections.h: Finding the right defendant too late

body.text: Azman learns the real employer's name only after the limitation period for his claim has run out.
He asks to amend the writ and substitute the correct company. This is where two topics collide.
Courts distinguish correcting a name from changing the defendant. The first is usually allowed. The second may not be.

body.caption: Three ways the wrong name goes wrong
rows: The right entity, misspelt or given its trading name
Yes
That defendant knew the claim was aimed at it, so nothing is taken away.
The wrong entity altogether, found while time still runs
Yes, by adding or substituting
Expect to pay the costs of the party you wrongly named.
The wrong entity altogether, found after time has run
Often not
Substitution would strip the new defendant of a limitation defence it has already acquired.
body.alt: Three situations. The right entity named with a misspelling, or by its trading name, is usually fixable, because that defendant knew the claim was aimed at it. The wrong entity found while time still runs is fixable by adding or substituting, though you will usually pay the wrongly named party's costs. The wrong entity found after time has run is often not fixable, because substitution would strip the new defendant of a limitation defence it has already acquired.

body.text: Limitation is a defence a defendant must plead, and a defendant added late will plead it. Check the identity of every defendant well before the clock gets close.

body.q: A writ names Sri Maju Construction Sdn Bhd. The correct name is Sri Maju Constructions Sdn Bhd, the same company, and the slip is spotted a month after time expired. What is the best argument?
options: That limitation has no application to amendments at all
That the company waived the point by not correcting the writ itself
That this is a misnomer, because the intended defendant was always identifiable and knew the claim was aimed at it
body.why: A misnomer corrects the label on a defendant who was always the intended target and knew it. Nothing is being taken away, because that company was the party sued from the beginning. The other two answers ask the court to ignore a limitation defence, rather than to show that none ever arose.

sections.keypoint: One claim can stand for many with the same interest, and a defendant can pull in whoever should indemnify him.
sections.h: Representative actions, and bringing in a third party

body.text: Two devices deal with numbers, one on each side of the record.
A representative action lets one or more people sue, or be sued, on behalf of others who share the same interest in the claim.
Same interest is a real requirement rather than a formality. Malaysia has no general class action procedure, and claims where the loss differs from person to person usually cannot be run this way.
Third party proceedings work in the other direction. A defendant who says somebody else must indemnify him brings that person into the same action.
The developer sued by Azman brings in the scaffolding subcontractor. Liability and indemnity are then decided once, instead of in two separate trials on the same facts.
Both devices save the cost of running the same facts twice. Both have their own steps in the Rules, so build the time into the timetable.
